questions.stem: Compared with ordinary Portland cement, Portland pozzolana cement (PPC) has:
options: Higher heat of hydration and faster early strength gain
Higher heat of hydration and slower early strength gain
Lower heat of hydration and slower early strength gain
Lower heat of hydration and faster early strength gain
questions.solution:
**Lower heat of hydration and slower early strength gain.**

PPC is made by blending OPC clinker with a **pozzolana** — fly ash, calcined clay or silica fume — typically 15 to 35% by mass. The pozzolana is not itself cementitious; it reacts with the **calcium hydroxide** released by cement hydration:

> Pozzolana + Ca(OH)₂ + water → additional C–S–H gel

That secondary reaction is **slower** than the primary hydration of the clinker, which explains both properties at once:

| Property | PPC vs OPC | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Heat of hydration** | **Lower** | Suits **mass concrete** — dams, rafts, thick sections — where thermal cracking is the risk |
| **Early strength** | **Slower** | Formwork stays longer; needs **longer curing** |
| **Long-term strength** | **Equal or higher** | Catches up and overtakes OPC after 28–90 days |
| **Permeability** | **Lower** | The extra C–S–H fills capillary pores |
| Sulphate and chloride resistance | **Better** | Less free Ca(OH)₂ to be attacked |
| Workability | Better | Fly ash particles are spherical |

So the trade is **early strength for durability and lower heat** — which is why PPC is preferred for mass concrete and aggressive exposure, and OPC where early strength or fast formwork reuse matters.

The practical requirement that follows: PPC needs **curing for at least 10 to 14 days**, against 7 for OPC, precisely because the pozzolanic reaction is still proceeding. Cutting the curing short forfeits the durability that was the reason for choosing it.

examTip.trick: Blended cements (PPC, PSC) replace part of the clinker with **pozzolana or slag**, which reacts **slowly with the Ca(OH)₂** released by cement hydration — so heat and early strength both fall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slower early, EQUAL OR BETTER ultimate strength, less heat, better durability.** The lower heat is why blended cements suit **mass concrete**; the slower gain is why they need **longer curing (10–14 days against 7)**. Not a weaker cement — a differently paced one.

questions.stem: The purpose of adding gypsum during the grinding of cement clinker is to:
options: Improve the colour of the cement
questions.solution:
**To retard the setting time.**

Gypsum (calcium sulphate, CaSO₄·2H₂O) is ground with the clinker at **3 to 5%** by mass. Without it the cement would be unusable, because of one compound in particular:

> **C₃A (tricalcium aluminate)** hydrates almost instantly, causing a **flash set** — the paste stiffens within minutes, long before it could be placed and compacted.

Gypsum reacts preferentially with C₃A to form **ettringite**, a coating that seals the C₃A grains and delays their hydration. That buys the working time the initial setting time requires:

> **Initial setting time ≥ 30 minutes** — enough to mix, transport, place and compact
> **Final setting time ≤ 600 minutes (10 hours)** — so work can proceed

**The dose matters in both directions.** Too little gypsum and the flash set returns; **too much** leaves unreacted sulphate in the hardened paste, which later forms expansive ettringite and causes **unsoundness** — delayed expansion and cracking after setting. That is why IS 269 caps the SO₃ content, and why the **Le Chatelier soundness test** (limit 10 mm expansion) exists.

Why the other options are wrong: strength (c) comes from the calcium silicates C₃S and C₂S, not from gypsum; colour (d) comes chiefly from **iron oxide**; and (b) is the opposite of what gypsum does — accelerating the set is the job of an **admixture** such as calcium chloride.

Do not confuse **setting** (loss of plasticity, hours) with **hardening** (gain of strength, months) — gypsum affects only the first.

examTip.trap: "Accelerate the setting" is the natural but exactly backwards reading — an additive sounds like an accelerator.
examTip.trick: Ask what problem it solves. Without gypsum, **C₃A causes a FLASH SET** within minutes and the cement could never be placed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gypsum guards against the flash set.** Roughly 3–5% is added at the grinding stage. Too little and the cement flash sets; too much and it causes **unsoundness** through delayed expansion — which is exactly what the Le Chatelier test checks.

questions.stem: The characteristic compressive strength of concrete is defined as the strength below which not more than:
options: 1% of test results are expected to fall
2% of test results are expected to fall
10% of test results are expected to fall
5% of test results are expected to fall
questions.solution:
**5% of test results are expected to fall.**

Concrete strength is inherently variable — the same mix, batched and cured identically, gives a scatter of cube results. So a single "strength" is meaningless; the code defines a value with a stated **probability of being exceeded**:

> **f_ck** = the strength below which not more than **5%** of results fall — the **5th percentile**

Assuming a normal distribution, that fixes the target the mix must actually be designed for:

> **Target mean strength f_m = f_ck + 1.65 σ**

where σ is the standard deviation and **1.65** is the standard normal deviate for 5%.

The assumed standard deviations in IS 10262:

| Grade | σ (N/mm²) |
|---|---|
| M10 – M15 | 3.5 |
| **M20 – M25** | **4.0** |
| M30 – M50 | 5.0 |

So an **M25** mix must be designed for a mean of 25 + 1.65 × 4.0 = **31.6 N/mm²** — appreciably above its nominal grade. Designing for 25 would mean roughly **half** the results falling below the specified strength.

**The testing regime** that goes with it: 150 mm cubes, cured in water at 27 ± 2°C, tested at **28 days**, in sets of three whose individual results must not differ from their mean by more than ±15%.

The same 5% convention defines the characteristic strength of **steel**: Fe 500 means f_y = 500 N/mm² at the 5th percentile. And note the separate step from characteristic to **design** strength, using the partial safety factors — **0.446 f_ck** for concrete and **0.87 f_y** for steel.

examTip.trap: "5% expected to EXCEED" is the reversed distractor and is easy to pick under pressure. Characteristic strength is the **lower** 5% fractile — results fall **below** it.
examTip.trick: **f_ck = f_mean − 1.65σ**, where 1.65 is the standard normal value for 5%.
examTip.mnemonic: **M25 means 95% of results BEAT 25 N/mm² — it is not an average.** So the **target mean strength** for mix design is always higher than the grade: f_target = f_ck + 1.65σ, with σ from 4 to 5 N/mm² depending on the grade.

questions.stem: In the Vicat apparatus, the standard consistency of a cement paste is that at which the plunger penetrates to a point:
options: 2 to 4 mm from the bottom of the mould
5 to 7 mm from the bottom of the mould
10 to 12 mm from the bottom of the mould
Right down to the bottom of the mould
questions.solution:
**5 to 7 mm from the bottom of the mould.**

The test establishes the **standard (normal) consistency** of the paste — the water content, expressed as a percentage of the cement mass and denoted **P**, at which a 10 mm diameter plunger settles to between 5 and 7 mm above the base of the Vicat mould.

For ordinary Portland cement **P is typically 26 to 33%**.

**Why the test exists at all.** On its own the consistency figure is of no direct use in concrete design — its purpose is to fix a **reproducible reference water content** so that the other cement tests are comparable between laboratories:

| Test | Water content used |
|---|---|
| **Setting time** (initial and final) | **0.85 P** |
| **Soundness** (Le Chatelier) | **0.78 P** |
| Compressive strength (mortar cubes) | **0.40 P + 3%** |

Without a standard consistency, two laboratories mixing "by feel" would get different setting times for the same cement, and the results would mean nothing.

**The same apparatus, different attachment**, which is the point most often confused:

| Attachment | Determines |
|---|---|
| **10 mm plunger** | **Standard consistency** |
| **1 mm square needle** | **Initial** setting time — fails to penetrate to within 5–7 mm of the base |
| **Annular attachment** | **Final** setting time — leaves no impression |

Note that the 5–7 mm figure appears in two of those rows, for the plunger and the needle, which is why the wording of a question must be read carefully.

The requirements the tests then check: initial set **≥ 30 min**, final set **≤ 600 min**, soundness **≤ 10 mm** expansion, fineness **≥ 225 m²/kg**.

examTip.trick: Standard consistency is the water content at which the **10 mm Vicat plunger** penetrates to within **5 to 7 mm of the bottom** of the mould — normally about **26–33%** water by weight of cement.
examTip.mnemonic: **Standard consistency is not an end in itself — it is the REFERENCE paste for the setting time and soundness tests**, so those results are comparable between cements. Vicat uses **needles and plungers**; Le Chatelier uses an **expanding mould**. Different apparatus, different property.

questions.stem: Shoring is provided in building construction to:
options: Give temporary lateral support to an unsafe or bulging wall
Retain the sides of an excavation
Support a working platform for masons
Transfer the load of a wall to a new foundation
questions.solution:
**To give temporary lateral support to an unsafe or bulging wall.**

Shoring is a **temporary** measure, used while a wall is repaired, while an adjoining building is demolished, or where a wall has begun to lean, bulge or crack.

The three temporary-works terms are constantly interchanged, and the distinction is worth fixing:

| Term | Supports | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Shoring** | **A wall, laterally** | Prop an unsafe or bulging wall |
| **Underpinning** | **A wall from below** | Provide a **new, deeper foundation** beneath an existing one |
| **Timbering / strutting** | **The sides of an excavation** | Prevent the trench faces collapsing |
| **Scaffolding** | **Workers and materials** | A working platform — not a structural support |

So option (b) describes **timbering**, (c) **scaffolding**, and (d) **underpinning**.

**The types of shoring:**

| Type | Arrangement | Used when |
|---|---|---|
| **Raking shore** | Inclined members bearing on the wall and on the ground | The commonest; wall needs lateral support |
| **Flying shore** | Horizontal struts spanning **between two parallel walls** | The intermediate building has been removed; leaves the ground clear |
| **Dead (vertical) shore** | Vertical props carrying a **needle** through the wall | The wall itself must be **cut into** — a new opening, or the foundation rebuilt |

The **flying shore** is the one to remember for its advantage: because it spans between the two walls it obstructs nothing at ground level, so traffic and access continue.

**Practical points examined alongside:** rakers should meet the wall at **40° to 70°** (the ideal being 45–60°), bear against a **wall plate and needles** rather than directly on the masonry, and be founded on a **sole plate** on firm ground. And the order matters — shoring is erected **before** any cutting or demolition begins, never after movement has started.

examTip.trap: **Underpinning** is the near-miss and works on the **FOUNDATION**; **scaffolding** is a working platform. Shoring supports the **superstructure**, temporarily.
examTip.trick: Ask what is being supported and for how long. Temporary + superstructure = shoring.
examTip.mnemonic: **SHoring SHores up a wall; UNDERpinning goes UNDER the foundation.** Types of shoring: **raking** (inclined props), **flying** (spanning between two walls across a gap), **dead/vertical** (supporting from below, as when removing a wall beneath).

questions.stem: A queen closer in brick masonry is:
options: A brick cut along its length into two equal halves
A brick cut across its width
A brick cut lengthwise so that its width is halved
questions.solution:
**A brick cut lengthwise so that its width is halved.**

A **queen closer** is a half-brick in **width** — full length, full height, half width (so 190 × 45 × 90 mm from a modular brick). It is inserted next to the quoin (corner) header to close the course and establish the correct **lap**.

The cut bricks, which are examined as a set:

| Cut | Description |
|---|---|
| **Queen closer** | **Half the width**, full length |
| **King closer** | One corner cut off, so **half a header and half a stretcher** face outward |
| **Bevelled closer** | Full length, but the width **bevelled** along the length |
| **Mitred closer** | End cut at an angle (30° to 60°) |
| **Half bat** | **Half the length** |
| **Three-quarter bat** | Three quarters of the length |

The key distinction is that a **closer** is cut along the **length** (reducing width), whereas a **bat** is cut across the length (reducing length). Option (a) describes a bat cut differently and (d) names a bat outright.

**Why closers are needed at all.** The whole purpose of a **bond** is that vertical joints do not line up between successive courses — a continuous vertical joint would be a plane of weakness through the wall. At a corner or a stopped end, whole bricks alone cannot produce the required **quarter-brick lap**, so a closer is inserted to shift the course along.

Hence the rule: **closers are placed next to the quoin header, never in the middle of a wall**, where whole bricks give the lap naturally.

In **English bond** — the strongest, with alternate courses of headers and stretchers — a queen closer is placed after the quoin header in every heading course. **Flemish bond**, which alternates headers and stretchers within the *same* course, needs closers at the quoins too but has more cut bricks overall, which is part of why it is weaker than English bond despite its better appearance.

examTip.trap: **Queen closer** and **king closer** are easily swapped. A **king** closer is cut diagonally across one corner; a **queen** closer is cut lengthwise, halving the width.
examTip.trick: Closers exist to **break the vertical joint (perpend)** at a wall end or quoin, so the bond is maintained and no continuous vertical joint runs up the wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Queen = cut lengthwise, half width, placed next to the QUOIN header.** Without a closer, English bond degenerates into a stack of aligned joints — which is precisely the weakness bonding exists to prevent.

questions.stem: The polar moment of inertia of a solid circular shaft of diameter d is:
questions.solution:
**πd⁴/32.**

The polar moment of inertia is taken about the **longitudinal axis** of the shaft, and by the perpendicular axis theorem it is the sum of the two rectangular moments of inertia:

> **J = I_xx + I_yy**

For a circle, symmetry gives I_xx = I_yy = πd⁴/64, so

> J = πd⁴/64 + πd⁴/64 = **πd⁴/32** ✓

So **J = 2I** for a circular section — a relation worth remembering in its own right, because it is exactly where the factor of 2 in the combined bending-and-torsion ratio σ/τ = 2M/T comes from.

The values to keep apart, and the traps among the options:

| Quantity | Circle of diameter d |
|---|---|
| **I** — moment of inertia about a diameter | **πd⁴/64** |
| **J** — polar moment of inertia | **πd⁴/32** |
| **Z** — section modulus (bending) | πd³/32 |
| Z_p — polar section modulus (torsion) | πd³/16 |

Note that option (a) is **I**, and option (d) is the **section modulus** — which has units of m³, not m⁴, so it can be eliminated dimensionally.

**Where J is used** — the torsion equation:

> **T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L**

giving τ_max = 16T/(πd³) at the surface and an angle of twist θ = TL/(GJ). The product **GJ** is the **torsional rigidity**.

For a **hollow** shaft, J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32 — which is why hollow sections are so efficient in torsion: removing the lightly stressed core near the axis saves weight while barely reducing J, since the material's contribution scales with the **fourth power** of its distance from the centre.

examTip.trick: By the **perpendicular axis theorem**, **J = I_xx + I_yy = πd⁴/64 + πd⁴/64 = πd⁴/32** — exactly **twice** the diametral value.
examTip.mnemonic: **64 for a diameter, 32 for polar — halve the denominator, double the value.** Then **τ_max = Tr/J = 16T/πd³**. Note the **fourth power** in J: doubling a shaft's diameter multiplies its torsional stiffness by **sixteen**.

questions.stem: The centroid of a semicircular area of radius r, measured from its diameter, lies at:
questions.solution:
**4r/3π** from the diameter — about **0.424 r**.

The centroids most often confused with one another, and every one of them appears among these options:

| Shape | Centroid from the base |
|---|---|
| **Semicircular area (lamina)** | **4r/3π ≈ 0.424 r** |
| **Semicircular arc (wire)** | **2r/π ≈ 0.637 r** |
| **Solid hemisphere** | **3r/8 = 0.375 r** |
| Hemispherical shell | r/2 = 0.5 r |
| Solid cone | h/4 |
| Triangle | h/3 |

So option (a) is the **solid hemisphere**, (b) the **hemispherical shell**, and (c) the **semicircular arc** — three plausible near-misses, which is what makes this worth asking.

**A sanity check that separates the area from the arc.** The **arc** has all its material at radius r, so its centroid must lie further out (0.637 r); the **area** has material spread from the centre outward, pulling the centroid inward (0.424 r). Any answer for a lamina larger than that of the corresponding arc is wrong.

**Where the value is used.** Chiefly in **composite sections** — a section built from rectangles, triangles and part-circles — where the centroid of the whole is

> ȳ = Σ(A_i ȳ_i)/ΣA_i

and each part's own centroid must be known first. It also appears when applying the **parallel axis theorem** to a semicircle, since the moment of inertia about the base (πr⁴/8, equivalently πD⁴/128) and about the centroid (≈ 0.11 r⁴) differ by A·ȳ² using exactly this 4r/3π.

That difference is substantial — the base value is nearly four times the centroidal one — which is the general reminder that **a moment of inertia is meaningless without naming its axis.**

examTip.trap: **3r/8** is the **solid hemisphere**, a three-dimensional body. This question asks about a two-dimensional **semicircular AREA**.
examTip.trick: **4r/3π ≈ 0.424r.** Check the family: semicircular **area** 4r/3π; semicircular **arc** 2r/π; **solid** hemisphere 3r/8; **hollow** hemisphere r/2.
examTip.mnemonic: **Area 4r/3π, arc 2r/π** — the area value is exactly two thirds of the arc value. Four figures, four values; read carefully which one is asked.

questions.stem: In levelling, a back sight is a reading taken on:
options: A point whose elevation is to be determined
The last point before the instrument is shifted
A point of known elevation, taken immediately after setting up the instrument
Any intermediate point between two turning points
questions.solution:
**On a point of known elevation, taken immediately after setting up the instrument.**

The three kinds of staff reading, in the order they occur at any instrument station:

| Reading | Taken on | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Back sight (BS)** | A point of **known** elevation — a benchmark or the previous change point | Establishes the **height of instrument** |
| **Intermediate sight (IS)** | Points whose elevation is wanted | Detail levels |
| **Fore sight (FS)** | The **last** point before the instrument is moved | The **change point**, carrying the level forward |

So option (b) describes a **fore sight**, (d) an **intermediate sight**, and (a) is true of IS and FS but not of a back sight — whose defining feature is that the elevation there is **already known**.

**How the reduction works** — the **height of collimation** method:

> **HI = RL of the known point + BS**
> **RL of any other point = HI − its staff reading**

So the back sight is what ties the instrument into the existing datum; without it no reduced level can be computed at all. At every change point a **fore sight and a back sight are taken from different instrument positions on the same staff position**, which is what transfers the level forward without loss.

**The arithmetic check** that must always be applied:

> **ΣBS − ΣFS = Last RL − First RL**

and, for the rise-and-fall method, ΣBS − ΣFS = Σrise − Σfall = last RL − first RL. That check catches reduction errors but **not** field errors, which is why levelling is run in **closed circuits** back to the starting benchmark, with the misclosure compared against a permissible limit (commonly 24√K mm, K in kilometres).

**Instrument errors and how they are removed:** keeping back sight and fore sight distances **equal** at each station eliminates **collimation error, curvature and refraction** — which is why balanced sight lengths are standard practice rather than a refinement.

examTip.trick: The **backsight** is the first reading after setting up, taken on a point of **known** elevation — it establishes the height of the instrument. The **foresight** is the last reading before moving.
examTip.mnemonic: **BS = known point, FS = last reading before shifting, IS = everything in between.** Then **HI = RL + BS** and **RL = HI − FS**. Check: **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL** for the height-of-instrument method; the **rise-and-fall** method adds a third leg (ΣRise − ΣFall) and is therefore the better check.

questions.stem: In the preparation of a detailed estimate, the quantity of excavation for a foundation trench is measured in:
questions.solution:
**Cubic metres.**

Excavation is a volume of material removed, so it is measured in **m³** — length × breadth × depth.

The units of measurement under IS 1200, which is what this question is really testing:

| Item | Unit |
|---|---|
| **Excavation, earthwork, filling** | **m³** |
| Concrete (PCC, RCC) | **m³** |
| Brickwork, stone masonry | **m³** |
| **Plastering, pointing, painting** | **m²** |
| Flooring, DPC, waterproofing | **m²** |
| Formwork (shuttering) | **m²** |
| **Reinforcement, structural steel** | **kg or tonne (weight)** |
| Skirting, kerb, cornice, pipes | **running metre** |
| Doors, windows (sometimes) | number or m² |

The pattern is worth internalising: items with **thickness that matters** are volumes; items applied as a **layer of fixed thickness** are areas; items that are essentially **linear** are running metres; and steel is always by **weight**.

**Conventions specific to excavation:**
- Measured on the **authorised** dimensions, not on what was actually dug — over-excavation is at the contractor's cost.
- **No deduction** is made for the volume the footing will occupy; the whole trench is paid for.
- Rates are classified by **soil type** — soft/ordinary soil, hard soil, soft rock, hard rock — and by **depth range**, since deeper work is slower.
- **Shoring, timbering and dewatering** are separate items where required, not included in the excavation rate.

For reinforcement, the weight follows from **w = d²/162 kg/m** (d in mm), with laps and hooks included in the measured length. And note the deduction thresholds that catch candidates: **no deduction for openings up to 0.1 m² in brickwork**, but **0.5 m² in plaster**.

examTip.trick: The general IS 1200 rule: measure by the dimension that **varies**. Excavation varies in all three dimensions, so it is measured by **volume**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Thin layers by AREA (plaster, DPC, painting); bulk work by VOLUME (excavation, concrete, brickwork); linear items by LENGTH (skirting, cornice); and steel by WEIGHT.** Then add **lead** (horizontal transport) and **lift** (vertical) as separate items — both cost money without adding volume.

questions.stem: The specific gravity of soil solids is normally determined in the laboratory using a:
questions.solution:
**A pycnometer or density bottle.**

Specific gravity of solids is the ratio of the mass of a given volume of soil solids to the mass of an equal volume of water at the same temperature. The pycnometer measures it by **water displacement**:

> **G = (W₂ − W₁) / [(W₂ − W₁) − (W₃ − W₄)]**

where W₁ is the empty pycnometer, W₂ pycnometer + dry soil, W₃ pycnometer + soil + water, and W₄ pycnometer + water only. The difference (W₃ − W₄) is the mass of water **displaced** by the solids, which fixes their volume.

Matching the apparatus to the test, since all four options are real soil-testing equipment:

| Apparatus | Determines |
|---|---|
| **Pycnometer / density bottle** | **Specific gravity of solids** (also water content of sands) |
| **Casagrande apparatus** | **Liquid limit** — 25 blows to close a 12.7 mm groove |
| **Core cutter** | **Field dry density** of cohesive soil |
| **Hydrometer** | **Particle size distribution** of the fraction finer than 75 μm |

The **density bottle** (50 ml) is used for fine-grained soils and gives the more accurate result; the larger **pycnometer** (900 ml) suits sands and gravels.

**Typical values**, worth carrying as a check on any computed result:

| Soil | G |
|---|---|
| Sand | 2.65 – 2.67 |
| Silt | 2.67 – 2.70 |
| Clay | 2.70 – 2.80 |
| Organic soil | < 2.60 |

So a G outside roughly **2.6 to 2.8** should prompt a re-check rather than being accepted.

**Why G matters.** It appears in almost every phase relation: **Se = wG**, γ_d = Gγ_w/(1+e), the **zero-air-voids line** γ_d = Gγ_w/(1+wG), the critical hydraulic gradient **i_cr = (G−1)/(1+e)**, and hydrometer analysis. An error in G therefore propagates widely — which is why the entrapped air must be fully removed by vacuum or boiling before the W₃ weighing, this being the commonest source of error in the test.

examTip.trick: The pycnometer works by **displacement**: weigh it with soil and water, then with water alone, and the difference gives the volume the solids occupy.
examTip.mnemonic: **G for most soils is 2.65–2.75** — quartz sand about 2.65, clays a little higher. A result outside that band means an **error, not an exotic soil** — usually trapped **air bubbles**, which is why the sample is de-aired before weighing.

questions.stem: A soil has a liquid limit of 45% and a plastic limit of 25%. Its plasticity index is:
questions.solution:
**20%.**

> **PI = LL − PL = 45 − 25 = 20%**

The plasticity index is the **range of water content over which the soil behaves plastically** — it can be remoulded without cracking or flowing. A wide range indicates a clay-rich soil.

Option (a) adds the limits instead of subtracting; (c) divides them; (d) restates the plastic limit.

**Classifying this soil.** With PI = 20% it is of **medium to high plasticity**:

| PI | Description |
|---|---|
| 0 | Non-plastic (sand) |
| < 7 | Low plasticity |
| 7 – 17 | Medium plasticity |
| **> 17** | **High plasticity** |

And on the **plasticity chart** the A-line is PI = 0.73(LL − 20) = 0.73 × 25 = **18.25**. Since PI = 20 lies **above** the A-line with LL < 50, the soil classifies as **CI — inorganic clay of medium plasticity**. Below the A-line it would have been a silt (MI).

That is the practical use of the calculation: the PI and LL together place the soil on the chart, and the chart decides whether it is a **clay or a silt** — a distinction that governs drainage, strength and compressibility, and which cannot be made by grain size alone for fine soils.

**The related indices**, distinguished by which limits they combine:

| Index | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Plasticity index** | **LL − PL** |
| Shrinkage index | PL − SL |
| **Liquidity index** | (w − PL)/PI — where the natural water content sits in the plastic range |
| Consistency index | (LL − w)/PI |
| Toughness index | PI / flow index |

The **liquidity index** is the one with immediate engineering meaning: above 1 the soil is at or beyond its liquid limit and behaves as a viscous fluid — the condition of a **sensitive quick clay**, which loses nearly all its strength on remoulding.

examTip.trick: **PI = LL − PL = 45 − 25 = 20%.** It measures the **range of water content over which the soil behaves plastically**.
examTip.mnemonic: **PI wide = fat clay; PI near zero = silt.** The companion is the **liquidity index LI = (w − PL)/PI**, which says where the *natural* water content sits in that range — **above 1 and the soil behaves as a liquid**, which is the condition of a sensitive clay when remoulded.

questions.stem: At a depth of 4 m in a saturated soil deposit with the water table at the ground surface, the saturated unit weight being 20 kN/m³, the effective vertical stress is approximately:
questions.solution:
**40.8 kN/m².**

**Step 1 — total vertical stress:**
> σ = γ_sat × z = 20 × 4 = **80.0 kN/m²**

**Step 2 — pore water pressure**, the water table being at the surface:
> u = γ_w × z = 9.81 × 4 = **39.24 kN/m²**

**Step 3 — effective stress**, by Terzaghi's principle:
> **σ′ = σ − u** = 80.0 − 39.24 = **40.76 ≈ 40.8 kN/m²** ✓

Equivalently, use the **submerged (buoyant) unit weight** directly:
> γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w = 20 − 9.81 = 10.19 kN/m³
> σ′ = γ′ × z = 10.19 × 4 = **40.8 kN/m²** ✓

That second route is the quicker one and is worth adopting as the default whenever the water table is at the surface.

Note how the distractors are placed: **80.0** is the **total** stress, **39.2** the **pore pressure**, and **119.2** their sum — so every intermediate quantity appears as an option, and only the subtraction gives the answer.

**Why effective stress is the quantity that matters.** Everything mechanical depends on σ′, not σ:

> **Shear strength:** τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′
> **Consolidation:** settlement occurs as u dissipates and σ′ rises
> Bearing capacity, earth pressure and slope stability are all computed on σ′

Water cannot sustain shear and presses equally in all directions, so it does not push grains together and contributes nothing to strength — hence it is called the **neutral** stress.

**The consequence to carry:** raising the water table raises u, lowers σ′, and **reduces strength with no change in total load**. That single mechanism explains monsoon slope failures, quick sand (where upward seepage drives σ′ to **zero**), liquefaction under seismic shaking, and why excavations collapse after rain.

examTip.trick: With the water table at the surface, **σ′ = γ′ × depth**, using the **submerged** unit weight **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w ≈ 20 − 9.81 ≈ 10.2 kN/m³**. So σ′ = 10.2 × 4 ≈ **40.8 kPa** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Use γ′ below the water table — it is roughly HALF γ_sat, so the effective stress builds at half the rate.** That single fact is why a rising water table weakens soil, why bearing capacity on sand is nearly halved, and why **σ′ = σ − u** is the most important equation in the subject.

questions.stem: For a soil deposit consisting of horizontal layers of differing permeability, the equivalent permeability for flow perpendicular to the layers is the:
options: Weighted arithmetic mean of the layer permeabilities
Simple average of the layer permeabilities
Weighted harmonic mean of the layer permeabilities
Geometric mean of the layer permeabilities
questions.solution:
**The weighted harmonic mean.**

The two cases must be kept apart, because they behave quite differently:

| Flow direction | Equivalent permeability | Governed by |
|---|---|---|
| **Parallel** to the layers (horizontal) | **k_h = Σ(k_i H_i)/ΣH_i** — weighted **arithmetic** mean | The **most permeable** layer |
| **Perpendicular** to the layers (vertical) | **k_v = ΣH_i / Σ(H_i/k_i)** — weighted **harmonic** mean | The **least** permeable layer |

**The reasoning is an exact analogy with electrical resistance.** Flow **parallel** to the layers is like resistors in **parallel** — the water takes the easiest path, so a single highly permeable seam carries most of the flow and dominates the average. Flow **perpendicular** is like resistors in **series** — every drop must pass through *all* the layers, so the tightest layer throttles the whole flow.

**A worked illustration** makes the asymmetry vivid. Take two equal layers, k₁ = 10⁻³ m/s (sand) and k₂ = 10⁻⁹ m/s (clay):

> k_h = (10⁻³ + 10⁻⁹)/2 ≈ **5 × 10⁻⁴ m/s** — essentially the sand's value
> k_v = 2/(1/10⁻³ + 1/10⁻⁹) ≈ **2 × 10⁻⁹ m/s** — essentially the clay's value

So **k_h/k_v ≈ 250,000**. The same deposit is a quarter of a million times more permeable sideways than downwards.

**Why it matters in practice.** Natural deposits are almost always layered, so **k_h ≫ k_v** as a rule, commonly by one to two orders of magnitude. The consequences:

- **Seepage** beneath a dam or into an excavation travels predominantly **horizontally**, so cut-offs and sheet piling must interrupt the horizontal path.
- **Consolidation** of a clay layer sandwiched between sand seams occurs far faster than a vertical-only analysis predicts, because water escapes **sideways** to the drainage layers — which is the principle **sand drains** exploit deliberately.
- Flow nets in anisotropic soil must be drawn on a **transformed section**, scaling one coordinate by √(k_z/k_x), with the equivalent isotropic permeability **√(k_x k_z)**.

That last point is how the flow-net technique is rescued for real ground: transform, draw orthogonally, then transform back.

examTip.trick: Reason physically. **Perpendicular** to the layers the water must cross **every** layer, so the **least permeable one controls** — that is a **harmonic** mean. **Parallel** to them it takes the easiest path, so the most permeable dominates — an **arithmetic** mean.
examTip.mnemonic: **Across the layers, the WORST one wins (harmonic). Along them, the BEST one wins (arithmetic).** Hence **k_horizontal is always ≥ k_vertical**, often by a factor of 2 to 10 — which is why seepage nets are drawn on a **transformed section** with the horizontal scale reduced by √(k_v/k_h).

questions.stem: In the direct shear test, a principal limitation compared with the triaxial test is that:
options: It cannot be used for cohesionless soils
It requires a much larger specimen
It cannot measure the angle of internal friction
The failure plane is predetermined and drainage cannot be controlled
questions.solution:
**The failure plane is predetermined and drainage cannot be controlled.**

The direct shear (box shear) test forces the specimen to fail on the **horizontal plane** between the two halves of the shear box. That plane is imposed by the apparatus, not chosen by the soil — so if the soil's weakest plane lies elsewhere, the measured strength is not the soil's true minimum.

The test's limitations in full:

| Limitation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Failure plane forced horizontal** | Not necessarily the weakest plane |
| **Drainage cannot be controlled** | No UU / CU / CD distinction possible |
| **Pore pressure cannot be measured** | Only **total**-stress parameters obtainable |
| Stress distribution non-uniform | Stress concentrates at the edges |
| Area changes during shear | Correction needed |
| No control of the intermediate principal stress | — |

By contrast the **triaxial test** encloses the specimen in a membrane inside a pressure cell, so drainage can be opened or closed, pore pressure measured at the base, and the specimen fails on **its own weakest plane**. That is what makes the three test conditions possible:

| Test | Drainage | Models |
|---|---|---|
| **UU** | Closed throughout | Rapid loading on saturated clay — end of construction |
| **CU** | Consolidated, then sheared undrained | Loading after consolidation |
| **CD** | Open, sheared slowly | **Long-term** stability; gives **c′ and φ′** |

The distinction between **total-stress (c_u, φ_u)** and **effective-stress (c′, φ′)** parameters is the whole reason this matters: a clay slope may stand safely on excavation and fail years later as pore pressures equalise, and only a drained or pore-pressure-measured test can predict that.

**Why the direct shear test survives nonetheless.** It is quick, simple and cheap, and for **sand** the objections largely evaporate — drainage is so rapid that the test is effectively drained however it is run, so it gives φ′ directly. Its natural use is therefore **cohesionless soils**, which is precisely why option (a) is wrong: sand is what it is *best* suited to.

Option (c) is also wrong — the test plots τ against σ across several normal loads and reads φ from the slope of the failure envelope.

examTip.trick: The box must split along its **own horizontal plane**, which may not be the soil's weakest plane, and it cannot be sealed — so pore pressure can be neither measured nor controlled.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear box: cheap, quick and BLIND.** Acceptable for a drained sand test; useless whenever pore pressure matters — which is whenever clay is involved. The **triaxial** cell fixes both defects: sealed (so drainage is controlled and u is measured) and the failure plane finds itself.

questions.stem: Taylor's stability number for a slope in cohesive soil is defined as:
questions.solution:
**S_n = c/(γH)** — strictly the **mobilised** cohesion, c_m/(γH).

It is a **dimensionless** grouping, which is the quickest way to check it:

> c [kN/m²] ÷ (γ [kN/m³] × H [m]) = dimensionless ✓

Option (c) is its reciprocal, and option (d) is dimensionally wrong.

**How it is used.** Taylor published charts of S_n against the **slope angle β** and the **angle of internal friction φ**, derived from the friction-circle method. Two questions can then be answered without a full stability analysis:

| Given | Read off | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Slope angle and φ | S_n from the chart | **Critical height** H_c = c/(γ S_n) |
| Height and φ | S_n = c/(γH) | The **safe slope angle** |

So the stability number packages the whole analysis into one dimensionless figure, which is why it survives as a rapid check even though modern practice uses computer methods.

**A value worth carrying:** for a **purely cohesive** soil (φ = 0) with a vertical slope, S_n = 0.261, giving

> **H_c ≈ 3.85 c/γ**

which is the maximum unsupported height of a vertical cut in clay — the figure that decides whether a trench needs timbering. For a 4 m deep trench in a clay of c = 25 kPa and γ = 18 kN/m³, H_c = 3.85 × 25/18 = 5.3 m, so the cut stands — but with a factor of safety of only 1.3, which is why supports are used regardless.

**The contrast with a cohesionless slope** is instructive. There, as Set 4 Q68 showed, the factor of safety is

> FoS = tan φ′/tan β

**independent of height** — so a sand slope is equally at risk at any depth and its critical angle is simply φ′ (the angle of repose). Cohesion is what introduces a **critical height** at all, because it contributes strength that does not grow with depth while the driving weight does.

And recall the dominant practical caveat: **steady seepage roughly halves the factor of safety**, so a slope analysed dry must be re-checked saturated — which is why drainage, not geometry, is usually the effective remedy.

examTip.trick: **S_n = c/(F γ H)** is **dimensionless** — c, γ and H combine to cancel. That is exactly what lets one chart serve every slope of a given angle and φ.
examTip.mnemonic: **Taylor's charts give S_n from the slope angle and φ; the formula then gives the safe height.** Since **H ∝ 1/S_n**, a *small* stability number means a *tall* safe slope — the relation is inverse, which is easy to get backwards.

questions.stem: In the standard penetration test, the N-value is the number of blows required to drive the split-spoon sampler through:
options: The last 300 mm of a 450 mm penetration
questions.solution:
**The last 300 mm of a 450 mm penetration.**

The sampler is driven **450 mm** in total, recorded in three 150 mm increments:

| Increment | Treated as |
|---|---|
| First 150 mm | **Seating drive — discarded** |
| Second 150 mm | Counted |
| Third 150 mm | Counted |
| **Sum of the last two (300 mm)** | **The N-value** |

**Why the first 150 mm is discarded.** The bottom of the borehole is disturbed by the drilling itself — loosened, or heaved by stress relief. Blows in that zone measure the disturbance, not the soil, so they are used only to seat the sampler in undisturbed ground below.

**The standard conditions:** a **63.5 kg** hammer falling freely through **750 mm**, driving a split-spoon sampler of 50 mm outside and 35 mm inside diameter. The test is stopped at 50 blows for any increment — recorded as **refusal**.

**Corrections applied before use**, which is where candidates most often stop too early:

> **N_corrected = N × C_N (overburden) × C_E, C_B, C_S, C_R (energy, borehole, sampler, rod length)**

plus a **dilatancy correction** for fine saturated sands and silts. The overburden correction matters most: the same sand gives a higher N deeper down simply because it is more confined, so raw N-values from different depths are not comparable.

**What N is used for:**

| Parameter | Relation |
|---|---|
| **Relative density** of sand | N < 4 very loose, 4–10 loose, 10–30 medium, 30–50 dense, > 50 very dense |
| **Angle of internal friction** φ | Correlations with corrected N |
| Undrained strength of clay | c_u ≈ 6N kPa (crude) |
| **Allowable bearing pressure** | Via Teng's or Peck's charts |
| **Liquefaction potential** | Corrected (N₁)₆₀ against cyclic stress ratio |

That last row is important in Nepal: **liquefaction assessment** in the Terai's saturated sands is based on (N₁)₆₀, and the 2015 earthquake produced widespread liquefaction where those values were low.

**Its limitation** is worth stating plainly: the split-spoon has an **area ratio of about 110%**, so the sample it recovers is thoroughly **disturbed** — usable for classification and index tests, never for strength or consolidation testing. For those, a thin-walled sampler with an area ratio **≤ 10%** is required.

examTip.trap: "450 mm" is the whole drive and is the obvious wrong pick. The **first 150 mm is the SEATING drive and is discarded.**
examTip.trick: The spoon is driven in three 150 mm increments; N is the sum of the **second and third** only, using a **63.5 kg hammer falling 750 mm**.
examTip.mnemonic: **150 seating, 300 counted.** Two corrections always apply: **overburden** (N₁) and **dilatancy** in saturated fine sand (N above 15 corrected to 15 + ½(N − 15)). The test is **least reliable in gravel** (a stone jams the shoe) and **in very soft clay** (the spoon sinks under its own weight).

questions.stem: A cantilever sheet pile wall derives its stability principally from:
options: Passive resistance of the soil in front of the embedded depth
The weight of the wall itself
Anchors or tie rods near the top
Friction along the back face of the wall
questions.solution:
**Passive resistance of the soil in front of the embedded depth.**

A cantilever sheet pile has no anchors and negligible weight. It is driven to a depth below excavation level, and the **passive pressure mobilised in front of that embedded portion** is the only thing resisting the active pressure pushing from behind. The wall acts as a vertical cantilever fixed by the soil below dredge level.

The design consequence is direct: **embedded depth is everything**. It is found by taking moments about the point of rotation, equating the active thrust behind to the passive resistance in front, and then increasing the theoretical depth by a factor of safety — commonly **20 to 40%**, or by applying a factor of 1.5 to 2 to the passive pressure.

**Why the passive side needs a factor of safety of its own.** As Set 3 Q11 noted, full active pressure develops after movement of only **0.1 to 0.5%** of the wall height, whereas full **passive** resistance needs **2 to 5%** — often more movement than the structure or adjacent property can tolerate. So passive resistance is deliberately discounted rather than taken at face value.

**The types of sheet pile wall**, which the distractors name:

| Type | Stability from | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | **Passive resistance of the embedded depth** | Heights up to about **6 m** |
| **Anchored (tied-back)** | Passive resistance **plus** anchors or tie rods near the top | Greater heights |
| Braced (strutted) | Internal struts across the excavation | Trenches, cofferdams |
| **Gravity wall** | **Its own weight** | Masonry and concrete retaining walls |

So option (b) describes a **gravity** wall and (c) an **anchored** sheet pile — a different structure, and the usual answer once the height exceeds what a cantilever can manage. The height limit exists because the required embedment and the bending moment both grow rapidly: the moment varies roughly with the **cube** of the height.

**Where sheet piling is used:** waterfront quays and bulkheads, cofferdams, deep excavations in soft ground, and as a **cut-off** to lengthen the seepage path beneath a hydraulic structure — recall that vertical cut-offs are far more effective than horizontal floor length at cutting the exit gradient, which is precisely Lane's and Khosla's correction to Bligh's creep theory.

examTip.trick: A cantilever sheet pile has **no anchor and no prop** — its only source of stability is the **passive resistance** of the soil in front of the embedded length, plus the passive wedge behind the toe.
examTip.mnemonic: **No anchor means the embedded depth does ALL the work — which is why cantilever sheet piles are limited to about 6 m of retained height.** Beyond that the required embedment and the deflection both become unreasonable, and an **anchored** or **strutted** wall is needed instead.

questions.stem: An under-reamed pile is used principally to:
options: Reduce the cost of boring in rock
Resist uplift and to found in expansive soils below the active zone
Increase the skin friction along the entire shaft
questions.solution:
**To resist uplift and to found in expansive soils below the active zone.**

An under-reamed pile is a bored cast-in-situ pile with one or more **enlarged bulbs** (under-reams) formed near its base, typically **2 to 2.5 times** the shaft diameter.

The bulb does two things that a plain shaft cannot:

| Function | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Resists uplift** | The bulb must lift a cone of soil above it to move upward — a large **anchoring** resistance |
| **Founds below the active zone** | Carries the structure on soil below the depth of seasonal moisture change |
| Increases end bearing | Larger bearing area at the base |

**Why expansive soils demand this.** **Black cotton soil** and similar expansive clays swell on wetting and shrink on drying, and the movement is concentrated in the upper **active zone** — typically 1.5 to 3.5 m deep. A shallow footing on such soil is lifted in the monsoon and dropped in the dry season, cracking the structure. An under-reamed pile passes through that zone and anchors below it, so:

- the **bulb resists the uplift** the swelling soil exerts on the shaft;
- the load is transferred to soil of **stable moisture content**.

That combination — uplift resistance plus a stable founding level — is why under-reamed piles are the standard Indian and Nepali solution for light structures on expansive soil, and why they are used for **transmission tower** foundations, where uplift from wind on one leg is the governing case.

**Design points:** shaft diameter usually 200 to 500 mm; bulb diameter **2 to 2.5 D**; the topmost bulb at least **1.75 times the bulb diameter** below ground and below the active zone; spacing between multiple bulbs 1.25 to 1.5 times the bulb diameter.

Why the other options fail: boring in **rock** (a) is not what the technique is for, and the bulb adds nothing there; **skin friction along the entire shaft** (c) is unchanged by a local bulb; and **driving through boulders** (d) describes a driven pile problem — an under-reamed pile is **bored**, so boulders obstruct rather than favour it.

The general pile classification, for context: by **material** (concrete, steel, timber, composite), by **installation** (driven, bored, driven cast-in-situ), and by **load transfer** — **end-bearing**, **friction**, or **uplift/tension** piles, of which the under-reamed pile is the classic example of the last.

examTip.trick: Expansive clay **swells on wetting** and drags a plain shaft **upward**. The **bulb anchors** the pile: to lift it, the swelling force would have to lift the cone of soil above the bulb as well.
examTip.mnemonic: **The bulb must sit BELOW the ACTIVE ZONE** — the depth over which moisture changes seasonally, typically 1.5–3.5 m in black cotton soil. Bulb diameter **2–2.5 × shaft**; pile spacing **2 × the BULB diameter**, not the shaft. Locating the bulb inside the active zone defeats the whole design.

questions.stem: The total settlement of a footing on saturated clay consists of immediate settlement, primary consolidation settlement and:
questions.solution:
**Secondary consolidation (creep) settlement.**

The three components, in the order they occur:

| Component | Cause | Time scale |
|---|---|---|
| **Immediate (elastic)** | Undrained distortion at constant volume | **On loading** |
| **Primary consolidation** | **Expulsion of pore water**; excess pore pressure dissipates and σ′ rises | **Months to years** in clay |
| **Secondary consolidation (creep)** | **Rearrangement of the soil skeleton** at essentially constant effective stress | **Years to decades** |

> **Total settlement = S_i + S_c + S_s**

**What distinguishes secondary from primary.** Primary consolidation is driven by water leaving the voids, and it ends when the excess pore pressure has dissipated. **Secondary** consolidation continues **after** that — the effective stress is no longer changing, but the particles and their adsorbed water films continue to creep into a denser arrangement. It is plotted as a straight line against **log time**:

> S_s = C_α H log₁₀(t₂/t₁)

where C_α is the coefficient of secondary compression.

**When it matters.** Usually secondary settlement is small and is neglected — but not always:

| Soil | Secondary settlement |
|---|---|
| Inorganic clay of low plasticity | Small; commonly ignored |
| **Highly plastic and organic clays, peat** | **Large — can exceed the primary settlement** |

So on peat or organic soil, ignoring creep is a serious error, and it is one reason such deposits are avoided or pre-loaded.

Why the other options are not components of settlement: **elastic rebound** is *recovery* on unloading, **frost heave** is an upward movement from ice formation, and **differential settlement** is not a component at all but the **difference** in total settlement between two points — which is what actually damages a structure.

That last distinction is the practically important one. A building can tolerate large **uniform** settlement (Mexico City has sunk metres) but very little **differential** settlement, because it is differential movement that racks the frame and cracks the cladding. IS 1904 accordingly limits differential settlement and **angular distortion** rather than total settlement alone — typically 1/500 for framed buildings — and it is why a **raft** is chosen to even out settlement across erratic ground.

examTip.trick: Three components in sequence: **immediate (elastic)** during construction, **primary consolidation** as pore water is expelled over months to years, and **secondary (creep)** at constant effective stress afterwards.
examTip.mnemonic: **Immediate dominates in SAND; primary consolidation dominates in CLAY; SECONDARY dominates in PEAT and organic soils.** That last is why building on peat is treated as a special problem — the settlement never really stops.

questions.stem: An ideal fluid is one which is:
questions.solution:
**Incompressible and having zero viscosity.**

An ideal (or perfect) fluid is a **mathematical idealisation** — no real fluid has zero viscosity. Its two defining properties are chosen to make the equations tractable:

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Zero viscosity (inviscid)** | **No shear stress**, so **no friction loss** and no boundary layer |
| **Incompressible** | Constant density, so continuity is simply A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ |

**Why the idealisation is useful despite being false.** Assuming zero viscosity is exactly what permits **Bernoulli's equation**:

> p/γ + v²/2g + z = constant

Because there is no friction, total head is conserved along a streamline. Real flows lose head, so the equation is extended with a loss term, h_L — but the inviscid solution remains the starting point, and away from boundaries it is often very accurate.

**Where the idealisation breaks down** is at the boundary. Viscosity, however small, forces the fluid velocity at a solid surface to **zero** — the no-slip condition — so a thin **boundary layer** always forms in which viscous effects dominate. Prandtl's insight was to treat the flow as inviscid outside that layer and viscous within it, which is the basis of modern fluid mechanics.

The fluid classifications, for contrast:

| Fluid | Character |
|---|---|
| **Ideal** | **μ = 0, incompressible** — theoretical only |
| **Real** | Has viscosity; every actual fluid |
| **Newtonian** | τ = μ(du/dy) with **μ constant** — water, air, thin oils |
| Non-Newtonian | μ varies with shear rate — paint, blood, fresh concrete |
| Ideal plastic | Needs a **yield stress** before flowing — toothpaste, drilling mud |

Note the trap in that table: a **real** fluid need not be **Newtonian**. Paint and toothpaste are real and non-Newtonian — so "real fluid" and "Newtonian fluid" are not synonyms.

One consequence of the incompressibility assumption worth remembering: it is precisely what a **water hammer** analysis must abandon, since the pressure wave speed c = √(K/ρ) ≈ 1449 m/s exists only because water is slightly compressible.

examTip.trick: An ideal fluid has **zero viscosity and constant density** — so no shear stress ever, no boundary layer, and free slip at a wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **No viscosity, no drag — which is D'ALEMBERT'S PARADOX**, resolved only by real flow **SEPARATING**. Ideal theory works well in **accelerating (converging)** flow and badly in **decelerating** flow — hence a venturi's steep 20° inlet and gentle 6° diffuser.

questions.stem: The property of a liquid responsible for the rise of sap in plants and for water rising in a fine tube is:
questions.solution:
**Surface tension.**

Surface tension **σ** arises because a molecule at the surface has neighbours only on one side, so the surface behaves like a stretched membrane in tension. Its unit is **N/m** (force per unit length), and for water at 20°C **σ ≈ 0.073 N/m**.

**How it produces capillary rise.** Where the liquid **wets** the solid, adhesion exceeds the liquid's own cohesion, the meniscus curves concave upward, and the vertical component of the surface tension around the perimeter lifts the column:

> **h = 4σ cos θ/(ρgd)**

So the rise is **inversely proportional to the diameter** — the finer the tube, the higher the water climbs.

**Wetting decides the direction:**

| Liquid in glass | Contact angle θ | Meniscus | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water** | ≈ 0° | Concave | **Rise** |
| **Mercury** | ≈ 130–140° | Convex | **Depression** |

Because cos θ is negative for mercury, h comes out negative — a depression.

**The other manifestations of surface tension**, which are examined as a set:

| Case | Excess pressure inside |
|---|---|
| Liquid **droplet** (one surface) | **4σ/d** |
| **Soap bubble** (two surfaces) | **8σ/d** |
| Liquid **jet** (cylindrical) | 2σ/d |

All inversely proportional to diameter — so a **smaller bubble has a higher internal pressure**, which is why two connected bubbles of unequal size end with the small one emptying into the large one.

**Why it matters in civil engineering, not just in plants:**
- **Capillary rise in soils** follows the same 1/d law with pore size in place of tube diameter, which is why fine silts draw water far higher than coarse sands. It governs the depth at which a **damp proof course** is needed and drives **frost heave**.
- It holds **capillary water** in the soil against gravity — the fraction actually available to plants, between field capacity and the wilting point.
- **Bulking of sand**: films of water hold grains apart, increasing bulk volume by 20 to 40%.
- **Manometer tubes** are kept above about 6 mm bore so the capillary correction can be neglected.

Surface tension **decreases with rising temperature** and vanishes at the critical point.

examTip.trick: Surface tension makes a liquid surface behave as a **stretched membrane**, and in a fine tube it pulls the column up: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **h ∝ 1/d — fine pores, big rise.** In soils: sand 0.1–2 m, **silt 1–10 m**, clay 10 m+. Silt's combination of high rise **and** workable permeability is exactly what makes it the most **frost-susceptible** soil, and it also explains the **apparent cohesion** that lets damp sand stand in a vertical cut.

questions.stem: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m deep has its top edge 1 m below the water surface. The total hydrostatic force on the gate is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 147 kN.**

**Step 1 — depth of the centroid.** The gate spans from 1 m to 4 m below the surface, so its centroid is at
> x̄ = 1 + 3/2 = **2.5 m**

**Step 2 — area:**
> A = 2 × 3 = **6 m²**

**Step 3 — total force**, which acts at the centroid depth regardless of the gate's orientation:
> **F = γ A x̄** = 9.81 × 6 × 2.5 = **147.15 kN** ✓

Note that option (b), 88 kN, is what you get using x̄ = 1.5 m (forgetting the 1 m submergence), and (c) uses x̄ = 1 m — so the whole question turns on locating the centroid correctly.

**Where the force acts** — the centre of pressure, which is always **below** the centroid:

> h_cp = x̄ + I_G/(A x̄)
> I_G = bd³/12 = 2 × 27/12 = 4.5 m⁴
> h_cp = 2.5 + 4.5/(6 × 2.5) = 2.5 + 0.30 = **2.80 m** below the surface

The offset appears because pressure grows linearly with depth, so the lower strips carry disproportionately more force. That offset **shrinks as the gate is submerged deeper** — at great depth the pressure is nearly uniform over the gate and the centre of pressure approaches the centroid.

**The special case worth memorising:** if the top edge is **at** the water surface, the general result collapses to

> **h_cp = 2d/3**

the familiar two-thirds-of-the-depth answer.

**For a curved surface** the same total-force approach does not work directly; instead resolve into components:

| Component | Equals |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal** | Pressure force on the **vertical projection** |
| **Vertical** | **Weight of the fluid** above the surface (real or imagined) |

That projected-area rule is what gives the axial force **πP₀R²** on a hemispherical vessel end, and it is why a flat cap and a domed cap of the same radius transmit the same total thrust to the shell.

examTip.trick: **F = γh̄A**, and h̄ is the depth of the **CENTROID** = 1 + 3/2 = **2.5 m**. So F = 9.81 × 2.5 × 6 = **147 kN** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Centroid for the FORCE; centre of pressure for its LOCATION.** Here h_cp = h̄ + I_G/(Ah̄) = 2.5 + (2×27/12)/(6×2.5) = 2.5 + 0.3 = **2.8 m** — always **below** the centroid, because the correction term is always positive.

questions.stem: A body floats in water with 60% of its volume submerged. Its specific gravity is:
questions.solution:
**0.60.**

By **Archimedes' principle**, a floating body displaces its own weight of fluid:

> Weight of body = Weight of displaced fluid
> ρ_body × V_total × g = ρ_water × V_submerged × g

Cancelling and rearranging:

> **ρ_body/ρ_water = V_submerged/V_total**
> **G = 0.60** ✓

So for **any** floating body the specific gravity equals the **submerged fraction** of its volume — a result worth carrying, because it turns a geometric observation directly into a material property, and vice versa.

The familiar checks: ice floats with about **90%** submerged (G ≈ 0.9), and a body of G = 1 floats **just fully submerged**, in neutral buoyancy. Option (b) is the reciprocal, and (a) the *emergent* fraction.

**Buoyancy and stability are separate questions**, and it is worth keeping them apart:

| Question | Governed by |
|---|---|
| Will it **float**? | **Archimedes** — G < 1 |
| Will it float **upright**? | **Metacentric height** GM |

For a floating body:

> **GM = I/V − BG**

where I is the second moment of area of the **water-plane** section and V the displaced volume. Stability requires **M above G**, that is **GM positive** — then the buoyant force through the shifted centre of buoyancy and the weight through G form a **righting** couple.

| GM | Equilibrium |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | **Stable** |
| Zero | Neutral |
| Negative | **Unstable** — capsizes |

So a body can satisfy Archimedes perfectly and still overturn, which is why a heavily laden barge with a high centre of gravity is dangerous even though it clearly floats.

Note the contrast for a **fully submerged** body — a submarine or a balloon: the displaced shape does not change on tilting, so the metacentre concept does not apply, and stability requires simply that **B lie above G**.

examTip.trick: A floating body displaces **its own weight**, so the **submerged fraction equals the ratio of densities**: S_body/S_fluid = 0.60 in water.
examTip.mnemonic: **Submerged fraction = specific gravity, in water.** So **ICE (S = 0.917) floats with about 92% submerged** — nine tenths below the surface, not one tenth, which is the opposite of the popular image of an iceberg.

questions.stem: The continuity equation for steady incompressible flow expresses the conservation of:
questions.solution:
**Mass.**

The continuity equation states that mass cannot accumulate in a control volume in steady flow — what enters must leave:

> ρ₁A₁v₁ = ρ₂A₂v₂

and for an **incompressible** fluid the density cancels:

> **Q = A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ = constant**

The immediate consequence, and the reason it is so useful: **velocity is inversely proportional to area**. A pipe that narrows to half its area doubles the velocity — which is the whole principle of a **venturimeter, nozzle and orifice meter**.

**The three conservation laws** of fluid mechanics, each giving a different equation, must be kept apart:

| Law | Equation | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| **Mass** | **Continuity**, Q = Av | Velocities from areas |
| **Energy** | **Bernoulli**, p/γ + v²/2g + z = const | Pressures from velocities |
| **Momentum** | **Impulse–momentum**, F = ρQ(v₂ − v₁) | **Forces** on boundaries |

That table is worth internalising because it tells you **which equation to reach for**:

- Need a **velocity or discharge**? Continuity.
- Need a **pressure**? Bernoulli.
- Need a **force** — on a bend, a gate, a plate, a thrust block? **Momentum**.

The momentum equation is the one candidates under-use. It is indispensable where **energy loss is unknown in advance**, because it does not require the loss to be quantified. That is exactly why the **hydraulic jump** is analysed by momentum — giving the sequent depths

> y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1)

— and the energy loss is then computed **afterwards** from E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂). Attempting the jump by energy alone is impossible, since the loss is the unknown.

Similarly the **sudden enlargement** loss (V₁ − V₂)²/2g is derived by combining momentum with energy, which is why it is one of the few minor losses that can be derived rather than measured.

A caution on Bernoulli: its constant belongs to **one streamline**, and is the same for all streamlines only in **irrotational** flow. Continuity, by contrast, applies to the whole stream tube without qualification.

examTip.trick: Continuity is conservation of **mass**: **ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂**. For constant density it reduces to the volumetric statement A₁V₁ = A₂V₂.
examTip.mnemonic: **Continuity gives VELOCITIES; Bernoulli gives PRESSURES — a varying-section problem needs both.** Together they say a throat is a region of **high velocity and low pressure**, which is why a venturi measures flow from a pressure reading and also why cavitation starts there.

questions.stem: In a venturimeter, the coefficient of discharge is generally:
options: Higher than that of an orifice meter
Lower than that of an orifice meter
Equal to that of an orifice meter
questions.solution:
**Higher than that of an orifice meter**, because the gradual taper keeps the flow attached and reduces the loss.

| Device | C_d | Head loss |
|---|---|---|
| **Venturimeter** | **0.95 – 0.98** | **Low** — 10 to 20% of the differential |
| Nozzle meter | 0.93 – 0.98 | Moderate |
| **Orifice meter** | **0.60 – 0.65** | **High** — 60 to 80% of the differential |

**Why the difference is so large.** A venturimeter has a **gradual convergent cone** (about 20°) and a much gentler **divergent cone** (5 to 7°). The flow follows the boundary without separating, so most of the pressure drop is **recovered** downstream.

An orifice meter is a flat plate with a hole. The jet **separates** at the sharp edge, contracts to a **vena contracta**, and then expands abruptly into turbulent eddies — exactly the sudden-enlargement situation whose loss is (V₁ − V₂)²/2g. Most of the differential is destroyed.

The low C_d of the orifice is chiefly a **contraction** effect rather than friction, since C_d = C_v × C_c with C_v ≈ 0.97 but C_c only ≈ 0.62.

**The discharge relation is common to both:**

> **Q = C_d · A₁A₂√(2gh)/√(A₁² − A₂²)**

where h is the differential head read from a manometer.

**The trade-off that decides which to use** — and the reason the orifice survives despite its poor performance:

| | Venturimeter | Orifice meter |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy and C_d | **Better** | Poorer |
| Head loss | **Low** — matters for permanent installations | High |
| **Cost and length** | **High**; needs a long straight run | **Cheap and compact** |
| Maintenance | Harder to clean | Plate easily replaced |

So a venturimeter is chosen where the **energy loss is a running cost** — a large water main or a pumping installation — and an orifice where **first cost and simplicity** dominate.

Note option (d): **C_d can never exceed 1**, since it is the ratio of actual to theoretical discharge, and real flow always loses something. Any computed C_d above unity means an arithmetic or measurement error — a useful sanity check in the laboratory.

The divergent cone's shallow angle (5–7°) is the same principle as a turbine's **draft tube**: expand gradually and you recover pressure; expand abruptly and you make eddies.

The gradual taper reduces the loss.

examTip.trick: The venturi's **long gentle diffuser** decelerates the flow **without separating**, so most of the pressure is recovered. An orifice plate's jet expands abruptly and dissipates the energy in eddies.
examTip.mnemonic: **Venturi: C_d 0.98, permanent loss only ~10%, but bulky and costly. Orifice: C_d 0.62, permanent loss 50–70%, but cheap and fits between flanges.** Choose by whether **head or capital** is the scarcer commodity. The orifice's operational weakness: its **sharp edge WEARS**, and the meter then reads high with no obvious symptom.

questions.stem: Two pipes are connected in parallel between the same two points. For the two pipes:
options: The discharges are equal and the head losses add
The head losses are equal and the discharges are equal
Both the discharges and the head losses add
The head losses are equal and the discharges add
questions.solution:
**The head losses are equal and the discharges add.**

The two arrangements are exact opposites, and the reasoning is the same as for electrical circuits:

| Arrangement | Discharge | Head loss |
|---|---|---|
| **Series** | **Same** in each pipe (continuity) | **Adds**: h_f = h_f1 + h_f2 |
| **Parallel** | **Adds**: Q = Q₁ + Q₂ | **Same** in each pipe |

**Why the head losses must be equal in parallel.** Both pipes join the **same two junctions**, so both experience the same difference in piezometric head between those points. Head loss is a property of the endpoints, not of the route — so however the flow divides, each branch loses the same head.

That single fact is what lets a parallel network be solved:

> **h_f1 = h_f2**, so **f₁L₁Q₁²/(12.1 D₁⁵) = f₂L₂Q₂²/(12.1 D₂⁵)**

giving the ratio in which the total discharge divides. The flow naturally takes the path of least resistance — the shorter, larger, smoother pipe carries proportionally more.

**The Darcy–Weisbach relation** behind it:

> h_f = fLV²/(2gD) = **fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵)**

The **D⁵** is the striking term: head loss varies inversely with the **fifth power** of diameter. Doubling a pipe's diameter cuts its head loss by a factor of 32 for the same discharge — which is why a modest increase in diameter is such an effective remedy for an inadequate main, and why the **economic diameter** calculation balances pipe cost against a lifetime of pumping energy.

**Why parallel pipes are used in practice:**
- **Increase capacity** without replacing an existing main — lay a second pipe alongside it.
- **Reliability**: one branch can be isolated for repair while supply continues.

That second reason is precisely the argument for a **grid iron** distribution layout over a dead-end tree: water reaches any point by more than one route, so a burst does not cut off everything downstream. The cost is that the flow distribution becomes **indeterminate**, requiring iterative solution by the **Hardy Cross** method — balancing heads around each loop until the corrections vanish.

An **equivalent pipe** is the single pipe of stated diameter that would carry the same discharge with the same total head loss as the actual system, and it is the standard way to simplify a series–parallel network before analysis.

examTip.trick: Both pipes join the **same two points**, and each point has a single value of head — so the head loss must be identical for either route, while the discharges add to the total.
examTip.mnemonic: **Series: same Q, ADD the losses. Parallel: same loss, ADD the discharges.** Exactly like resistors — except hydraulic resistance is **non-linear (h ∝ Q²)**, which is why networks need iteration. And **Q ∝ D^2.5**, so a half-diameter parallel pipe adds only about **18%** capacity.

questions.stem: The hydraulic gradient line of a pipeline falling below the pipe axis indicates that:
options: The pressure in the pipe is below atmospheric
The pipe friction has become negligible
questions.solution:
**The pressure in the pipe is below atmospheric.**

The HGL plots the **piezometric head**, z + p/γ. Its height above any point of the pipe is therefore the **pressure head** at that point:

> HGL **above** the pipe axis → p/γ positive → **pressure above atmospheric**
> HGL **below** the pipe axis → p/γ **negative** → **sub-atmospheric (partial vacuum)**

So the position of the HGL relative to the pipe is a direct reading of the pressure, which is exactly why the two are plotted on the same diagram.

**Why negative pressure is dangerous** — four distinct problems, all serious:

| Problem | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Cavitation** | If the pressure reaches the **vapour pressure**, water boils; the bubbles collapse downstream and pit the pipe |
| **Air release** | Dissolved air comes out of solution and collects at summits, throttling the flow |
| **Contamination** | A leaking joint under vacuum **draws in** groundwater and pollutants — a public-health failure in a water main |
| **Collapse** | A thin-walled pipe in external compression can **buckle inward** |

That third row is the reason codes are strict about it: a pressurised main leaks outward and merely wastes water, but a main under vacuum leaks *inward* and can contaminate the supply.

**Where it arises, and the remedies:**

| Situation | Remedy |
|---|---|
| A **summit** in the pipeline, especially a long siphon | Keep the summit below the HGL; provide **air valves** |
| Rapid **valve closure** — water hammer | Surge tank, slow-closing valve, relief valve |
| Pump suction lift too great | Reduce the static suction lift; check **NPSH** |
| Draining a pipeline | **Air inlet valves** at high points |

The practical rule for a siphon or an inverted-siphon summit: the **absolute** pressure must stay above the vapour pressure, which in practice limits the height of a summit above the hydraulic grade line to roughly **7 m** of water rather than the theoretical 10.3 m.

Why the other options are wrong: **supercritical flow** (a) is an open-channel concept requiring a free surface, which a pressurised pipe does not have; discharge (b) affects the *slope* of the HGL, not whether it lies above or below the axis; and negligible friction (d) would make the HGL nearly **horizontal**, not low.

Recall the companion relation: the **EGL always lies above the HGL by the velocity head**, and the EGL always **falls** in the direction of flow — its slope being the energy slope h_f/L.

examTip.trick: The HGL plots **p/γ + z**. If it lies below the pipe centreline elevation z, then p/γ must be negative.
examTip.mnemonic: **The serious risk is CONTAMINATION** — a main at negative pressure passing through polluted ground **draws it IN** through any joint. A positive pressure leaks harmlessly outward; a negative one imports pathogens. Hence the code requirement for a **minimum positive residual head** everywhere, at all times.

questions.stem: A hydraulic jump can occur only when the upstream flow is:
questions.solution:
**Supercritical**, that is with **Fr₁ > 1**.

A hydraulic jump is the abrupt transition from **supercritical to subcritical** flow — shallow and fast becoming deep and slow, with a turbulent roller at the front and a substantial loss of energy.

The direction is fixed by the second law: a jump **dissipates** energy, so it can only proceed from the high-energy-per-unit-mass state to the lower one. A "reverse jump" from subcritical to supercritical would have to *create* energy, so it cannot occur — the transition in that direction happens smoothly instead, through a drawdown.

**The governing relation**, obtained from **momentum** (not energy, because the loss is unknown in advance):

> **y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1)**

with the energy loss computed **afterwards**:

> **E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂)**

The two depths y₁ and y₂ are called **sequent** (or conjugate) depths — equal **momentum**, not equal energy. They must not be confused with **alternate** depths, which have equal **specific energy** and lie on the two limbs of the specific-energy curve.

**Classification by upstream Froude number:**

| Fr₁ | Type | Energy loss |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 – 1.7 | Undular | Negligible |
| 1.7 – 2.5 | Weak | 5 – 15% |
| 2.5 – 4.5 | Oscillating | 15 – 45% |
| **4.5 – 9.0** | **Steady** | **45 – 70%** |
| > 9.0 | Strong | 70 – 85% |

The **steady** range is the one designers aim for: it dissipates a large fraction of the energy in a stable, predictable position. The **oscillating** range is avoided because the jump wanders and generates waves that travel downstream and attack the banks.

**Where it is used deliberately.** The jump is the standard means of destroying the energy of water leaving a spillway, a canal fall or a sluice gate, so that it enters the downstream channel without scouring it. The **stilling basin** is simply a paved apron long enough to contain the jump — its length taken as **5 to 7 times the jump height**, since the length cannot be derived from momentum theory and comes from experiment.

The critical design requirement is that the **tail water depth must match the required y₂**. Too little and the jump sweeps out of the basin, sending a high-velocity jet along the river bed; too much and it drowns, losing its dissipating action. That comparison is what selects the energy dissipater — a **stilling basin** where tail water matches, a **ski jump** where it is deficient, and a **roller bucket** where it is excessive.

examTip.trick: A jump **dissipates** energy, which is thermodynamically permitted. The reverse would have to **create** energy, which is not — so supercritical → subcritical must be a jump, while the downward transition happens smoothly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use MOMENTUM across a jump, not energy** — the loss is large and unknown, but the external forces are small. **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1].** Design in the **steady range Fr 4.5–9** and avoid the **oscillating range 2.5–4.5**, which throws waves far downstream.

questions.stem: In a hydrograph, the portion representing groundwater contribution to the stream is called:
questions.solution:
**Base flow.**

A stream hydrograph — discharge plotted against time — is made up of two contributions:

| Component | Source | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct runoff** | Rainfall reaching the channel over and through the surface | **Fast**, produces the peak |
| **Base flow** | **Groundwater** draining slowly into the channel | **Slow**, sustains flow between storms |

Base flow is what keeps a perennial river running in the dry season, long after the rain has stopped. Its recession is gradual and roughly exponential.

**The parts of the hydrograph**, which the other options name:

| Part | Description |
|---|---|
| **Rising limb** (concentration curve) | Discharge rising as more of the catchment begins contributing |
| **Crest segment** | Around the peak — the maximum discharge |
| **Recession limb** (falling limb) | Withdrawal of water from storage after rainfall ceases |

So options (c) and (d) are **shapes** on the curve, not sources of water.

**Why base flow separation matters.** **Unit hydrograph** theory applies only to **direct runoff**, so the base flow must be stripped out before a unit hydrograph is derived, and added back when a flood is synthesised. The standard separation methods are the **straight-line**, **fixed-base** and **variable-slope** methods — all somewhat arbitrary, which is a recognised weakness of the technique.

Recall the definition that depends on it: a **unit hydrograph** is the **direct runoff** hydrograph from **1 cm of effective rainfall** falling uniformly over the catchment in a specified duration. And its standard check is that the **area under it equals 1 cm of runoff over the catchment area** — a check that fails if the base flow separation was wrong.

**The time characteristics**, examined alongside:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Time of concentration** | Time for runoff to travel from the remotest point to the outlet |
| **Basin lag** | Time from the centroid of rainfall to the peak discharge |
| Time base | Total duration of direct runoff |

Catchment shape controls these strongly: a **fan-shaped** basin delivers runoff from all parts simultaneously and gives a **sharp, high peak**, while a **fern-shaped** basin staggers the arrivals and produces a flatter, drawn-out hydrograph of the same volume.

examTip.trick: Split streamflow by **speed of arrival**: **overland flow** (hours), **interflow** (intermediate), **base flow** (weeks to months, from groundwater). Direct runoff is the first two.
examTip.mnemonic: **Base flow is what keeps a perennial river alive between storms.** Its separation from direct runoff has **no uniquely correct method** — what matters is using the **same** method to derive a unit hydrograph and to apply it. **N = 0.83 A^0.2 days** after the peak is the usual convention for where direct runoff ends.

questions.stem: In a simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load over its whole span, the maximum bending moment occurs:
options: At mid-span, where the shear force changes sign
questions.solution:
**At mid-span, where the shear force changes sign.**

The reasoning matters more than the answer. Because

> **dM/dx = V**
