the bending moment is stationary — a maximum or minimum — exactly where the **shear force is zero**. For a symmetric UDL the shear varies linearly from +wL/2 at one support to −wL/2 at the other, crossing zero at the **centre**. Hence the maximum moment is at mid-span:

> **M_max = wL²/8**

That relation, **maximum moment where shear changes sign**, is the general tool. It locates the maximum for *any* loading, which is far more useful than memorising individual cases.

The standard results for this beam:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Reactions | wL/2 each |
| **Shear force** | **±wL/2 at supports, zero at centre** — linear |
| **Bending moment** | **wL²/8 at centre, zero at supports** — parabolic |
| Maximum deflection | 5wL⁴/384EI at centre |

Note the shapes: a UDL gives a **linear** shear diagram and a **parabolic** moment diagram, one integration apart. A point load gives a **step** in shear and a **kink** in moment; an applied **couple** gives no change in shear and a **step** in moment.

Why the other options fail: at the **supports** of a simply supported beam the moment is **zero** by definition (a pin cannot carry moment) — that is where **shear** is maximum, which is the common confusion. And a **constant** moment along the span (d) requires zero shear everywhere, the pure-bending condition, which a UDL cannot produce.

**A caution for moving loads.** This mid-span answer holds for a **fixed** UDL covering the span. For a **train of wheel loads** crossing a bridge girder the maximum moment always occurs **under one of the wheels**, never necessarily at mid-span — because the moment diagram is then piecewise linear and can only peak at a break point. That is a different problem, solved with **influence lines**.

The companion relation, dV/dx = −w, completes the set: load intensity is the negative slope of the shear diagram, so the three curves are successive integrals of one another.

examTip.trick: **V = dM/dx**, so the moment is stationary where the shear is zero — and a genuine maximum where the shear also **changes sign**, which for a symmetric UDL is at midspan.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear peaks at the SUPPORTS, moment at MIDSPAN.** They peak at different sections, which is the whole basis of efficient detailing: **stirrups close together near the supports, main bars fully provided at midspan.** The values: **V = wL/2, M = wL²/8.**

questions.stem: For an overhanging beam, the point of contraflexure is the section at which:
options: The slope of the beam is zero
questions.solution:
**The bending moment changes sign.**

At a point of contraflexure the curvature of the beam reverses — **sagging becomes hogging** or vice versa — so the bending moment passes through **zero while changing sign**. The name states it: *contra-flexure*, opposite bending.

The conditions that are constantly confused, and every one appears among the options:

| Condition | Locates |
|---|---|
| **BM = 0 and changes sign** | **Point of contraflexure** |
| **SF = 0 (changes sign)** | Point of **maximum bending moment** |
| **Slope dy/dx = 0** | Point of **maximum deflection** |
| SF maximum | Usually at a support |

Option (a) is the classic trap: since S = dM/dx, zero **shear** marks where the moment diagram is flat — a **maximum**, not a zero crossing.

**Where points of contraflexure occur.** Only in beams that carry **both** sagging and hogging moments:

| Beam | Points of contraflexure |
|---|---|
| **Overhanging** | **Yes** — hogging over the support, sagging in the span |
| **Continuous** | Yes — hogging at supports, sagging at mid-span |
| **Fixed** | Yes — two, at 0.211L from each end under UDL |
| **Simply supported** with downward load | **None** — sags throughout |
| Cantilever | None — hogs throughout |

**Why it matters practically**, which is the reason the concept is taught rather than merely defined:

- The moment is **zero** there, so it is the natural place to **curtail reinforcement**, to locate a **splice or lap**, or to place a **construction joint**.
- In a continuous beam it marks where the **main steel must migrate** from the top face to the bottom — top steel over the supports where the beam hogs, bottom steel at mid-span where it sags. Getting that crossover wrong leaves the beam with no tensile capacity where it needs it.
- In approximate frame analysis, a **hinge may be assumed** at a point of contraflexure, which is the basis of the portal and cantilever methods.

For a fixed beam under UDL the points sit at **0.211L** from each support, dividing the span into a hogging region at each end and a sagging region in the middle — the pattern that dictates where the top and bottom bars run.

examTip.trap: "Bending moment is zero" alone is not enough — the moment is zero at both ends of every simply supported beam, and those are not contraflexure points. It must **change sign**.
examTip.trick: At contraflexure the beam switches from sagging to hogging, so the **tension face swaps** from bottom to top.
examTip.mnemonic: **It locates where reinforcement can be curtailed — and it MOVES with the load pattern**, so curtail on the **envelope** of all load cases, never on one analysis. It is also the basis of **effective length**: between two contraflexure points a member behaves as a pin-ended strut.

questions.stem: A steel bar is held rigidly between two fixed supports and its temperature is raised. The bar develops:
questions.solution:
**Compressive stress.**

Heating makes the bar want to **expand**. The rigid supports prevent it, so the restraint pushes back — putting the bar into **compression**.

The magnitude follows from the strain that was prevented:

> Free thermal strain: ε = **αΔT**
> Prevented entirely, so the stress is **σ = E α ΔT**

Note what the expression does **not** contain: the **length**. A bar 1 m long and one 100 m long develop exactly the same thermal stress for the same temperature rise, because the strain — not the extension — is what is resisted.

**A worked feel for the magnitude.** For steel, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C and E = 200 GPa. A rise of just 20°C gives

> σ = 200,000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 20 = **48 N/mm²**

nearly a fifth of the yield stress of mild steel, from a very modest temperature change. That is why thermal effects cannot be dismissed.

**Partial restraint** is the general case. If the supports yield by an amount δ:

> σ = E(αΔT·L − δ)/L

so any accommodation of movement reduces the stress proportionally — which is precisely how thermal stress is designed out.

**How structures avoid it:**

| Provision | Where |
|---|---|
| **Expansion joints** | Buildings — IS 456 requires them at about **45 m** spacing |
| **Expansion bearings, roller supports** | Bridges — one end fixed, the other free to slide |
| **Expansion loops and joints** | Pipelines, penstocks |
| **Expansion joints in rigid pavements** | Concrete roads, 50 to 140 m apart |
| Rail expansion gaps | Track |

**The key structural insight.** Thermal stress arises only from **restraint**. A **determinate** structure is free to expand and develops **no** thermal stress at all; only **indeterminate** structures do. That is the hidden cost of continuity: an indeterminate frame is stiffer, safer and more redundant, but it develops stresses from **temperature change, shrinkage and support settlement** that a determinate structure simply accommodates by moving.

The same logic explains why a **three-hinged arch** is insensitive to temperature and settlement while a **two-hinged or fixed arch** develops secondary stresses from both.

Cooling, of course, reverses the sign — a restrained bar in falling temperature goes into **tension**, which is what cracks concrete slabs and is why shrinkage and temperature reinforcement is provided.

examTip.trick: Heating makes the bar want to **expand**; the fixed supports prevent it, so the bar is **compressed**: **σ = αΔT·E**.
examTip.mnemonic: **FREE expansion causes no stress; RESTRAINT causes stress — and the LENGTH does not appear in the formula.** A 1 km restrained rail develops exactly the same stress as a 1 m bar. For steel, a 30 °C rise gives **72 MPa** — a substantial fraction of yield, so thermal stress is not a minor effect.

questions.stem: On the Mohr circle for a two-dimensional state of stress, the radius of the circle represents:
options: The sum of the principal stresses
questions.solution:
**The maximum shear stress.**

On the Mohr circle, normal stress is plotted horizontally and shear stress vertically. So:

| Feature of the circle | Represents |
|---|---|
| **Radius** | **τ_max = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2** |
| **Centre** | **Average normal stress, (σ₁ + σ₂)/2** |
| **Rightmost point** | σ₁ — **major** principal stress, with τ = 0 |
| **Leftmost point** | σ₂ — minor principal stress, with τ = 0 |
| **Top and bottom** | Planes of **maximum shear** |

So option (b) is the **centre**, not the radius, and (c) is the rightmost **point**.

Algebraically:

> σ₁, σ₂ = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 **±** √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²]

where the first term is the centre and the square root is the **radius** — so the radius is literally what is added and subtracted to reach the principal stresses.

**Two geometric facts that follow, and are examined:**

1. **Principal planes carry no shear.** They are the points where the circle crosses the horizontal axis, and the normal stress there is stationary — maximum or minimum. "Shear zero" and "normal stress extreme" are the same statement.
2. **Planes of maximum shear lie at 45° to the principal planes.** Angles on the Mohr circle are **double** the physical angles, and the top of the circle is 90° round from the rightmost point — hence 45° in the material.

On those maximum-shear planes the normal stress is **not** zero; it equals the average, (σ₁ + σ₂)/2 — the centre.

**Where this shows up in practice:**

| Material | Fails on | Because |
|---|---|---|
| **Ductile** (mild steel) | The **45° plane of maximum shear** | Weak in shear — hence the **cup-and-cone** fracture |
| **Brittle** (cast iron, concrete) | The **principal plane** | Weak in tension — breaks square across the bar |

Same load, two different failure planes, decided by which stress the material cannot resist.

**A caution for soils.** The failure plane in soil is **not** the plane of maximum shear but at **45° + φ/2**, because the Mohr–Coulomb envelope slopes upward at φ and touches the circle before its top. Normal stress helps resist sliding, so failure occurs where the *ratio* of shear to normal stress is critical. The two coincide only when φ = 0, as in an undrained clay.

examTip.trick: The circle's centre is at **(σ₁ + σ₂)/2** and its radius is **(σ₁ − σ₂)/2**, which is precisely **τ_max**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Centre = mean stress, RADIUS = maximum shear.** The maximum-shear points are the **top and bottom** of the circle — 90° from the principal points on the circle, hence **45° in reality**. That 45° is why a **ductile** tensile specimen fails on a cone and a **brittle** one fails square across.

questions.stem: For no tension to develop at the base of a short masonry column of rectangular section under an eccentric axial load, the eccentricity must not exceed:
questions.solution:
**d/6** — the **middle-third rule**.

Under an eccentric axial load the extreme-fibre stresses are the sum of direct and bending stress:

> **σ = P/A ± Pe/Z**

with Z = bd²/6 for a rectangle, so

> σ = (P/bd)(1 ± 6e/d)

No tension requires the smaller stress to remain compressive:

> 1 − 6e/d ≥ 0
> **e ≤ d/6** ✓

Since the load may be eccentric either side of the centre, the permissible zone spans from d/6 left to d/6 right — a band of **d/3** centred on the axis. Hence the resultant must fall **within the middle third** of the base, which is where the rule gets its name. Option (b), d/3, is that band's total width — the trap.

**Why tension must be avoided.** Masonry, plain concrete and soil have negligible tensile strength. Once tension is implied at an edge:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| The joint **opens** | Contact area reduces, so the real compressive stress is higher than calculated |
| Water enters the crack | In a dam, this **raises the uplift pressure**, worsening stability |
| Progressive failure | The crack extends, further reducing the contact area |

**Where the rule governs:**

| Structure | Application |
|---|---|
| **Gravity dam** | Resultant within the middle third → no tension at the **heel** |
| **Retaining wall** | No tension at the heel; also checked for overturning and sliding |
| **Masonry column, chimney** | Eccentric load within d/6 |
| **Footing on soil** | Resultant within the middle third → **whole base in contact**, pressure everywhere compressive |

That last case is the everyday one: if the resultant on a footing falls outside the middle third, part of the base **lifts off** the soil and the pressure distribution becomes triangular over a reduced width, with a much higher peak than the elastic formula predicts.

**Note the code allowance for masonry**, which softens the rule in practice: IS 1905 permits the **permissible stress to be increased by 25%** where the eccentricity ratio e/t exceeds 1/24, recognising that masonry yields locally and redistributes stress, so the calculated elastic peak is conservative.

For a **circular** section the corresponding limit is e ≤ d/8, since Z = πd³/32 and A = πd²/4.

examTip.trick: The **middle third rule**: for no tension anywhere on the base, the resultant must fall within the middle third, so **e ≤ d/6** for a rectangular section.
examTip.mnemonic: **e ≤ d/6 keeps the WHOLE section in compression** (p = P/A(1 ± 6e/d), and at e = d/6 the stress just reaches zero at one edge). Beyond it, **part of the base LIFTS OFF**, the contact area shrinks, the resultant moves further toward the edge — and the process is **progressive**, which is why the limit is enforced rather than advised.

questions.stem: In the theory of simple bending, one of the assumptions is that:
options: The material has different moduli in tension and compression
Plane sections become curved after bending
Plane sections remain plane after bending
questions.solution:
**Plane sections remain plane after bending.**

This is the central assumption, and everything in simple bending theory follows from it. If a section stays flat as the beam curves, the strain at any fibre must be proportional to its distance from the neutral axis:

> ε = y/R

and for a linearly elastic material σ = Eε = Ey/R — a **linear** stress distribution. Combining with moment equilibrium gives the flexure formula:

> **M/I = σ/y = E/R**

So "plane sections remain plane" is what makes the stress distribution linear, and hence what makes the whole theory work.

The full set of assumptions:

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **Plane sections remain plane** | The key kinematic assumption |
| Material is **homogeneous and isotropic** | — |
| Material is **linearly elastic**, obeying Hooke's law | Needed for σ ∝ ε |
| **E is the same in tension and compression** | Option (a) contradicts this |
| Beam is **initially straight**, of constant cross-section | Option (b) contradicts this |
| Load acts in a **plane of symmetry** | No twisting |
| Radius of curvature is large compared with the depth | Small deflections |

So options (a), (b) and (c) each contradict one of these directly.

**Where the assumptions break down**, which is the useful part:

| Case | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Curved beam** (crane hook, chain link) | Sections still plane, but stress becomes **hyperbolic**; the neutral axis shifts towards the centre of curvature |
| Beyond the elastic limit | Stress block flattens; fully **plastic** at M_p |
| **Deep beam** | Shear deformation matters; plane sections **do not** remain plane |
| **RCC section** | E differs between steel and concrete; handled by the transformed-section or limit-state method |

Note that the plane-sections assumption **survives** into plastic analysis and into RCC design — it is what lets the strain diagram stay linear even when the stress diagram is not. IS 456's limit-state method assumes exactly this: a linear strain distribution with concrete reaching 0.0035 at the extreme fibre, while the *stress* follows a parabolic-rectangular block.

That is why the assumption is so durable: it is a statement about **geometry**, not about material behaviour, so it holds long after Hooke's law has been abandoned.

examTip.trick: "Plane sections remain plane" is the **kinematic** assumption from which everything else follows — it is what makes the **strain vary linearly** with distance from the neutral axis, and hence the stress too.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plane sections → linear strain → (with Hooke) linear stress → σ = My/I.** The other assumptions: the material is homogeneous, isotropic and elastic; E is the same in tension and compression; the beam is initially straight and of constant section; and the loads are in a plane of symmetry.

questions.stem: Maxwell's reciprocal theorem states that in a linearly elastic structure:
options: The deflection at A due to a unit load at B equals the deflection at B due to a unit load at A
The strain energy equals the external work done
The deflection is proportional to the applied load
The sum of the internal and external work is zero
questions.solution:
**The deflection at A due to a unit load at B equals the deflection at B due to a unit load at A.**

Written as flexibility coefficients:

> **δ_AB = δ_BA**, or more generally **f_ij = f_ji**

where f_ij is the displacement at i caused by a unit load at j. The theorem holds for any **linearly elastic** structure obeying superposition, and it applies to rotations caused by moments as well as to deflections caused by forces.

The other options are all real principles, but different ones:

| Statement | Principle |
|---|---|
| **δ_AB = δ_BA** | **Maxwell's reciprocal theorem** |
| Strain energy = external work | **Conservation of energy** (the basis of Castigliano) |
| Deflection ∝ load | **Hooke's law / linearity** — the *precondition* for Maxwell |
| Total virtual work = 0 | **Principle of virtual work** |

**Why it is genuinely useful**, and not merely elegant:

1. **It halves the work.** Building an influence line or a flexibility matrix requires only the coefficients on and above the diagonal; the rest follow by symmetry.
2. **It makes the flexibility and stiffness matrices symmetric**, which is a property every structural-analysis program relies on for storage and for solution efficiency. The symmetry of **[K]** in the stiffness method is Maxwell's theorem in matrix form.
3. **It gives influence lines by a single loading.** Applying one unit load and reading the deflected shape yields the influence line for deflection at that point — which is the idea generalised in **Muller-Breslau's principle**, where releasing a restraint and imposing a unit displacement traces the influence line for the corresponding force.

That third use is the practically important one: it converts the tedious business of moving a load step by step across a span into a single calculation of a deflected shape.

**Betti's law** is the generalisation: for two independent load systems P and Q on the same structure, the work done by P through the displacements caused by Q equals the work done by Q through the displacements caused by P. Maxwell's theorem is the special case where each system is a single unit load.

**The limitation** to keep in mind: linear elastic behaviour and small displacements are essential. The theorem fails once a member yields, or where the geometry changes enough for superposition to break down.

examTip.trick: **Maxwell's reciprocal theorem** — a direct consequence of the symmetry of the flexibility (and stiffness) matrix for any **linear elastic** structure.
examTip.mnemonic: **It halves the work in influence line and flexibility calculations** — compute one coefficient and you have its mirror free. It is also the theoretical foundation of **MÜLLER-BRESLAU'S principle**: the influence line for a quantity has the shape of the deflected form when the corresponding restraint is released.

questions.stem: The strain energy stored in a bar of length L and cross-sectional area A carrying an axial load P is:
questions.solution:
**P²L/(2AE).**

The load builds up from zero to P as the bar extends, so the work done — and hence the stored strain energy — is **half** the product of the final load and the final extension:

> Extension δ = **PL/AE**
> **U = ½ P δ = ½ P × PL/AE = P²L/(2AE)** ✓

The factor of ½ is the whole point, and it is what option (c) omits.

**Two checks that eliminate the wrong options at once:**

1. **Energy must be quadratic in P.** Doubling the load quadruples the energy, because both the force and the distance it acts through double. Any option linear in P — (a) and (d) — cannot be an energy.
2. **Dimensions.** P²L/(AE) has units N²·m/(m²·N/m²) = N·m ✓, a work. Option (a), PL/AE, is a **length** — it is the extension δ, not the energy.

So option (a) is the deflection, offered as a trap.

**The strain energy expressions for the four modes of loading**, worth holding as one set:

| Mode | Strain energy |
|---|---|
| **Axial** | **P²L/(2AE)** |
| **Bending** | ∫M²dx/(2EI) |
| **Torsion** | T²L/(2GJ) |
| **Shear** | ∫V²dx/(2AG) × form factor |

Each has the same shape: (action)² × length ÷ (2 × rigidity). Recognising that pattern makes them reconstructible rather than memorised — and the shear term is usually negligible for slender members.

**Where it leads.** Strain energy is the basis of the energy methods:

> **Castigliano's second theorem:** δ = ∂U/∂P — differentiate the strain energy with respect to a load to get the deflection at that load, in its direction.

Applied to the bar above: ∂U/∂P = 2P L/(2AE) = **PL/AE** = δ ✓, which is a satisfying internal consistency check.

The **limitation** of that theorem is worth recalling: it gives the deflection only **at, and along, an applied load**. To find a displacement elsewhere, a fictitious load must be introduced there and set to zero afterwards — which is the idea formalised in the **unit load (virtual work)** method, the general tool.

For a simply supported beam with a central point load, the same ½Wδ reasoning gives U = W²L³/(96EI), since δ = WL³/48EI.

examTip.trick: **U = ½Pδ = ½P(PL/AE) = P²L/(2AE).** The **½** is because the load builds up **gradually** — the work is the triangular area under the load–extension curve.
examTip.mnemonic: **A SUDDENLY applied load does work Pδ, not ½Pδ — so it produces DOUBLE the stress and double the deflection.** The bar overshoots to twice the static deflection, then oscillates back. Counter-intuitive corollary: under impact, a **more flexible** member is better.

questions.stem: A plane truss with m members, j joints and r support reactions is statically determinate when:
questions.solution:
**m + r = 2j.**

At each joint of a **plane** truss the member forces are concurrent, so only **two** equilibrium equations are available — ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0. With j joints that gives **2j** equations, against **m + r** unknowns (the member forces plus the reactions). Determinacy requires the two to match:

> **m + r = 2j** → **determinate**
> m + r > 2j → **indeterminate**, by (m + r − 2j) degrees
> m + r < 2j → **unstable** (a mechanism)

Option (a), m + r = 3j, is the **rigid frame** condition, where each joint transmits moment and so provides three equations. Keeping the two apart is the point of the question:

| Structure | Equations per joint | Determinacy condition |
|---|---|---|
| **Plane truss** | **2** | **m + r = 2j** |
| **Plane rigid frame** | **3** | m + r = 3j |
| Space truss | 3 | m + r = 3j |

**A worked check.** A simply supported triangular truss with m = 3, j = 3, r = 3: m + r = 6 = 2j ✓ determinate — as the simplest rigid truss must be.

**A caution the formula cannot catch.** Satisfying m + r = 2j is **necessary but not sufficient**. A truss can meet the count and still be unstable if the members are badly arranged — for instance four members forming a parallelogram, which is a mechanism however the numbers add up, or a truss whose reactions are **concurrent or parallel** so they cannot resist a general load. That is **geometric** instability, and it must be checked by inspection.

**The assumptions behind truss analysis**, which the counting presupposes: **pin joints**, **loads applied only at joints**, and **straight members** — so every member carries pure axial force with no bending. Real trusses have bolted or welded joints that transmit some moment, but the resulting **secondary stresses** are small and normally neglected, provided loads really are brought to the panel points. That is why purlins are placed at joints rather than mid-panel.

Once determinacy is established, the analysis follows: the **method of joints** (two equations, so start where at most **two** members are unknown) for all member forces, or the **method of sections** (three equations, cutting at most **three** members) for a few specific ones. Spotting **zero-force members** first shortens the work considerably.

examTip.trick: **m + r = 2j** for determinacy: each pin joint gives **two** equations (ΣH, ΣV), and each member has one unknown (its axial force).
examTip.mnemonic: **TRUSS m + r − 2j (pins carry no moment); FRAME 3m + r − 3j (rigid joints do).** Critical caveat: **the count checks DEGREE, not STABILITY.** Three parallel or three concurrent reactions, or an unbraced rectangular panel, give a valid count and an unstable structure — always look at the geometry too.

questions.stem: In the moment distribution method, the distribution factor for a member at a joint is the ratio of:
options: Its length to the total length of members at that joint
Its moment of inertia to the total moment of inertia at that joint
Its stiffness to the sum of the stiffnesses of all members at that joint
Its fixed end moment to the total fixed end moment at that joint
questions.solution:
**Its stiffness to the sum of the stiffnesses of all members meeting at that joint.**

> **DF = k / Σk**

where the member stiffness depends on how its **far** end is held:

| Far end | Stiffness k |
|---|---|
| **Fixed** | **4EI/L** |
| **Hinged (pinned)** | **3EI/L** |

The distribution factors at any joint necessarily **sum to 1**, which is the standard arithmetic check. At a **fixed support** DF = 0 (it absorbs any moment without rotating) and at a **hinged end** DF = 1.

**Why stiffness and not length or I alone.** When a joint rotates, all the members meeting there rotate together by the same amount. The moment each one attracts is proportional to how much moment it takes to rotate *it* through that angle — its stiffness. Since k = 4EI/L, both I **and** L matter, and so does the far-end condition. Options (a) and (b) each capture only part of k, which is why they fail: a long stiff member and a short flexible one can have the same k.

**The method in outline:**

1. Compute **fixed end moments** for every member, assuming all joints locked.
2. Compute **distribution factors** at each joint.
3. **Release** a joint: the unbalanced moment is distributed among its members in proportion to their DFs, with the sign reversed.
4. **Carry over half** of each distributed moment to the far end — the **carry-over factor is ½** for a member fixed at the far end, and **zero** for one pinned there.
5. Repeat until the unbalanced moments are negligible.

The **modified stiffness of 3EI/L** for a member pinned at its far end is the standard shortcut: it avoids carrying moments over to a support that cannot resist them.

**The standard fixed end moments**, needed at step 1:

| Loading (fixed–fixed) | FEM |
|---|---|
| UDL w over span L | **wL²/12** |
| Central point load W | **WL/8** |
| Point load at distance a, b | Wab²/L², Wa²b/L² |

with **wL²/8** and **3WL/16** for the corresponding propped (far end pinned) cases.

**Why the method matters.** Moment distribution is an **iterative** hand method that solves indeterminate frames and continuous beams without setting up and inverting simultaneous equations — which is why it dominated design offices before computers. It remains the best way to develop a feel for how moments actually redistribute around a frame, and its two coefficients, **4EI/L and ½**, are the same ones that appear in the slope-deflection equation and in the stiffness matrix.

examTip.trick: **Distribution factor = member stiffness ÷ sum of stiffnesses at the joint**, so the factors at any joint sum to **1** — a useful arithmetic check at every step.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stiffness 4EI/L (far end FIXED) or 3EI/L (far end HINGED); carry-over factor ½ (fixed) or ZERO (hinged).** Those four numbers are the whole of moment distribution: **distribute in proportion to stiffness, carry over half, repeat.** It is the clearest expression of the principle that **load flows toward stiffness.**

questions.stem: The characteristic load in limit state design is defined as the load which:
options: Is certain never to be exceeded during the design life
Equals the average of all recorded loads
Has a 95% probability of not being exceeded during the design life
Equals the design load divided by the partial safety factor
questions.solution:
**The load with a 95% probability of not being exceeded** during the life of the structure.

Loads, like material strengths, are variable — so limit state design defines them **statistically** rather than as fixed values. The characteristic load is the **95th percentile** of the load distribution, mirroring the definition of characteristic **strength** as the **5th percentile**:

| Quantity | Percentile | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| **Characteristic load** | **95th** — only 5% of cases exceed it | Take the load **high** |
| **Characteristic strength** | **5th** — only 5% of results fall below | Take the strength **low** |

Both choices err in the safe direction, and then partial safety factors are applied **on top**:

> **Design load** = characteristic load × γ_f  (1.5 for DL + LL)
> **Design strength** = characteristic strength ÷ γ_m  (1.5 concrete, 1.15 steel)

So option (d) has the relation inverted — the design load is the characteristic load **multiplied** by γ_f.

**Why not option (a).** No load can be guaranteed never to be exceeded; there is always a finite probability of a larger one. Design accepts a **small, quantified** probability of failure rather than pretending to eliminate it, which is the essential shift from working-stress to limit-state thinking.

**In practice** the codes tabulate characteristic loads rather than requiring the designer to do the statistics: IS 875 Part 1 for **dead** loads (unit weights), Part 2 for **imposed** loads (2 kN/m² residential, 3–4 kN/m² office), Part 3 for **wind** (basic wind speed by zone, 47 m/s and 55 m/s in Nepal), Part 4 for **snow**, and IS 1893 / NBC 105 for **seismic**.

**The two limit states**, and the different factors each uses:

| Limit state | Concerns | Factors |
|---|---|---|
| **Collapse** | Strength, stability, overturning | γ_f = 1.5; γ_m = 1.5 / 1.15 |
| **Serviceability** | **Deflection, cracking, vibration** | All factors **1.0** |

Serviceability uses unfactored values because the question there is how the structure behaves under the loads it will **actually** experience — not whether it will collapse.

And note the exception that catches candidates: where dead load **stabilises** against overturning or uplift, the factor becomes **0.9**, deliberately under-estimating the weight that is doing the resisting.

examTip.trick: Characteristic **load** and characteristic **strength** are defined from opposite tails: the load has a **95% chance of NOT being exceeded** (upper fractile), while the strength is the value **95% of results beat** (lower fractile).
examTip.mnemonic: **Characteristic LOAD: 95% chance of NOT being exceeded. Characteristic STRENGTH: 95% chance of BEING exceeded.** Both are then made safer by **partial factors** — loads multiplied (1.5), strengths divided (1.5 concrete, 1.15 steel). That two-sided treatment is the essence of limit state design.

questions.stem: In seismic design, the base shear of a building is proportional to:
options: The seismic weight of the building
The inverse of the seismic weight
The square of the building height
questions.solution:
**The seismic weight of the building.**

> **V_B = A_h × W**

where W is the **seismic weight** and A_h the design horizontal seismic coefficient:

> **A_h = (Z/2) × (I/R) × (S_a/g)**

Earthquake loading is **inertial** — the ground moves and the building's own mass resists that motion, so the force is F = ma. More mass means proportionally more force, which makes seismic design fundamentally different from gravity design.

**The consequence, and it is the central lesson of the topic:** reducing mass **directly reduces the demand**. In a wind-loaded structure, extra weight is helpful (it resists uplift and overturning). In a seismic one, extra weight is the *load itself*. That is why:

- **light roofing** (CGI sheet rather than heavy tile or mud) is preferred in Nepali hill construction;
- **lightweight partitions** are favoured over solid masonry infill;
- heavy **stone or mud-mortar** construction performs so badly — its mass generates the force that destroys it.

**What counts as seismic weight:** full **dead load** plus a fraction of the **imposed load** — 25% for live loads up to 3 kN/m² and 50% above that. Imposed load on the **roof is not** included, since it is unlikely to be present during an earthquake.

**The other factors, each accounting for something distinct:**

| Factor | Accounts for |
|---|---|
| **Z** | **Seismic hazard** of the zone |
| **I** | **Importance** — hospitals, schools, lifeline structures |
| **S_a/g** | **Structural period** and the **soil type** |
| **R** | **Ductility and energy absorption** of the structural system |

**R** is the one with an obligation attached: claiming a high R (5.0 for a special moment resisting frame, against 3.0 for an ordinary one and 1.5 for unreinforced masonry) is a **promise about detailing** — closely spaced closed stirrups with 135° hooks, strong column–weak beam proportioning, and capacity design for shear. Taking SMRF values without SMRF detailing under-designs the structure by nearly a factor of two, which was a repeated failure in the **2015 Gorkha earthquake**, alongside the **soft storey** created by open ground floors.

Height enters only indirectly, through the **period** T and hence S_a/g — so option (c) is wrong, and the base shear is then **distributed** up the height in proportion to W_i h_i².

examTip.trick: **V_B = A_h W**, where W is the **seismic weight** — the earthquake force is an **inertia** force, so it is proportional to the **mass** being shaken.
examTip.mnemonic: **Earthquake load is proportional to WEIGHT — so a lighter building attracts a smaller force.** That is why lightweight roofing and partitions are a genuine seismic measure, and why heavy overhanging water tanks and masonry infill are a liability. Seismic weight = full dead load + a **fraction** of the imposed load (25–50%).

questions.stem: For a very dry concrete mix of low workability, the most suitable test is the:
questions.solution:
**The Vee-Bee consistometer test.**

The slump test loses sensitivity at low workability — a very dry mix simply does not subside, so several quite different mixes all record a slump of zero and the test cannot distinguish them. The **Vee-Bee** test instead measures the **time in seconds** for a moulded cone of concrete to remould into a cylinder under vibration, which remains discriminating in exactly that range.

Matching the test to the workability:

| Test | Suits | Measures |
|---|---|---|
| **Vee-Bee consistometer** | **Very low to low** | **Time (seconds) to remould under vibration** |
| **Compaction factor** | **Low to medium** | Ratio of partially to fully compacted density |
| **Slump** | **Medium to high** | Subsidence in mm |
| **Flow table** | **High to very high**, flowing concrete | Spread in mm |

So the four tests cover a continuum, and the choice depends on where the mix sits on it. Note that the **compaction factor** test is the other correct answer for stiff mixes and is often paired with Vee-Bee in the same range.

**Typical correspondence:**

| Workability | Slump (mm) | Vee-Bee (s) | Compaction factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Very low | 0 – 25 | **20 – 10** | 0.78 |
| Low | 25 – 50 | 10 – 5 | 0.85 |
| Medium | 50 – 100 | 5 – 2 | 0.92 |
| High | 100 – 150 | < 2 | 0.95 |

Note that the Vee-Bee time runs **opposite** to slump — a **longer** time means a **drier**, less workable mix.

**Why dry mixes are used at all**, given the difficulty of placing them. By **Abrams' law**, strength varies inversely with the water–cement ratio, so a drier mix is stronger and less permeable. The permissible slump therefore **falls as the compaction method improves**:

| Compaction | Slump |
|---|---|
| **Power-driven vibrator** | **< 25 mm** |
| Hand compaction | 25 – 50 mm |
| Mechanical vibrator | 50 mm |

That is the governing principle: **better compaction permits a lower water content, hence higher strength and durability**. A mix too dry for the available plant, however, will be left full of voids — which defeats the purpose entirely. The right resolution is a **plasticiser**, which raises workability at constant w/c, never added water at the mixer.

examTip.trick: For a **very dry** mix the slump reads near zero and is useless — it cannot distinguish between mixes. The **Vee-Bee** test measures the **time to remould** the cone under vibration, which is meaningful at that end of the range.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slump for medium to high workability; COMPACTION FACTOR for low; VEE-BEE for very low.** Match the test to the range, or the number carries no information. And remember: **slump measures the yield stress and says NOTHING about strength** — a high slump from excess water means weaker concrete.

questions.stem: An air-entraining admixture is added to concrete principally to improve its:
questions.solution:
**Resistance to freezing and thawing.**

Air entrainment deliberately introduces **billions of microscopic air bubbles** (10 to 100 μm, typically 4 to 7% by volume) uniformly through the paste. Those voids act as **pressure-relief chambers**: when water in the capillaries freezes and expands by about 9%, it can escape into the nearest bubble instead of bursting the paste apart.

Without them, repeated freeze–thaw cycling progressively spalls and disintegrates the surface — the mechanism that destroys concrete in cold climates.

**The trade-off**, which is why it is not used everywhere:

| Effect | Direction |
|---|---|
| **Freeze–thaw durability** | **Greatly improved** |
| **Workability** | Improved — the bubbles act as a lubricant |
| Bleeding and segregation | Reduced |
| Permeability | Reduced |
| **Compressive strength** | **Reduced — roughly 5% per 1% of entrained air** |

So strength is **sacrificed** for durability, which is exactly why option (a) is wrong. Part of the loss is recovered because the improved workability permits a lower water content.

**Where it matters in Nepal:** high-altitude structures and hill roads experience many freeze–thaw cycles each winter, so air entrainment is appropriate there and unnecessary in the Terai. Note that the same freeze–thaw mechanism attacks the **aggregate** as well as the paste, which is what the **soundness test** (sulphate crystallisation, limit 12%) screens for.

**The families of admixture**, so the functions are distinct:

| Admixture | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Air-entraining** | **Freeze–thaw resistance** |
| **Plasticiser / superplasticiser** | Workability at **constant w/c** — hence strength |
| **Accelerator** (CaCl₂) | Faster set and early strength; cold weather |
| **Retarder** | Slower set; hot weather, long hauls, mass pours |
| Waterproofing / integral | Reduced permeability |
| Air-detraining | Removes unwanted entrapped air |

One caution on accelerators: **calcium chloride must not be used in reinforced or prestressed concrete**, because the chloride ions destroy the passive film on the steel and initiate corrosion.

Distinguish **entrained** air — intentional, fine, uniformly distributed, beneficial — from **entrapped** air, which is accidental, coarse, irregular, and simply a compaction defect to be removed by vibration.

examTip.trick: Air entrainment deliberately introduces **billions of tiny disconnected air bubbles**, which give the freezing water **somewhere to expand into** instead of cracking the paste.
examTip.mnemonic: **Air entrainment: excellent freeze–thaw durability and improved workability, at a cost of about 5% strength per 1% of air.** Relevant to Nepal's **high-altitude** construction, where freeze–thaw cycling is severe. Note the bubbles must be **fine and disconnected** — accidentally entrapped air voids from poor compaction do the opposite and cost strength for nothing.

questions.stem: A rectangular RCC slab is designed as a one-way slab when the ratio of its longer span to its shorter span:
questions.solution:
**Exceeds 2.**

| Ratio L_y/L_x | Behaviour | Design as |
|---|---|---|
| **> 2** | Load spans predominantly the **short** way | **One-way slab** |
| **≤ 2** | Load shared in **both** directions | **Two-way slab** |

**Why the ratio decides it.** A slab supported on all four edges sheds load along whichever path is stiffer, and stiffness varies as **1/L³**. So when the long span is twice the short one, the long-direction strips are 2³ = **8 times more flexible** and carry a negligible share. Beyond that ratio the slab behaves, to a good approximation, as a series of one-way strips spanning the short direction.

**What follows for the reinforcement**, which is the practical content:

| | One-way slab | Two-way slab |
|---|---|---|
| **Main steel** | **Short span only** | **Both** directions |
| Other direction | **Distribution steel**, 0.12% (HYSD) minimum | Main steel |
| Moment coefficients | Simple beam analysis | IS 456 **Annex D** tables |
| Corner reinforcement | Not required | **Required** where corners are held down |

The distribution steel in a one-way slab is not there to carry the load — it resists **shrinkage and temperature** movement and distributes concentrated loads, and it holds the main bars in position.

**Cases that are one-way regardless of ratio:** a slab supported on **only two opposite edges** spans one way whatever its proportions, since there is no support in the other direction to share the load.

**The depth is fixed by deflection, not strength** — the point most often missed. IS 456 cl. 23.2.1 gives basic span/effective-depth ratios:

| Support | Basic span/d |
|---|---|
| Cantilever | **7** |
| Simply supported | **20** |
| Continuous | **26** |

modified by the tension-steel percentage. So a slab is proportioned for **deflection** first, then checked for flexure and shear — and shear rarely governs a slab, except as **punching shear** around a column in a flat slab.

Other slab detailing limits: minimum thickness 100 to 125 mm for a floor slab, main bar spacing not exceeding **3d or 300 mm**, distribution steel not exceeding 5d or 450 mm, and clear cover 20 mm for moderate exposure.

examTip.trick: When one span is more than twice the other, the slab sheds **almost all** its load along the **short** span, and the long-span moment becomes negligible — so it is designed as spanning one way only.
examTip.mnemonic: **L_y/L_x > 2 → one-way; ≤ 2 → two-way.** But a one-way slab still needs **distribution steel** in the long direction (0.12% for HYSD) to resist shrinkage, temperature and any incidental transverse moment — omitting it is a real detailing error.

questions.stem: In an RCC beam, the effective depth is measured from the:
options: Top of the beam to the bottom of the beam
Top of the beam to the bottom of the tension reinforcement
Neutral axis to the extreme compression fibre
Extreme compression fibre to the centroid of the tension reinforcement
questions.solution:
**From the extreme compression fibre to the centroid of the tension reinforcement.**

> **d = D − (clear cover + bar diameter/2)** for a single layer

where D is the overall depth. For **two layers** of bars, d is measured to the **centroid of the group**, not to the nearest layer.

**Why the centroid and not the bar edge.** The tensile force acts through the centroid of the steel area, so the **lever arm** of the internal couple is measured from there:

> **M_u = 0.87 f_y A_st (d − 0.42 x_u)**

Everything in flexural design depends on d, so a small error in it propagates directly into the moment capacity.

The depths to keep apart:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Overall depth D** | Full depth of the section |
| **Effective depth d** | **Compression fibre to centroid of tension steel** |
| **Effective cover** | D − d |
| **Clear cover** | Concrete face to the **outer surface** of the steel |
| Neutral axis depth x_u | Compression fibre to the neutral axis |

So option (a) is the **overall** depth and (c) is **x_u** — a quite different quantity, and one limited by IS 456 to **x_u,max** = 0.48d for Fe 415 and 0.46d for Fe 500, so that the section stays **under-reinforced** and fails ductilely.

**Nominal cover requirements** (IS 456 Table 16), which determine d in practice:

| Exposure | Nominal cover |
|---|---|
| **Mild** | 20 mm |
| **Moderate** | **30 mm** |
| Severe | 45 mm |
| Very severe | 50 mm |
| **Extreme** | **75 mm** |
| Footing (cast against soil) | **50 mm** |

Cover is not a detailing nicety — it is the reinforcement's **only protection** against corrosion, and it also provides the **fire resistance** and the **bond** development. Insufficient cover is among the commonest causes of premature deterioration in Nepali construction, and it is why **cover blocks** are specified rather than leaving bars propped on stones or, worse, on binding wire.

A practical consequence of the definition: using **larger-diameter bars** in a single layer reduces d slightly, while **two layers** reduce it appreciably — so for the same steel area, many small bars in one layer give a deeper effective section as well as better crack control.

examTip.trap: **Effective depth** and **overall depth** are constantly confused. Effective depth is measured to the **centroid of the tension steel**, not to the bottom of the section.
examTip.trick: **d = D − cover − (bar diameter/2) − stirrup diameter.** It is the internal lever arm that actually resists moment.
examTip.mnemonic: **Every flexural formula uses d, never D.** Using overall depth overstates the capacity by 10% or more — and the error is always unconservative, which is why it matters.

questions.stem: In the Freyssinet system of prestressing, the tendons are anchored by means of:
options: Threaded nuts bearing on a plate
A conical concrete or steel plug wedged into a cone
Button heads formed on the wires
Looping the wires around the anchor block
questions.solution:
**A conical plug wedged into a female cone.**

In the Freyssinet system a group of wires (typically 8, 12 or 18) is splayed around the inside of a **female cone** cast into the end of the member, and a **male conical plug** is then driven in. The plug grips the wires by friction against the cone, and the whole assembly locks tighter as the tendons try to pull back.

The major **post-tensioning** systems, distinguished by their anchorage:

| System | Anchorage |
|---|---|
| **Freyssinet** | **Conical plug wedged into a female cone** |
| **Magnel–Blaton** | Flat sandwich plates with **wedges**, wires in pairs |
| **Gifford–Udall** | Individual **wedge grips**, one per wire, in a bearing plate |
| **Lee–McCall** | **Threaded bars with nuts** bearing on a plate — option (a) |
| CCL / Dywidag strand systems | Barrel and wedge, or threaded couplers |

Option (c) describes the **BBRV** system's button heads, and (d) is not a recognised anchorage — a looped tendon would crush the concrete at the bend.

**Why anchorage design is critical.** The entire prestressing force — often hundreds of kilonewtons — is delivered into a very small area of concrete at the end of the member. That produces:

- very high local **bearing stress** under the anchorage;
- **transverse tensile (bursting) stresses** in the end block, which require dedicated **anchorage zone reinforcement** in the form of spirals or closed links;
- the **anchorage slip (draw-in)** loss when the wedges seat, typically a few millimetres — significant on a short tendon and one of the losses unique to post-tensioning.

That is why prestressed members demand **high-grade concrete, M40 for post-tensioned work**, and why the end block is the most heavily reinforced part of the member.

**The two methods**, for context:

| | Pre-tensioning | Post-tensioning |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence | Stress wire **first**, cast around it | Cast **first**, stress against hardened concrete |
| Force transfer | **Bond** along the wire | **Anchorages** at the ends |
| Suits | Factory precast — sleepers, piles, planks | **Site work**, long spans, bridges, curved tendons |
| Elastic shortening loss | **Yes** | **No** for a single cable |
| Friction and anchorage slip losses | No | **Yes** |
| Total losses (IS 1343) | ≈ 20% | ≈ 15% |

After stressing, the ducts are **grouted** — which both bonds the tendon and, more importantly, protects it from corrosion, to which high-tensile steel at 1500 to 1900 N/mm² is acutely vulnerable.

examTip.trick: The Freyssinet system grips the wires between a **conical concrete or steel plug** and a matching **female cone**, the tendon force itself wedging the plug tighter.
examTip.mnemonic: **The load locks the anchorage — the harder it pulls, the tighter it grips.** That self-anchoring principle is common to nearly all post-tensioning systems (Freyssinet cones, Magnel sandwich plates, Gifford-Udall barrels and wedges). The associated loss is **ANCHORAGE SLIP** — a few millimetres of draw-in, which matters most on **short** tendons.

questions.stem: In a T-beam, the effective width of the flange is limited because:
options: The flange would otherwise fail in tension
The code restricts the total steel area
The compressive stress is not uniform across the full flange width
The flange carries no compression at all
questions.solution:
**Because the compressive stress is not uniform across the full flange width.**

In a T-beam the slab acts as the compression flange, but the compression does not spread indefinitely. It is **highest over the web** and diminishes with distance from it, because the flange must transfer its share of the force into the web by **shear**, and that transfer is not instantaneous.

Rather than integrate a varying stress, the code replaces the real distribution with an **equivalent uniform stress over a reduced width** — the **effective flange width b_f** — chosen so the total compressive force is the same. It is a design convenience, not a physical boundary.

**The limits (IS 456 cl. 23.1.2):**

| Beam | Effective flange width, the **least** of |
|---|---|
| **T-beam** | **l₀/6 + b_w + 6D_f**; or b_w + half the clear distance to the next beam; or the actual flange width |
| **L-beam** | **l₀/12 + b_w + 3D_f**; or b_w + half the clear distance; or the actual width |

where l₀ is the distance between points of zero moment (about **0.7 × effective span** for a continuous beam), b_w the web width and D_f the flange thickness.

Note that l₀ appears in the formula: the effective width **grows with span**, because a longer span gives the shear more length over which to distribute the force.

**Why the T-beam form is so efficient.** The neutral axis usually falls **within the flange**, so:

- a large **compression area** is available where it is needed, high in the section;
- the **web** carries the shear and holds the tension steel low, maximising the lever arm;
- material is removed from the region near the neutral axis, where it contributes least.

In a monolithic floor the slab and beam are cast together, so this action is automatic — the designer gets the flange free, which is why monolithic construction is so much more economical than a rectangular beam of the same depth.

**Two design consequences:**

1. If x_u ≤ D_f, the section behaves as a **rectangular beam of width b_f** — the usual case, and the simplest to design.
2. If x_u > D_f, the compression extends into the web and the analysis must be split into flange and web contributions.

And note the reversal at a **support** in a continuous beam: the moment is hogging, the flange is in **tension**, and the beam must be designed as a **rectangular section of width b_w** — the flange contributes nothing. That is exactly where the main steel migrates to the top face.

examTip.trick: Compressive stress in the flange is **highest over the web** and falls away toward the tips — the flange does not work uniformly. The **effective width** is a fiction that gives the same total force at a uniform stress.
examTip.mnemonic: **That is SHEAR LAG, and the same idea appears in steel design.** IS 456's effective width for a T-beam: **b_f = L₀/6 + b_w + 6D_f** (least of that, the actual flange width, and the beam spacing). Assuming the full flange acts overestimates the capacity.

questions.stem: In a steel tension member made of a single angle connected through one leg only, the design strength is reduced to allow for:
options: Shear lag due to the eccentric connection
questions.solution:
**Shear lag due to the eccentric connection.**

When only one leg is bolted or welded, the force enters the angle through that leg alone. The **outstanding (unconnected) leg** can pick up its share of the load only by transferring it through the fillet — and that transfer requires length. So near the connection the outstanding leg is **under-stressed** while the connected leg is over-stressed. The stress distribution is non-uniform, and the member cannot develop the strength its full area suggests.

That effect is **shear lag**, and the connection's **eccentricity** compounds it by introducing bending as well.

**How IS 800 handles it.** The rupture strength of the net section is factored:

> **T_dn = α A_n f_u / γ_m1**

with **α = 0.6 to 0.8** depending on the number of fasteners in the line — fewer fasteners give a shorter transfer length and therefore a lower α. The code also gives the fuller expression

> T_dn = 0.9 A_nc f_u/γ_m1 + β A_go f_y/γ_m0

separating the **connected** leg (net area, at ultimate strength) from the **outstanding** leg (gross area, at yield) — which makes the mechanism explicit.

**The three checks on any tension member**, the capacity being the **least**:

| Mode | Strength | γ |
|---|---|---|
| **Gross section yielding** | A_g f_y/γ_m0 | **1.10** |
| **Net section rupture** | 0.9 A_n f_u/γ_m1 (× α for shear lag) | **1.25** |
| **Block shear** | From the shear and tension paths round the bolt group | 1.25 |

Note the different partial factors: rupture is a **brittle** failure at ultimate strength, so it carries the larger factor, whereas gross yielding is ductile.

**How the penalty is avoided in practice:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| Connect **both legs** | Removes the eccentricity and most of the lag |
| Use a **lug angle** | Brings the outstanding leg into the connection |
| **More fasteners in line** | Longer transfer length, higher α |
| Use a **double angle** back to back, either side of the gusset | Symmetric — no eccentricity |

Why the other options fail: **buckling** (a) is a *compression* phenomenon and a tension member cannot buckle; corrosion (c) is addressed by protection, not by a strength factor; and thermal expansion (d) causes stress only where movement is restrained.

A related detail: **bolt holes** are the other reason net area matters — hole diameter is the bolt plus 2 mm for 16 to 24 mm bolts, and the minimum pitch of **2.5d** exists partly so staggered bolting can raise the net area.

examTip.trick: An angle connected through **one leg only** transfers the load eccentrically, so the stress does not spread uniformly across the section — the outstanding leg is under-stressed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear lag is why the NET section is reduced further by a factor (IS 800's β).** Two practical remedies: connect **both legs**, or use a **longer connection** (more bolts in line), which gives the stress more length over which to distribute. It is the same phenomenon as the T-beam's effective flange width, in a different guise.

questions.stem: The permissible stresses for structural timber given in IS 883 are specified for three groups A, B and C based on the timber's:
questions.solution:
**Its modulus of elasticity and strength.**

IS 883 sorts structural timber into three groups by measured mechanical properties — chiefly the **modulus of elasticity** and the **extreme fibre stress in bending**:

| Group | Modulus of elasticity | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **≥ 12.6 kN/mm²** | Strongest — sal, teak (better grades) |
| **B** | 9.8 – 12.6 kN/mm² | Medium |
| **C** | 5.6 – 9.8 kN/mm² | Weakest of the structural grades |

Timber below Group C is not admitted for structural use at all.

**Why grouping is necessary.** Timber is a **natural, anisotropic and highly variable** material — far more so than steel or concrete. Its strength depends on species, density, growth conditions, moisture content, and the size and position of defects. Grouping reduces that variability to a manageable set of design values.

**The three location classes**, which modify the permissible stress further:

| Location | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Inside** | Continuously dry |
| **Outside** | Alternately wet and dry |
| **Wet** | Continuously damp or in contact with water |

A member in the wet class takes a substantially lower permissible stress than the same timber inside.

**The anisotropy that governs design**, and the reason a single "strength" would be meaningless:

| Direction | Relative strength |
|---|---|
| **Parallel to the grain**, compression and tension | **Highest** |
| **Perpendicular to the grain**, compression | Much lower — bearing at a support governs |
| **Shear parallel to the grain** | **Low** — timber splits readily along the grain |

So timber connections are the usual weak point: bolts and nails bear across the grain and the member tends to split, which is why end distances and spacings are generously specified.

**Moisture content**, option (d), is a real and important variable — permissible stresses are quoted at 12% and reduced for wetter service — but it modifies the values rather than defining the groups.

The **defect limits** complete the grading: knots, shakes, checks, wane and slope of grain are restricted by size **and position**, since a knot in the tension face of a beam is far more damaging than the same knot in compression.

The slenderness limits from the same code: **S/d ≤ 50** for a solid column and 80 for a built-up or box column.

examTip.trick: Timber's permissible stresses are grouped by **strength class**, established from its **modulus of elasticity and its strength** — the two properties that govern both stiffness and capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Timber is highly ANISOTROPIC — strength along the grain is many times that across it**, so every permissible stress is quoted with a direction. Then apply modification factors for **moisture content, duration of load, and size**. A single 'strength of timber' figure means nothing without those qualifiers.

questions.stem: The permissible limit of turbidity in drinking water, in the absence of an alternative source, is:
questions.solution:
**10 NTU** as the permissible limit, with **5 NTU** the desirable value.

Turbidity measures the **cloudiness** caused by suspended matter — clay, silt, finely divided organic and inorganic material, and microorganisms. It is determined with a **nephelometer**, which measures light **scattered at 90°** to the incident beam, and reported in **Nephelometric Turbidity Units**.

Nepal's drinking water standard sets 5 NTU as desirable and permits up to 10 NTU where no better source exists; the WHO guideline for water entering distribution is **below 1 NTU** where disinfection is practised.

**Why turbidity matters more than its appearance suggests.** It is not merely aesthetic:

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Shields pathogens from disinfection** | Organisms adsorbed on or embedded in particles are protected from chlorine |
| **Exerts chlorine demand** | Particles consume the disinfectant, reducing the free residual |
| Indicates treatment failure | Rising filter effluent turbidity signals breakthrough |
| Consumer rejection | Cloudy water is refused, and users return to unsafe sources |

That first row is decisive, and it is why turbidity must be reduced **before** disinfection rather than after: chlorinating turbid water gives a false sense of safety. The treatment train is ordered accordingly —

> screening → aeration → **coagulation and flocculation** → **sedimentation** → **filtration** → **disinfection**

with the first four steps existing largely to deliver water clear enough for the last to work.

**The related quality parameters and their limits:**

| Parameter | Desirable | Permissible |
|---|---|---|
| **Turbidity** | **5 NTU** | **10 NTU** |
| **Colour** | 5 TCU | 15 TCU |
| pH | 6.5 – 8.5 | — |
| Total hardness (as CaCO₃) | 500 mg/L | — |
| **E. coli** | **Zero per 100 mL** | **Zero** |
| Free residual chlorine | 0.1 – 0.2 mg/L at the tap | — |

The **zero E. coli** requirement is absolute and admits no "permissible" relaxation, which marks the difference between an **aesthetic** parameter and a **health** one.

Note the historical unit: turbidity was formerly expressed as **ppm of silica** on the silica scale, which is why older texts and some exam keys give it in ppm rather than NTU. Both describe the same property.

examTip.trick: Two figures are in play and the question specifies which: the **desirable** limit is **5 NTU**, and the **permissible** limit where no better source exists is **10 NTU**.
examTip.mnemonic: **5 desirable, 10 permissible in the absence of an alternative.** Turbidity matters beyond appearance: **suspended particles SHIELD pathogens from chlorine**, so a turbid water cannot be reliably disinfected however much chlorine is added. That is why filtration must precede chlorination.

questions.stem: The arithmetical increase method of population forecasting is most suitable for:
options: A town whose growth rate is accelerating
A large, old city that has nearly reached saturation
A town with no historical census data
questions.solution:
**A large, old city that has nearly reached saturation.**

The arithmetical increase method assumes a **constant absolute increase** per decade:

> **P_n = P₀ + n·x̄**

where x̄ is the average increase per decade. That is a **linear** projection, which fits a city whose growth has slowed to a steady trickle — one that is largely built out, with limited land and a mature economy.

Applied to a **young, rapidly growing** town it **under-estimates** badly, because such a town grows by a roughly constant *percentage*, not a constant number.

The methods and where each fits:

| Method | Assumes | Suits | Tends to |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Arithmetical increase** | Constant **absolute** increase | **Old, saturated** cities | **Under-estimate** growing towns |
| **Geometrical increase** | Constant **percentage** growth, P_n = P₀(1+r)ⁿ | **Young, fast-growing** towns | **Over-estimate** on long projections |
| **Incremental increase** | Average increase **plus** the average of the increments | A **compromise** — generally the most reliable | Sits between the two |
| Decreasing rate of growth | Growth rate falls towards saturation | Cities approaching their limit | — |
| **Graphical / comparison** | Extrapolate the curve, or follow a similar city | Where good records exist | — |
| Logistic (S-curve) | Growth follows an S-curve to a saturation value | Long-term projection | — |

Because arithmetic under-estimates and geometric over-estimates, the **incremental increase** method is usually preferred in practice — it captures both the level and the trend of growth.

**Why the choice matters so much.** Every water supply and sewerage scheme is sized for a **future** population over a design period of 15 to 30 years:

> Design population × per capita demand = design demand

Under-forecast and the scheme is starved within a few years; over-forecast and the client pays for idle capacity. The forecast is the single most consequential assumption in the design.

**The caveat that dominates in Nepal:** **migration**, which none of these methods handles well. Kathmandu Valley's growth has been driven overwhelmingly by in-migration rather than natural increase, so a projection extrapolated from natural growth rates badly under-predicts it — part of why the Valley's water supply has lagged its population for decades. Where migration dominates, the **graphical comparison** method against a similar city, or explicit scenario planning, serves better than any of the arithmetic formulae.

examTip.trick: Match the method to the **stage of growth**: **arithmetic** (constant increment) suits a **large, old, saturating** city; **geometric** (constant percentage) suits a **young, rapidly growing** one; **incremental increase** suits a maturing town.
examTip.mnemonic: **Arithmetic = old and slow; geometric = young and fast; logistic = an S-curve with a saturation limit.** Over a 30-year design period these give wildly different populations — choosing the wrong one is the single largest source of error in water supply design.

questions.stem: The main purpose of providing a bell-mouthed entry to an intake pipe is to:
options: Reduce the entry head loss and prevent vortex formation
Increase the velocity of water entering the pipe
Provide a seat for the sluice valve
questions.solution:
**To reduce the entry head loss and prevent vortex formation.**

A sharp-edged pipe entry forces the flow to turn abruptly, so it **separates** and contracts to a vena contracta before re-expanding — dissipating a substantial part of the velocity head. A **bell mouth** guides the streamlines round smoothly, so the flow stays attached.

The difference in the entry loss coefficient is large:

| Entry | k in h_L = k V²/2g |
|---|---|
| **Sharp-edged (flush)** | **0.5** |
| Slightly rounded | 0.2 – 0.25 |
| **Bell-mouthed** | **0.04** |
| Re-entrant (projecting) pipe | 0.8 – 1.0 |

So a bell mouth cuts the entry loss by a factor of more than **ten**.

**The second function is at least as important.** A smooth, symmetric approach suppresses the **air-entraining vortex** that forms when water swirls into a submerged intake. That vortex is a real operational hazard:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| Air drawn into the conduit | **Reduced discharge**; the effective area falls |
| Air reaching a pump or turbine | **Vibration, noise, loss of efficiency**, cavitation damage |
| Intermittent air slugs | **Pressure surges** |

Hence the bell mouth works together with **adequate submergence** — the depth of the intake below the water surface, checked against criteria such as H_s > 1.5V²/2g and H_s > 0.5V√D, the greater governing. Anti-vortex baffles or a floating raft are added where the submergence available is marginal.

**Why the other options fail.** A bell mouth **reduces** the entry velocity locally by enlarging the area (b); filtering is the job of the **trash rack** and **screens** (c); and the valve seat is a separate detail (d).

**Where bell mouths appear:** water supply intakes and pump suctions, hydropower **penstock intakes** at a forebay, and — in the same spirit of gradual transition — the **morning glory (bell-mouth) spillway**, whose flared inlet is profiled so the nappe stays attached and the pressure along the crest remains atmospheric.

The general principle worth carrying: **gradual transitions preserve energy, abrupt ones destroy it.** It is the same reason a venturimeter loses far less head than an orifice meter, and why a turbine's draft tube expands slowly rather than suddenly.

examTip.trick: A square-cut entry forces the streamlines to turn a sharp corner, so they separate and form a **vena contracta**. A bell mouth guides them in smoothly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rounding an entry drops K from 0.5 to about 0.05 — a TENFOLD reduction for nothing but a radius.** The same shaping raises an orifice's C_d from 0.62 to 0.98. It also suppresses the **air-entraining vortex** that would otherwise draw air into the conduit.

questions.stem: In a centrifugal pump, cavitation is likely to occur when:
options: The delivery head is too high
The pump speed is too low
The discharge is throttled at the delivery valve
questions.solution:
**When the suction lift is excessive.**

Cavitation occurs where the pressure falls to the **vapour pressure** of the liquid — and in a centrifugal pump the lowest pressure is at the **impeller inlet (eye)**, on the suction side. Raising the pump too far above the water level lowers that pressure until vapour bubbles form; they are then carried into the higher-pressure impeller passages and **collapse violently**, pitting the impeller and casing.

The governing quantity is the **net positive suction head**:

> **NPSH_available = (p_atm/γ) − (p_vapour/γ) − h_s − h_fs**

where h_s is the static suction lift and h_fs the friction loss in the suction pipe. Safe operation requires

> **NPSH_available > NPSH_required** (the value the manufacturer states)

Every term in that expression is a lever the designer can pull:

| Remedy | Term affected |
|---|---|
| **Reduce the suction lift** — lower the pump, or place it below water level | **h_s** — the principal control |
| **Shorten and enlarge the suction pipe**, minimise bends and fittings | h_fs |
| Provide **adequate submergence** and a bell-mouthed foot | Prevents air entry and vortex |
| Avoid pumping hot liquids | Raises p_vapour |
| Note that **altitude reduces p_atm** | Less margin in the hills |

That last point matters in Nepal: at Kathmandu's elevation the atmospheric head is roughly 8.7 m rather than 10.3 m, so the permissible suction lift is correspondingly smaller — and smaller still at hill stations. A pump specification imported unchanged from the plains can cavitate.

**Why the other options are wrong.** A high **delivery** head (a) loads the pump and reduces its discharge, but the delivery side is the high-pressure side and does not cavitate. **Low speed** (b) raises pressures if anything. **Throttling the delivery valve** (c) is the normal method of regulating a centrifugal pump and is safe — note the contrast with throttling the **suction**, which is dangerous precisely because it lowers the inlet pressure.

**The symptoms**, which are the same as in a turbine: noise like gravel in the casing, vibration, a fall in head and efficiency, and **pitting** of the impeller on the low-pressure faces of the vanes.

The turbine parallel is exact. There the lowest pressure is at **runner exit into the draft tube**, and the criterion is **Thoma's cavitation factor** σ = (H_a − H_v − H_s)/H, with the same remedy — **lower the machine setting**, even below tailwater level.

examTip.trick: Cavitation occurs where the **absolute pressure falls to the vapour pressure**, and in a pump that is on the **suction** side. Excessive suction lift is the direct cause.
examTip.mnemonic: **NPSH_available must exceed NPSH_required.** The single most effective remedy is to **LOWER THE PUMP** — ideally below the water level, giving a flooded suction. And note the Nepali constraint: **NPSH_available falls about 1.1 m per 1000 m of altitude**, so a pump that works in the Terai may cavitate in Kathmandu.

questions.stem: In a rapid sand filter, backwashing is carried out to:
options: Remove the accumulated impurities and restore the filter's capacity
Increase the effective size of the sand
questions.solution:
**To remove the accumulated impurities and restore the filter's capacity.**

As filtration proceeds, floc and suspended matter accumulate in the pores of the bed. Two things then happen: the **head loss rises** (the filter "clogs"), and eventually **breakthrough** occurs, with turbidity appearing in the effluent. Backwashing reverses the flow to lift and scour the bed clean.

**How it works.** Clean water is forced **upward** at a high rate — about **0.6 m³/m²/min** — which **fluidises** the bed, expanding it by 25 to 50%. The grains are set in motion, rub against one another, and the dislodged floc is carried away in the wash water to waste. Air scour or surface wash jets are often used first to break up the surface mat.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Backwash rate** | ≈ 0.6 m³/m²/min |
| **Bed expansion** | 25 – 50% |
| **Duration** | 5 – 15 minutes |
| **Frequency** | Every **1 to 3 days** |
| Wash water used | 2 – 5% of the filtered output |

**Why option (c) is subtly wrong but instructive.** Backwashing *does* re-grade the bed — fluidisation sorts the grains **hydraulically**, leaving the finest at the top and the coarsest at the bottom. But that is a **side-effect**, not the purpose, and it is in fact a mild disadvantage: the fine layer at the surface does most of the straining and clogs fastest. **Dual-media filters** (anthracite over sand) are used to reverse the gradation deliberately, giving depth filtration and longer runs.

Option (d) is impossible — backwashing cannot change the size of the sand grains, only their arrangement.

**The contrast with a slow sand filter** is the clearest way to fix the distinction:

| | **Rapid sand filter** | **Slow sand filter** |
|---|---|---|
| **Cleaning** | **Backwashing**, every 1–3 days | **Scraping** the top 2–3 cm, every 1–3 months |
| Rate of filtration | 3000 – 6000 L/m²/h | 100 – 200 L/m²/h |
| Bed depth | 60 – 75 cm | 90 – 110 cm |
| Effective size | 0.35 – 0.55 mm | 0.2 – 0.3 mm |
| Pre-treatment | **Coagulation essential** | Plain sedimentation |
| Bacterial removal | 80 – 90% | **98 – 99%** |
| Mechanism | Largely **physical straining and adsorption** | Largely **biological** — the schmutzdecke |

The rapid filter is a physical device that must be washed; the slow filter is a biological one whose active layer must be **scraped off and allowed to re-form**. Backwashing a slow sand filter would destroy the very layer that does the work.

Either way, filtration is followed by **disinfection** — it reduces bacteria greatly but does not sterilise.

examTip.trick: Backwashing reverses the flow up through the bed, **expanding** it so the trapped floc is scoured off and carried away — restoring both the head loss and the capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rapid sand filter: BACKWASH (reverse flow). Slow sand filter: SCRAPE the top layer.** Different mechanisms, because the rapid filter traps floc **through the depth** while the slow filter works by the biological **schmutzdecke** at the surface. Backwash water is 2–5% of the throughput and must itself be treated.

questions.stem: Compared with chlorination, the principal disadvantage of ozone as a disinfectant is that it:
options: Is less effective against bacteria and viruses
Leaves no residual protection in the distribution system
Increases the turbidity of the water
questions.solution:
**It leaves no residual protection in the distribution system.**

Ozone is a powerful oxidant and a **more effective** disinfectant than chlorine — faster acting and effective against chlorine-resistant organisms such as *Cryptosporidium* and *Giardia*. But it is unstable and **decomposes back to oxygen within minutes**, so nothing remains in the water once it leaves the plant.

That is a serious operational gap. A distribution network can be re-contaminated **after** treatment — through a leaking joint, a section under sub-atmospheric pressure, a service reservoir, or during a repair. A **residual disinfectant** is the defence against exactly that, which is why Nepal's standard requires a **free residual chlorine of 0.1 to 0.2 mg/L at the consumer's tap**.

Hence ozonation is normally followed by a **small chlorine dose** purely to provide the residual — ozone doing the disinfecting, chlorine doing the guarding.

**The comparison in full:**

| | **Chlorine** | **Ozone** |
|---|---|---|
| Disinfecting power | Good | **Better** |
| **Residual** | **Yes — persists** | **No** |
| Taste and odour | Can **cause** them | **Removes** them |
| By-products | **Trihalomethanes (THMs)** — carcinogenic concern | Bromate (where bromide present) |
| Effect on colour and iron | Oxidises | Oxidises, more effectively |
| Cost and complexity | **Low; simple to dose** | **High — generated on site, needs power** |
| Suits | Almost all supplies | Large plants, difficult raw water |

So option (b) is the wrong way round: **THMs are a chlorine by-product**, formed when chlorine reacts with natural organic matter, and reducing them is one of the reasons for considering ozone in the first place.

**Why chlorine dominates despite its drawbacks.** It is cheap, simple to dose as gas, bleaching powder or hypochlorite, and it provides the residual. Its efficiency depends on:

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **pH** | Efficiency **falls as pH rises** — potent HOCl gives way to weak OCl⁻ above pH 7.5 |
| **Contact time** | Minimum **30 minutes**; expressed as the C·t product |
| **Temperature** | Higher temperature speeds the kill |
| **Turbidity** | Particles **shield** organisms — hence filter first |

The other alternatives: **UV** disinfection, which likewise leaves **no residual**, and **chloramines**, which give a weaker but far more persistent residual — useful in a large network where chlorine would decay before reaching the extremities.

examTip.trick: Ozone and UV are **excellent disinfectants at the point of application** but leave **nothing behind** in the water — so any recontamination in the distribution network goes unchecked.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chlorine's great virtue is its RESIDUAL** — 0.2 mg/l maintained to the far end of the network guards against ingress through joints and repairs. That is why ozone and UV plants usually add a **small chlorine dose afterwards** purely for residual protection. Chlorine's own drawback is **trihalomethane** formation with organic matter.

questions.stem: An egg-shaped sewer section is sometimes preferred to a circular one because it:
options: Carries a greater discharge when running full
Is easier to clean by rodding
Maintains a self-cleansing velocity better at low flows
questions.solution:
**It maintains a self-cleansing velocity better at low flows.**

Sanitary sewage varies widely through the day and grows over the design period, so a sewer must remain **self-cleansing at minimum flow** while not eroding at peak flow. The egg-shaped (ovoid) section addresses the first requirement directly.

**How.** Its **narrow invert** concentrates a small flow into a deeper, narrower stream than a circular pipe of the same capacity would. The hydraulic radius at low depth is therefore larger, and by Manning's equation

> V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}

the velocity is higher — so solids stay in suspension instead of settling.

**Why that matters so much.** If solids deposit at low flow they:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| Reduce the section | Capacity falls; blockage follows |
| **Decompose anaerobically** | Generate **hydrogen sulphide** |
| H₂S oxidised on the damp crown | **Sulphuric acid → crown corrosion**, destroying concrete sewers from the inside top |
