So a section that self-cleanses is not a refinement but a protection against the sewer destroying itself.

**The design limits it serves:**

> **Minimum velocity 0.6 – 0.9 m/s** at minimum flow — self-cleansing
> **Maximum velocity 2.4 – 3.0 m/s** at peak flow — non-eroding

**Why circular sections nonetheless dominate.** The egg shape has real drawbacks, and options (a), (b) and (c) are all wrong precisely because the circle wins on each:

| | Circular | Egg-shaped |
|---|---|---|
| Cost and manufacture | **Cheap, mass-produced pipe** | Cast in situ or special; **expensive** |
| Discharge when full, for the same material | **Greater** (best area-to-perimeter ratio) | Less |
| Structural strength | **Uniform** under external load | Weaker; needs care in the narrow invert |
| Handling and laying | Easy; no orientation issue | Must be laid the right way up |
| **Low-flow velocity** | Poorer | **Better** |

So the egg shape is reserved for **large combined sewers** where flows vary enormously between dry weather and storm conditions, and where the section is being built in situ anyway. For ordinary sanitary sewers the circular pipe's economy is decisive, and the low-flow problem is handled instead by **flushing manholes**, steeper local gradients, or laying the sewer to run **half to three-quarters full** at the design peak.

A useful circular-pipe fact in the same vein: velocity is **maximum at 0.81D** depth and discharge **maximum at 0.95D**, so a pipe running part full performs nearly as well as one running full — and rather better in places.

examTip.trick: An egg-shaped section is **narrow at the invert**, so at low flow the same discharge occupies a **deeper, narrower** channel — giving a higher velocity and a larger hydraulic radius than a circular pipe would.
examTip.mnemonic: **Egg-shaped sewers self-cleanse better at LOW flow — which is exactly the binding condition in sewer design.** Their drawback is cost and difficulty of manufacture and laying, which is why circular pipes dominate despite the hydraulic disadvantage.

questions.stem: In a separate sewerage system:
options: Sanitary sewage and storm water are carried in separate sewers
Sanitary sewage and storm water are carried together
Only industrial waste is carried separately
Sewage is treated separately at each house
questions.solution:
**Sanitary sewage and storm water are carried in separate sewers.**

The three systems:

| System | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| **Separate** | **Two sets of sewers** — sanitary sewage to treatment, storm water direct to a watercourse |
| **Combined** | **One sewer** carries both |
| **Partially separate** | Sanitary sewage plus the **roof and yard** drainage in one sewer; street storm water separate |

**Why separation is generally preferred**, and it comes down to what happens at the treatment works:

| Advantage | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Treatment plant is far smaller** | It receives only sanitary flow, not storm flow many times larger |
| **No overflow of raw sewage** | A combined sewer surcharged by a storm discharges **diluted sewage** to the river |
| Sanitary sewers are small, so **cheaper and self-cleansing** | Flow is more consistent |
| Storm water needs no treatment | Discharged directly, at nearby outfalls |

That second row is the decisive public-health argument: **combined sewer overflows** put untreated sewage into watercourses during exactly the heavy rainfall that makes them most used.

**Where a combined system still makes sense:** a **high, evenly distributed rainfall** with no marked dry season; **narrow streets** where two sets of sewers cannot be laid; and where the rainfall is sufficient to keep a large sewer self-cleansing. Its advantages are one set of pipes, lower initial cost in congested streets, and continuous flushing of the sewage by storm flow.

**Why separate suits Nepal.** The monsoon concentrates almost all the rainfall into a few months, so a combined sewer would be **enormously oversized and non-self-cleansing** for most of the year, then overwhelmed in the monsoon. The separate system is therefore the norm — and note the practical failure mode: illegal storm connections into sanitary sewers defeat the whole arrangement, flooding the treatment works in the monsoon.

**The design flows the two carry** are quite different in character:

| Sewer | Design flow |
|---|---|
| **Sanitary** | ≈ **80% of water supply** + infiltration; peak factor about **3** |
| **Storm** | From the **rational method**, Q = CIA, with the intensity read at the **time of concentration** |

Both must satisfy the same velocity limits — **0.6 to 0.9 m/s** minimum for self-cleansing, up to 2.4 to 3.0 m/s maximum to avoid erosion — though storm sewers take the higher minimum because they carry heavier grit.

examTip.trick: **Separate**: two pipe systems, one for sewage and one for stormwater. **Combined**: one system carrying both. **Partially separate**: some roof water admitted to the sewage system.
examTip.mnemonic: **Separate: smaller treatment works, no overflow of raw sewage in storms — but two sets of pipes. Combined: cheaper to lay, but the treatment works must handle storm flow, and COMBINED SEWER OVERFLOWS discharge dilute raw sewage to rivers.** Separate is the modern preference for exactly that reason.

questions.stem: A waste stabilisation pond system in which both aerobic and anaerobic conditions exist in the same pond, stratified by depth, is called a:
questions.solution:
**A facultative pond.**

A facultative pond is **stratified by depth**, with two quite different environments in one basin:

| Zone | Condition | Process |
|---|---|---|
| **Upper layer** | **Aerobic** — oxygen from surface reaeration and from **algal photosynthesis** | Bacteria oxidise dissolved organics |
| **Lower layer** | **Anaerobic** | Settled sludge is digested |
| Middle | Facultative | Organisms tolerate either condition |

Depth is typically **1 to 2.5 m**, with a detention time of **15 to 30 days** or more.

**The algal–bacterial symbiosis** is the elegant part, and the reason these ponds work with no energy input:

> **Algae** use sunlight to photosynthesise, releasing **oxygen**
> **Bacteria** use that oxygen to oxidise the organic matter, releasing **CO₂** and nutrients
> The algae consume the CO₂ and nutrients — and the cycle closes

So the pond is self-sustaining. There are **no mechanical aerators, no pumps and no power** required, which is exactly why it suits developing-country and rural conditions.

**The pond types in series**, a full system usually using all three:

| Pond | Depth | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Anaerobic** | 2 – 5 m | Heavy **BOD removal** and settling; no oxygen, no algae |
| **Facultative** | 1 – 2.5 m | Main **BOD removal**; aerobic top, anaerobic bottom |
| **Maturation** | 1 – 1.5 m | **Pathogen removal** — the polishing stage |

The **maturation pond** is worth distinguishing: it removes little further BOD but is extremely effective at killing **faecal coliforms and helminth eggs**, through sunlight (UV), high pH from algal activity, and long detention. Where the effluent will be reused for irrigation, that is the pond that matters.

**Advantages and limits:**

| Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|
| **No energy**, no mechanical parts | **Very large land area** |
| Very **low operating cost** | Odour if overloaded or if the anaerobic layer surfaces |
| Simple operation, minimal skill | Performance varies with **temperature and sunlight** |
| **Excellent pathogen removal** | Algae in the effluent raise suspended solids |
| Tolerates shock loads | Desludging needed every few years |

The land requirement is the binding constraint — which is why stabilisation ponds suit small towns and rural schemes in Nepal but not the Kathmandu Valley, where land value forces a compact mechanised plant such as **activated sludge** or a trickling filter instead.

examTip.trick: A facultative pond is **stratified**: the upper layer is **aerobic** (oxygen from algae and surface re-aeration) and the lower layer **anaerobic** (sludge digesting on the bottom), with a facultative zone between.
examTip.mnemonic: **Anaerobic pond (deep, high loading) → FACULTATIVE (the workhorse) → maturation (shallow, pathogen removal).** The algae–bacteria symbiosis drives it: **bacteria consume organics and release CO₂; algae consume CO₂ and release oxygen.** Cheap, simple, needs no power — but needs a lot of land.

questions.stem: The environmental study required for a project with moderate impacts, requiring Terms of Reference but not scoping, is:
questions.solution:
**Initial Environmental Examination (IEE).**

Under Nepal's **Environment Protection Act 2076** and Rules 2077, the tiers of environmental study step up with the significance of the impacts, and they are distinguished precisely by which procedural steps they require:

| Level | Impacts | **Scoping** | **ToR** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BES** — Brief Environmental Study | Small, minor | **No** | **No** |
| **IEE** | **Moderate** | **No** | **Yes** |
| **EIA** | Major, significant | **Yes** | **Yes** |

So the combination named in the question — **ToR required, scoping not** — identifies the IEE uniquely. That is a genuinely useful discriminator, because it is the one procedural difference between the two middle tiers.

**Why scoping is reserved for EIA.** Scoping is the formal exercise of identifying which issues are significant, setting the study boundaries, and deciding which **alternatives** will be examined. It involves public consultation and produces the approved Terms of Reference. For a project with only moderate impacts that machinery is disproportionate, so the IEE proceeds straight to a ToR and the study itself.

**The EIA sequence**, for contrast:

> **Screening** (which tier applies?) → **Scoping** and ToR approval → **baseline** data → **impact prediction and evaluation** → **mitigation** → **Environmental Management Plan** → **monitoring and auditing**

with public consultation and a **public hearing** throughout.

**Which tier applies** is set by schedules in the Rules, generally by project type and size — installed capacity for hydropower, length and class for roads, area for irrigation, population served for water supply. Approval authority also rises with the tier.

**Option (d), SEA**, is a real instrument but operates at a different level: a **Strategic** Environmental Assessment appraises **policies, plans and programmes** rather than individual projects — a national energy plan, say, rather than one hydropower scheme.

**What every tier must cover**, in proportion to its scope: air, water, soil, noise, flora, fauna and biodiversity; plus the **social** dimensions — resettlement and compensation, cultural and religious sites, occupational health and safety, and effects on livelihoods.

The practical point for a Nepali project: the **mitigation and monitoring commitments** in an approved study are legally binding conditions of approval, not aspirations — and land acquisition and resettlement are frequently the critical path of the whole project.

examTip.trick: The threshold is set by **project size and sensitivity**: below it, an **IEE**; above it, or in a sensitive area, a full **EIA**.
examTip.mnemonic: **IEE for smaller projects; EIA for large or sensitive ones — and a project in a protected area needs an EIA regardless of size.** The EIA sequence: **screening → SCOPING → terms of reference → study → report → review → approval → MONITORING.** The last step is the most often neglected and the one that makes the rest meaningful.

questions.stem: The overall irrigation efficiency of a scheme is the product of:
questions.solution:
**Conveyance efficiency × application efficiency.**

> **η_overall = η_c × η_a**

The two account for losses in the two distinct stages between the canal head and the crop's root zone:

| Efficiency | Definition | Losses it accounts for |
|---|---|---|
| **Conveyance, η_c** | Water delivered to the field ÷ water diverted at the head | **Seepage and evaporation** in canals and watercourses |
| **Application, η_a** | Water stored in the root zone ÷ water delivered to the field | **Deep percolation and surface runoff** in the field |

So the overall figure measures how much of the water taken from the river actually reaches the crop. Typical values: η_c of 0.6 to 0.8 in unlined canals, η_a of 0.6 to 0.8 for surface irrigation — giving an overall efficiency often as low as **40 to 60%**.

**The other efficiencies**, which are *not* multiplied into the overall figure:

| Efficiency | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Distribution, η_d** | **Uniformity** of application — (1 − D/d), where D is the mean deviation |
| **Use, η_u** | Water **beneficially used** ÷ water delivered |

Distribution efficiency is a **uniformity index**, not a loss ratio, which is why it does not belong in the product — a field could be watered with perfect uniformity and still lose half the water to percolation.

**Why the overall figure matters.** It is what converts the crop's requirement into the canal's design discharge:

> **GIR = NIR / η_overall**

and the canal is sized for the **gross** requirement. Design for the net and the tail-end farmers get nothing.

**Where the improvements come from**, in order of effect: **lining the canals** (attacks η_c, and simultaneously reduces the waterlogging that seepage causes), **sprinkler or drip irrigation** (raises η_a to 0.8–0.9, and drip to 0.9–0.95), and better **land levelling and scheduling**. Lining is usually the first move because canal seepage is both the largest single loss and the cause of the rising water table.

examTip.trick: Efficiencies **multiply** along the chain: water lost in the canal is gone before the field ever sees it. **η_overall = η_conveyance × η_application.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Efficiencies MULTIPLY, never average.** Two stages at 70% give **49%**, not 70%. That compounding is why a scheme can divert twice what the crops need and still fall short — and why **lining the canal** (conveyance) is often the cheapest single improvement available.

questions.stem: Field capacity of a soil is the moisture content:
options: Retained after free gravitational drainage has ceased
At which the plant permanently wilts
At which the soil is fully saturated
Held as hygroscopic water on the particle surfaces
questions.solution:
**The moisture retained after free gravitational drainage has ceased.**

After irrigation or heavy rain the soil is briefly saturated. Gravity then drains the excess over a day or two, and what remains — held in the pores by **surface tension** — is the field capacity, corresponding to a suction of about **⅓ bar**.

The moisture states, in decreasing order of water content:

| State | Suction | Water present |
|---|---|---|
| **Saturation** | 0 | All pores full |
| **Field capacity** | **⅓ bar** | **Capillary water, after free drainage** |
| **Permanent wilting point** | **15 bar** | Plant can no longer extract; does not recover |
| Hygroscopic | > 31 bar | Tightly adsorbed films only |

So option (c) is **saturation**, (b) the **wilting point** and (d) **hygroscopic** water — all real states, but different ones.

**The quantity irrigation design actually uses:**

> **Available moisture = Field capacity − Permanent wilting point**

That is the whole usable reservoir in the root zone. **Gravitational** water drains away too fast to be useful, and **hygroscopic** water is held far beyond root suction — only the **capillary** water between the two limits is available to the crop.

**How it fixes the irrigation schedule.** Water is applied before the soil dries to the wilting point, when a permitted fraction — the **readily available moisture**, commonly 50 to 75% of the total — has been depleted. The depth to apply follows directly:

> **d = γ_d × D × (FC − w_before)**

with D the root-zone depth. Aggregated over the season and divided by the irrigation efficiency, that becomes the **gross irrigation requirement** on which the canal is sized.

**Why the soil type matters so much.** Field capacity and available moisture both depend strongly on texture:

| Soil | Available moisture |
|---|---|
| Sandy | Low — drains fast, needs **frequent light** irrigation |
| **Loam** | **Highest** — the ideal |
| Clayey | Holds much water, but a large fraction is unavailable |

So a sandy soil is irrigated little and often, a clayey one heavily and seldom — the same seasonal total delivered on quite different schedules.

examTip.trick: **Field capacity** is what the soil **retains against gravity** after free drainage has stopped — the upper limit of water available to plants.
examTip.mnemonic: **Available water = FIELD CAPACITY − PERMANENT WILTING POINT.** Above FC the water drains away (and is wasted); below PWP it is held too tightly for roots. That difference is the entire basis of **irrigation scheduling** — and it is largest in loams, small in sands, and deceptively small in clays.

questions.stem: Kennedy's critical velocity in a canal is the velocity which:
options: Just causes scouring of the canal bed
Is the maximum permissible for the lining material
Keeps the channel free from both silting and scouring
Corresponds to critical flow, with a Froude number of unity
questions.solution:
**The velocity that keeps the channel free from both silting and scouring.**

Kennedy observed, from the Upper Bari Doab canal in 1895, that a stable channel maintains a velocity high enough to keep silt in suspension but not high enough to erode the bed. He attributed the suspension to **eddies generated from the bed**, and so related the critical velocity to the **depth**:

> **V₀ = 0.55 m y^{0.64}**

where y is the flow depth and **m** the critical velocity ratio, allowing for silt grade — m = 1.0 for the silt on which he calibrated it, rising to 1.1 or 1.2 for coarser material and falling to 0.8 or 0.9 for finer.

**Note carefully that this is not the "critical velocity" of open-channel hydraulics**, which is the velocity at **Fr = 1** separating subcritical from supercritical flow. The two share a name and nothing else, which is why option (d) is the trap.

**The limitation that Lacey corrected.** Kennedy's theory gives **one equation** but the design needs **three unknowns** — bed width, depth and slope. So the slope had to be assumed from experience (or from Kutter's equation), and the bed width guessed and iterated, which meant different engineers reached different sections for the same duty.

**Lacey's advance** was to supply enough independent relations to fix the section completely:

| Quantity | Lacey |
|---|---|
| Silt factor | **f = 1.76√d** (d in mm) |
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = 4.75√Q** |
| **Scour depth** | **R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Slope** | **S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** |
| Velocity | V = (Qf²/140)^{1/6} |

Lacey also replaced Kennedy's reliance on **bed** eddies with eddies from the **whole wetted perimeter**, and specified the **semi-ellipse** as the ideal regime shape.

Both theories apply only to a channel in **regime** — flowing in incoherent alluvium of the same grade as the material it transports. Neither applies to a **lined** canal, where the boundary is non-erodible and the design is simply a matter of maximum permissible velocity and Manning's equation.

examTip.trick: Kennedy observed that a canal in regime neither scours nor silts, and defined the **critical velocity V₀ = 0.55 m y^0.64** at which that balance holds.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kennedy fixed the VELOCITY; LACEY went further and fixed the whole SECTION** (P = 4.75√Q, R = 0.473(Q/f)^⅓, S = f^(5/3)/(3340Q^(1/6))). Lacey's advance was recognising that a regime channel adjusts its **width, depth AND slope**, not just its velocity. The modern successor is the **tractive force** method, checking τ₀ = γRS.

questions.stem: A canal aligned along a watershed or ridge line has the advantage that:
options: It can irrigate on one side only
It follows the shortest possible route
questions.solution:
**It needs no cross-drainage works.**

A **watershed (ridge) canal** runs along the highest line of the country. Since a watershed is by definition the divide between two drainage basins, **no natural stream crosses it** — every drain runs *away* from it, downhill on either side.

That single geometric fact produces the decisive economy: **cross-drainage works are the most expensive structures in an irrigation system**, and a ridge alignment eliminates them entirely.

The further advantage follows from the same position: the canal commands land falling away on **both sides**, so it can irrigate a much larger area by gravity. Option (c) states the reverse and describes a **contour canal**.

The alignments compared:

| Alignment | Runs | Cross-drainage | Irrigates |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Watershed (ridge)** | Along the **ridge line** | **None needed** | **Both sides** |
| **Contour** | Along a contour, across the slope | **Many** — every stream must be crossed | **One side only** (the lower) |
| Side-slope | Along the slope, parallel to the drainage | Few | Limited |

So a **contour** canal is unavoidable in hilly terrain, where no usable ridge line exists, and it pays for that with aqueducts, syphons and super-passages at every stream.

**Why the other options fail.** Least excavation (a) is not guaranteed — a ridge line usually requires more earthwork, since the natural surface undulates along it and the canal must hold a gentle uniform gradient. Shortest route (d) is also wrong: following the ridge is generally **longer** than a direct line.

So the trade is real: a ridge canal is **longer and needs more earthwork**, but it avoids the cross-drainage structures and commands twice the area. On the Terai plains, where broad watersheds exist between the major rivers, that trade is overwhelmingly favourable — which is why the main canals of the large Nepali schemes are ridge canals.

**The cross-drainage works a contour canal needs**, for reference: an **aqueduct** (canal over drain, drain flowing freely), **syphon aqueduct** (canal over drain, drain under pressure), **super passage** (drain over canal) and **canal syphon** (canal under drain, under pressure).

examTip.trick: A **ridge (watershed) canal** runs along the high ground, so **no natural drainage crosses it** — every stream flows away from the ridge on either side.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ridge canal: NO cross-drainage works, and it commands land on BOTH sides — but it needs a long lead to climb to the ridge. CONTOUR canal: reaches the command quickly but crosses every drain, so it needs aqueducts and syphons. WATERSHED alignment is preferred wherever the topography permits.**

questions.stem: The principal difference between a weir and a barrage is that a barrage:
options: Has gates over most of its length, so the water level is controlled by gate operation
Is always built of masonry rather than concrete
Stores water for the whole irrigation season
Is built only on non-alluvial rivers
questions.solution:
**A barrage has gates over most of its length, so the level is controlled by gate operation.**

Both are **diversion** works — they raise the upstream water level to feed a canal, and neither provides seasonal storage. The distinction is how that level is achieved:

| | **Weir** | **Barrage** |
|---|---|---|
| Level raised by | A **raised crest**, with small shutters | **Gates**, on a low crest |
| Control | Little or none | **Full control** by raising and lowering gates |
| Crest height | High | **Low** |
| **Afflux** in flood | **Large** — level rises with discharge | **Small** — gates opened to pass the flood |
| Submergence of land upstream | More | **Less** |
| Cost | **Lower** | Higher |
| Roadway | Rarely | **Usually carried across** |
| Silting upstream | More | Less; gates can be flushed |

**Why the gates matter so much.** Being able to pass a flood by opening the gates keeps the **afflux** small, so much less land is submerged upstream — which in a densely settled flood plain is often the decisive consideration, and one that outweighs the higher construction cost. Gate operation also allows silt to be **flushed** through rather than accumulating in the pond.

Option (c) is the key confusion to avoid: **neither** a weir nor a barrage stores water for the season. That is a **storage dam**, an entirely different structure with a reservoir behind it. A diversion work merely lifts the level enough to command the canal.

**The components of a barrage headworks**, examined as a set:

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Barrage with gates** | Raises and controls the level |
| **Under-sluices** | Low bays near the canal head; **flush accumulated silt** |
| **Divide wall** | Separates the under-sluice pocket from the main weir |
| **Head regulator** | Controls discharge into the canal |
| **Silt excluder** | Skims the silt-laden bottom layer away from the canal |
| **Fish ladder** | Lets fish migrate upstream |
| Guide banks, aprons, cut-offs | Train the flow; resist scour and seepage |

The floor is designed against seepage by **Khosla's theory**, with the **exit gradient** checked against piping at a factor of safety of 4 to 5 — the quantity that Bligh's and Lane's earlier creep theories could not supply.

examTip.trap: **Weir** and **barrage** are constantly confused. A **weir** is a mostly solid raised crest; a **barrage** is a low crest with **gates over most of its length**.
examTip.trick: Ask what controls the pond level. If gates do, it is a barrage; if the crest height does, it is a weir.
examTip.mnemonic: **Barrage: gates control the level, so afflux and submergence upstream are CONTROLLED and can be released in a flood. Weir: cheaper, no operating staff, but the pond level and the upstream flooding are fixed by the crest.** Barrages cost more and are almost always preferred on large alluvial rivers.

questions.stem: In Khosla's theory of seepage, the quantity that governs the safety of a hydraulic structure against piping is the:
options: Uplift pressure at the downstream end
questions.solution:
**The exit gradient.**

Piping begins at the **downstream exit**, where seepage water emerges. If the upward hydraulic gradient there is large enough to lift the soil grains, they are carried away; a small channel forms and works **backward** beneath the structure, undermining it. So the governing quantity is the gradient **at the point of emergence**, not the length of the seepage path.

Khosla gives it as

> **G_E = (H/d) × 1/(π√λ)**,  with λ = (1 + √(1 + α²))/2 and α = b/d

and the requirement is that G_E stay safely below the **critical hydraulic gradient** — that at which the effective stress reaches zero:

> **i_cr = (G_s − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1.0**

with a factor of safety of **4 to 5**. In practice permissible exit gradients are about **1/4 to 1/5 for shingle, 1/5 to 1/6 for coarse sand, and 1/6 to 1/7 for fine sand** — the finer the soil, the more easily it pipes.

**This is exactly what the earlier theories could not deliver.** Bligh's and Lane's creep theories give only a **creep length** and a coefficient, so they can say whether the path is long enough by empirical comparison, but they cannot compute the gradient at the exit — the thing that actually decides whether piping occurs. Options (a) and (b) belong to those older methods.

| Theory | Basis | Gives exit gradient? |
|---|---|---|
| **Bligh** | Uniform head loss; horizontal and vertical creep **equally** weighted | **No** |
| **Lane** | Vertical creep weighted **3×** horizontal | **No** |
| **Khosla** | **Potential flow theory** with correction factors | **Yes** |

Khosla also showed that head loss is **not uniform** along the path — contradicting the central assumption of both predecessors — and that **vertical cut-offs are far more effective** than horizontal floor length.

**Hence the design measures**, which follow directly from the formula: G_E falls as **d** (the depth of the downstream cut-off) increases, so a **deep downstream sheet pile or cut-off wall** is the primary remedy. Others are lengthening the impervious floor, providing a **drainage blanket or inverted filter** at the exit to load the emerging water, and relief wells.

**Uplift pressure** (option c) is a genuine and separate design consideration — it determines the required **thickness of the floor**, which must be heavy enough not to be lifted — but it is not the piping criterion.

examTip.trick: Khosla abandoned Bligh's creep length entirely and solved the **actual potential flow**, showing that the **exit gradient** at the downstream end governs safety against piping.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bligh counted length (and weighted vertical and horizontal EQUALLY, which is his fatal flaw); LANE weighted vertical 3:1; KHOSLA solved the flow.** Khosla's two practical outcomes: safety depends on the **EXIT GRADIENT**, and a **downstream cut-off is far more effective** than a longer horizontal floor.

questions.stem: A spur (groyne) projecting from a river bank is provided mainly to:
options: Increase the discharge capacity of the river
Deflect the flow away from the bank and protect it from erosion
questions.solution:
**To deflect the flow away from the bank and protect it from erosion.**

A spur is a structure projecting **transversely** from the bank into the river. By pushing the main current away from the bank it protects the bank itself, and it also induces **deposition** in the sheltered pockets between successive spurs, which reclaims the bank line over time.

**The types, distinguished by their inclination to the flow:**

| Type | Inclination | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Repelling** | Pointing **upstream**, at 60–70° | **Repels** the current strongly away from the bank; the most common |
| **Attracting** | Pointing **downstream** | Draws the flow towards itself; used to hold a channel in position |
| **Deflecting** | Perpendicular | Locally changes flow direction only |
| **Denehy's T-head** | T-shaped head | Keeps the scour hole away from the shank |
| Submerged (bed) spur | Below water level | Guides bed load; protects the bed |

**The critical design point** is that a spur creates its own hazard: the current, deflected around the nose, forms a **deep scour hole** there. That hole is the usual cause of spur failure, so the nose must be founded deep and heavily armoured with a **launching apron** — stone or gabions sized so that as the bed scours, the apron launches down the face of the hole and armours it.

The scour depth is estimated from **Lacey's regime depth** R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3}, with the design value at the nose taken as **2.0 to 2.5 R**.

**How spurs relate to the other river training works:**

| Work | Action |
|---|---|
| **Spurs / groynes** | **Deflect** flow away from the bank |
| **Guide banks** | **Guide** flow axially through a bridge or barrage waterway |
| **Revetment / pitching** | **Armour** the bank in place, without projecting |
| Cut-off | Shortens a meander loop |
| Levee / marginal bund | Confines flood water |

So a spur works by **redirecting** the flow while a revetment works by **resisting** it — an important distinction, since a revetment protects only the reach it covers whereas a spur influences the channel's alignment.

Spurs are normally built in a **series**, spaced at 2 to 4 times their length, so that the protection is continuous and the flow cannot re-attack the bank between them. A single isolated spur usually causes more trouble than it prevents.

examTip.trick: A spur projects into the river and **deflects the current away from the bank**, creating a slack zone behind it where sediment deposits and the bank is protected.
examTip.mnemonic: **Attracting, deflecting and repelling spurs — the angle to the bank decides which.** A **repelling** spur points upstream (about 60–70°) and is the usual protective type. All of them are protected by a **launching apron**, which is designed to be undermined and to fall into the scour hole that forms at the nose.

questions.stem: The sinuosity of a river is defined as the ratio of:
options: Length along the channel to length along the valley
Radius of curvature to channel width
questions.solution:
**Length along the channel ÷ length along the valley.**

> **Sinuosity = channel length / valley length**

It measures how much longer the winding channel is than the straight-line distance down the valley, so it is always **≥ 1**.

The classification:

| Sinuosity | River |
|---|---|
| < 1.05 | Straight |
| 1.05 – 1.5 | Sinuous |
| **> 1.5** | **Meandering** |

**Why rivers meander at all.** A perfectly straight alluvial channel is unstable. Any small disturbance sets up a slight curvature, and thereafter the flow attacks the **outer bank** (where velocity and depth are greatest) while depositing on the **inner bank** as a point bar. The bend therefore grows and migrates, and the pattern propagates downstream.

**The characteristic asymmetry of a bend** is worth carrying, because it dictates where protection is needed:

| Bank | Flow | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Outer (concave)** | **Faster, deeper** | **Erosion** — this is where spurs and revetments go |
| **Inner (convex)** | Slower, shallower | **Deposition** — point bar forms |

The **helicoidal (spiral) flow** within the bend is the mechanism: surface water moves outward, plunges down the outer bank, and returns along the bed carrying sediment to the inner bank.

**The other meander parameters**, which the distractors name:

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Meander length** | Distance between two successive bends of the same phase |
| **Meander belt width** | Width of the band the meanders occupy |
| **Radius of curvature** | Of an individual bend |

Empirically the meander length is roughly **6 to 10 times the channel width**, and both meander length and belt width correlate with the **dominant discharge** — the flow that does the most cumulative channel-forming work, commonly the bankfull flow of 1 to 2 year return period.

**Why it matters practically.** A meandering river continually shifts, so:

- a **bridge or barrage** must be sited where the channel is relatively stable, and protected by **guide banks** to hold the flow axially through the waterway;
- **land is lost** on the outer banks — a recurrent cause of boundary disputes in the Terai;
- an **oxbow lake** forms when a loop is finally cut off, either naturally or by an engineered **cut-off** that shortens the course deliberately.

examTip.trick: **Sinuosity = channel length ÷ valley length.** A perfectly straight river has sinuosity 1; the conventional threshold for calling a river **meandering** is about **1.5**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Straight ≈ 1, meandering > 1.5, and braided rivers have LOW sinuosity but MULTIPLE channels.** The distinction matters for bridge siting: a **braided** river (most of Nepal's Terai rivers) wanders across its whole belt, which is why **guide banks** are needed to confine it to the opening.

questions.stem: A canal outlet whose discharge depends on the water levels in both the distributary and the watercourse is called:
questions.solution:
**A non-modular outlet.**

Outlets are classified by **what their discharge depends on**, which is the whole basis of the topic:

| Outlet | Discharge depends on | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| **Non-modular** | **Both** the distributary and the watercourse level | Variable |
| **Semi-modular (flexible)** | The **distributary** level only | ≈ 1 for a proportional outlet |
| **Rigid module** | **Nothing** — discharge is constant | **Zero** |

A non-modular outlet is simply a **submerged pipe or orifice**: the discharge follows the **difference** in head across it, so it changes if either level changes.

**Why that is a problem.** A cultivator downstream can increase his own supply by lowering his watercourse level — deepening or clearing it — drawing more than his sanctioned share at the expense of others. The outlet gives no guarantee of equitable distribution, which is exactly what an irrigation system needs to provide.

Its advantages are simplicity, cheapness, and the ability to work with a very **small available head**, which is why non-modular outlets remain common despite the drawback.

**A semi-modular outlet** removes the downstream dependence by making the flow pass through a **free (supercritical) condition**, so conditions downstream cannot propagate back upstream. The standard forms are the **open flume** and the **Kennedy's gauge outlet**.

**The concepts used to compare them:**

> **Flexibility F** = (dq/q)/(dQ/Q) — the outlet's response relative to the distributary's
> **Sensitivity** = (dq/q)/(dG/G) — response to a change in distributary **depth**

| Outlet | Flexibility |
|---|---|
| **Proportional** | **F = 1** — the share stays constant as supply varies |
| Hyper-proportional | F > 1 — takes more than its share when supply rises |
| Sub-proportional | F < 1 |
| **Rigid module** | **Sensitivity 0** — fixed discharge whatever the level |

The **proportional** outlet is the ideal for equitable rotation: when the canal runs at reduced supply, every outlet's share falls by the same fraction, so no one is favoured. A **rigid module** guarantees the sanctioned discharge absolutely, but cannot pass a share of surplus water when the canal runs high.

examTip.trick: Classify outlets by what their discharge depends on: **non-modular** — both upstream and downstream levels; **semi-module (flexible)** — upstream level only; **rigid module** — neither, the discharge is constant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Non-modular is the WORST for equitable distribution**, because a farmer can increase his share by lowering his own watercourse level. A **rigid module** is the fairest — its **sensitivity is ZERO**, so the discharge is unaffected by anyone's interference.

questions.stem: The drainage coefficient of an agricultural drainage system is expressed as the:
options: Ratio of drained area to total area
Ratio of drain length to area served
Depth of water to be removed from the drained area in 24 hours
questions.solution:
**The depth of water to be removed from the drained area in 24 hours.**

It is expressed in **mm/day** or as a rate per unit area, and it is the design parameter for a drainage system — the analogue of the irrigation requirement, but for taking water **away** rather than supplying it.

Typical values: **6 to 12 mm/day** for surface drainage, and lower for sub-surface systems.

**What it must accommodate:**

| Source | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **Excess rainfall** not lost to evapotranspiration or deep percolation | The largest term |
| **Excess irrigation** water applied beyond the crop need | Significant where efficiency is poor |
| **Seepage** from canals and adjacent land | Often the dominant cause of a rising water table |
| Artesian or groundwater inflow | Site-specific |

Note the second and third rows: much of what a drainage system removes is water the **irrigation system itself** delivered. That is why drainage and irrigation must be designed **together** — a command area given canals without drains will waterlog within a decade or two.

**How the coefficient sizes the works.** It converts to a discharge:

> Q = (drainage coefficient × area) / (24 × 3600)

and that Q then fixes the drain sections by Manning's equation, and the spacing of sub-surface drains through the **Hooghoudt equation**, which relates drain spacing to permeability, the depth to the impermeable layer and the permitted height of the water table between drains.

**The two families of drainage:**

| Type | Removes | Methods |
|---|---|---|
| **Surface** | **Ponded water from the surface** | Open ditches, **bedding** with dead furrows, land grading, surface inlets |
| **Sub-surface** | **Lowers the water table** | **Tile drains**, perforated pipe, mole drains, French drains, **vertical drainage by tube wells** |

**Why it matters.** Waterlogging saturates the root zone and displaces soil air, so the crop suffocates; and a shallow water table brings salts to the surface by **capillary rise**, where evaporation concentrates them. Left long enough that produces a **sodic soil** with pH above 10 — structureless and practically infertile, requiring **gypsum** before it can even be leached.

So the drainage coefficient is ultimately a measure of how much water must be removed to keep the land productive at all.

examTip.trick: The **drainage coefficient** is the depth of water the system must remove from the whole area in **24 hours** — expressed as a depth so it scales directly with area.
examTip.mnemonic: **Expressed as a depth per day, so multiply by area for the discharge.** It is set by the **crop's tolerance to submergence** and the rainfall — rice tolerates standing water for days, most other crops for hours, which is why the coefficient differs so much between them.

questions.stem: A mass curve of inflow is used in hydropower and reservoir planning to determine the:
options: Firm power available at the site
Storage capacity required to meet a given demand
questions.solution:
**The storage capacity required to meet a given demand.**

A **mass curve** (Rippl diagram) plots the **cumulative** inflow volume against time. Its slope at any point is therefore the **rate of inflow**, and the demand can be drawn on the same axes as a line whose slope is the demand rate.

**How the storage is read off.** Draw tangents to the **peaks** of the mass curve, parallel to the demand line. The **maximum vertical intercept** between a tangent and the curve is the storage required — physically, the largest cumulative deficit the reservoir must cover during a dry spell.

| Feature of the diagram | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Slope of the mass curve** | Rate of **inflow** |
| **Slope of the demand line** | Rate of **draw-off** |
| Curve steeper than the demand line | Inflow exceeds demand — reservoir **filling** |
| Curve flatter than the demand line | Demand exceeds inflow — reservoir **emptying** |
| **Maximum vertical intercept** | **Required storage capacity** |

So the mass curve answers the storage question, and it can equally be used in reverse: given a fixed storage, it gives the **maximum uniform demand** the reservoir can sustain.

**Why the other options belong to different tools:**

| Question | Tool |
|---|---|
| **Storage required** | **Mass (Rippl) curve** |
| **Firm power / available power** | **Flow duration curve**, read at Q₉₀ or Q₉₅ |
| **Peak flood discharge** | Flood frequency analysis; rational method; unit hydrograph |
| Sediment yield | Sediment rating curve; reservoir sedimentation survey |

The **flow duration curve** is the one to keep distinct: it plots discharge against the **percentage of time exceeded**, and it answers *how much power is available and how reliably*. The mass curve plots **cumulative volume against time** and answers *how much storage is needed*. Both are built from the same streamflow record, for different purposes.

**Why storage matters so much in Nepal.** A run-of-river scheme generates whatever the river carries, and Himalayan dry-season flows are a small fraction of monsoon flows — so its **firm power may be only 20 to 30%** of installed capacity. Storage converts monsoon surplus into dry-season firm power, which is precisely the deficit the national system faces. The mass curve is the tool that sizes it.

A practical caution: the storage so determined must be increased for **evaporation losses** and for **dead storage** to accommodate the sediment expected over the project's life — which in Himalayan rivers is substantial.

examTip.trick: A **mass curve** plots **cumulative inflow against time**. Drawing demand lines tangent to its peaks and troughs gives the **maximum departure** — which is the **storage** needed to sustain that demand.
examTip.mnemonic: **The largest vertical gap between the tangent and the curve IS the required storage.** Its converse use is equally important: for a **given reservoir capacity**, the mass curve tells you the **maximum demand that can be sustained** — the firm yield. This is Rippl's method, and it is still the first tool in any storage study.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river hydropower scheme, the component that conveys water from the intake to the forebay under gravity at low pressure is the:
questions.solution:
**The headrace.**

The headrace is the **low-pressure** conveyance — a canal, tunnel or low-pressure pipe — carrying water from the intake and settling works to the forebay, at a gentle gradient under gravity.

Tracing the whole water route of a run-of-river scheme, which is the useful thing to have in order:

> **Intake → gravel trap → settling basin → headrace (canal or tunnel) → forebay → surge tank → penstock → turbine (spiral case → runner) → draft tube → tailrace**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Intake** | Diverts water from the river; **trash rack** excludes debris |
| **Gravel trap** | Removes coarse **bed load** |
| **Settling basin** | Removes finer **suspended sediment** — down to 0.1–0.2 mm |
| **Headrace** | **Low-pressure gravity conveyance** to the forebay |
| **Forebay** | Small balancing storage; final settling; houses the penstock intake |
| **Surge tank** | Absorbs **water hammer** on load change |
| **Penstock** | **High-pressure** pipe delivering the head to the turbine |
| **Draft tube** | Recovers residual kinetic energy at runner exit |
| **Tailrace** | Returns water to the river |

So the **penstock** (option a) is the *high-pressure* conveyance — the distinction the question is testing — and the **draft tube** and **tailrace** are on the downstream side of the machine.

**The key contrast:**

| | Headrace | Penstock |
|---|---|---|
| Pressure | **Low** — often free surface | **High** — full pipe |
| Gradient | **Gentle**, along the valley side | **Steep**, dropping to the powerhouse |
| Purpose | **Carry** water while conserving head | **Convert** head to pressure at the machine |
| Velocity | 1 – 2 m/s | **5 – 8 m/s** |
| Material | Concrete-lined canal or tunnel | **Steel** |

The design logic follows: the headrace **preserves** elevation by running nearly level along the contour, and the penstock then **spends** it in one steep drop. That is precisely why Nepal's terrain suits run-of-river schemes — a long headrace along the valley side can gain hundreds of metres of head relative to the river below without any dam at all.

The **surge tank** sits at the junction of the two because that is where the pressure regime changes: it confines the water-hammer pressure to the short penstock rather than letting it travel back along the whole headrace.

examTip.trick: Trace the water's path: **intake → headrace → settling basin → forebay (or surge tank) → penstock → turbine → tailrace.** The headrace is the low-pressure conveyance from intake to forebay.
examTip.mnemonic: **Headrace conveys at low pressure (canal or tunnel, near-horizontal); PENSTOCK delivers at high pressure (steep, closed pipe).** The forebay or surge tank sits between them precisely to keep the water hammer out of the long headrace — it protects only what is **upstream** of it.

questions.stem: The diversity factor of a power system is always:
options: Greater than or equal to unity
questions.solution:
**Greater than or equal to unity.**

> **Diversity factor = Σ(individual maximum demands) / (maximum demand of the system)**

Consumers do not all reach their peak at the same instant — a household peaks in the evening, an office at midday, a factory during its shift. So the **system** peak is always **less than or equal to** the sum of the individual peaks, and the ratio is therefore **≥ 1**.

It equals exactly 1 only in the limiting case where every consumer peaks simultaneously, which does not happen in a real system of any size. Typical values are **1.2 to 3.0**, rising as the mix of consumer types becomes more varied.

**Why it matters commercially and technically.** Diversity is what makes an electricity system economic: because the peaks do not coincide, the utility can serve a total connected load far larger than its installed capacity. A higher diversity factor means:

- **less generating and network capacity** needed per unit of connected load;
- better utilisation of the plant that exists;
- lower cost per unit supplied.

That is also the argument for **interconnecting** systems and for encouraging a **mixed** consumer base rather than a single dominant type.

**The factors, and which way each runs** — the point most often confused:

| Factor | Definition | Range |
|---|---|---|
| **Load factor** | Average load / peak demand | **≤ 1** |
| **Capacity factor** | Average load / **installed capacity** | ≤ 1 |
| **Utilisation factor** | Peak demand / installed capacity | ≤ 1 |
| **Demand factor** | Peak demand / **connected load** | ≤ 1 |
| **Diversity factor** | **Σ individual peaks / system peak** | **≥ 1** |

So the diversity factor is the **only one of the five that exceeds unity**, which is a reliable way to remember it. Option (c) is wrong because the load factor is a quite different ratio and is always ≤ 1.

Note the relationship **capacity factor = load factor × utilisation factor**, since (average/capacity) = (average/peak) × (peak/capacity).

**For Nepal**, the related and more binding constraint is **seasonal** rather than daily: run-of-river plants produce abundantly in the monsoon and little in winter, so the system's difficulty is not merely diversity of consumers within a day but the mismatch between generation and demand across the year — which is what storage projects and regional interconnection address.

examTip.trick: **Diversity factor = sum of individual maximum demands ÷ system maximum demand.** Because consumers do not all peak at the same instant, the sum of their individual peaks exceeds the system peak — so the ratio is always **≥ 1**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Diversity factor ≥ 1 (the ODD ONE OUT); load factor and capacity factor are both ≤ 1.** Diversity is what makes electricity supply economic at all — a utility can serve a thousand houses with far less than a thousand times one house's peak demand.

questions.stem: A load duration curve is obtained from the chronological load curve by:
options: Arranging the load ordinates in descending order of magnitude
Integrating the load curve over time
Plotting the cumulative energy against time
Differentiating the load curve with respect to time
questions.solution:
**By arranging the load ordinates in descending order of magnitude.**

The chronological **load curve** plots demand against the time of day (or year), in sequence. Re-sorting those same ordinates from largest to smallest gives the **load duration curve** — demand against the **percentage of time for which that demand is equalled or exceeded**.

The information is not changed, only reorganised, which has two useful consequences:

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Area under both curves is identical** | Both represent the same total **energy** |
| Ordinates re-sorted, not recomputed | The **peak** and the **minimum** demand are unchanged |
| Time axis becomes **duration**, not clock time | Chronological information is **lost** |

That last row is the trade: the load duration curve cannot tell you *when* the peak occurred, only *how long* demands of each level persisted.

**Why it is drawn.** It is the natural tool for deciding the **plant mix**, because it shows directly how much capacity is needed for how long:

| Region of the curve | Duty | Suitable plant |
|---|---|---|
| **Base** — the demand present nearly all the time | **Base load** | Hydro (storage), nuclear, large coal — **low running cost** |
| **Middle** | Intermediate | — |
| **Peak** — high demand for only a few hours | **Peak load** | **Gas turbine, diesel, pumped storage** — cheap to build, expensive to run |

That matching is the whole point: it is uneconomic to meet a two-hour peak with plant that must run continuously to justify its capital cost, and equally uneconomic to meet the base load with plant that burns expensive fuel.

**The related curves**, which the distractors describe:

| Curve | Plots | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Load curve** | Demand vs **time of day** | Daily pattern; peak timing |
| **Load duration curve** | Demand vs **% time exceeded** | **Plant mix** |
| **Mass (Rippl) curve** | **Cumulative inflow** vs time | **Reservoir storage** — option (c) |
| **Flow duration curve** | Discharge vs % time exceeded | **Firm power** at a hydro site |

Note the exact analogy between the last two rows: the **flow** duration curve is to a river what the **load** duration curve is to a demand, and at a fixed head the former converts directly into a **power** duration curve via P = ηγQH — from which the firm power is read at Q₉₀ or Q₉₅.

examTip.trick: A **load duration curve** is simply the **chronological load curve re-sorted** into descending order — so it shows for how many hours the load exceeds any given value, but loses all information about *when*.
examTip.mnemonic: **The AREA under both curves is the same — it is the total energy.** The load duration curve is what determines the **plant mix**: the flat base of the curve is met by low-running-cost **base load** plant, and the narrow peak by flexible, fast-starting **peaking** plant.

questions.stem: An arch dam is most suitable for a site with:
options: A wide valley and weak foundation
A wide valley and sound rock foundation
A narrow gorge with sound rock abutments
A broad flood plain with deep alluvium
questions.solution:
**A narrow gorge with sound rock abutments.**

An arch dam carries the water thrust **horizontally into the abutments** by arch action, rather than resisting it by its own weight. That mechanism dictates the site absolutely:

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Narrow gorge** | A short span makes arch action efficient; the ratio of crest length to height should be small |
| **Sound, strong rock abutments** | The entire thrust is delivered into the canyon walls — if they yield or fail, the dam fails |
| Sound foundation | As for any dam |

**The reward is material.** Because it does not rely on weight, an arch dam uses **far less concrete** than a gravity dam of the same height — often a third or less. Where the site suits it, that is a decisive economy.

**The risk is concentrated.** All the load goes into two points, so an arch dam is unforgiving of abutment weakness, and it is more sensitive to **foundation movement and temperature change** than a gravity dam. It is a genuinely indeterminate structure, so settlement and thermal effects induce real stresses in it.

**Matching the dam type to the site**, which is the general skill being tested:

| Site | Suitable dam |
|---|---|
| **Narrow gorge, sound rock** | **Arch** |
| Wide valley, **sound rock** | **Gravity** |
| Wide valley, **weak or variable** foundation | **Earthfill / rockfill** — flexible, spreads load |
| Sound rock, concrete or aggregate scarce | **Buttress** |
| Broad flood plain, deep alluvium | Embankment dam, or a **barrage** rather than a dam |

So options (a) and (b) describe embankment and gravity sites respectively, and (d) a site where no concrete dam is appropriate at all.

**The classifications to keep distinct**, since a dam is described by all three:

| Basis | Types |
|---|---|
| **Structural action / material** | **Gravity, arch, buttress, embankment** |
| **Hydraulic design** | **Overflow** (spillway section) and **non-overflow** |
| Function | **Storage, diversion, detention, debris** |

A large scheme normally combines hydraulic types in one barrier — a concrete overflow spillway section flanked by non-overflow embankment sections. And note that an **embankment dam can never be overtopped**, so it must always have a spillway located in competent separate ground, which is one reason **shaft (morning glory)** spillways are used with them.

examTip.trick: An arch dam carries its load **horizontally into the abutments** by arch action, so it needs **sound rock on both flanks** and a **narrow** valley for the arch to be efficient.
examTip.mnemonic: **Arch dam: narrow gorge, sound abutments, minimum concrete — the most material-efficient dam there is. GRAVITY dam: strong foundation, wide valleys acceptable. EARTH dam: weaker or variable foundations.** The **foundation and valley shape**, not the height, choose the dam type.

questions.stem: In a gravity dam, a drainage gallery is provided mainly to:
options: Intercept seepage and relieve uplift pressure on the base
questions.solution:
**To intercept seepage and relieve uplift pressure on the base.**

Water seeping through the foundation and through the concrete acts **upward** on the base of the dam. That **uplift pressure** reduces the effective weight — and since a gravity dam resists entirely **by its weight**, uplift directly undermines both stability checks:

| Check | Effect of uplift |
|---|---|
| **Overturning** about the toe | Reduces the resisting moment |
| **Sliding** on the base | Reduces the normal force, hence the frictional resistance |
| **Tension at the heel** | Makes it more likely, which then admits more water — a vicious circle |

A **drainage gallery** runs longitudinally near the upstream face, with **relief holes** drilled from it down into the foundation. Seepage is intercepted, led into the gallery and drained away, so the **uplift diagram is cut back** sharply behind the upstream face rather than building up across the whole base.

It works together with the **grout curtain** — a line of grouted holes near the heel that lengthens the seepage path and reduces the quantity of flow. The pairing is the standard arrangement:

> **Grout curtain reduces the seepage; drainage gallery relieves what still gets through.**

**The gallery's other uses** — which are real, but secondary:

- **Access** for inspection and for instrumentation readings (option a, incomplete rather than wrong);
- Housing **uplift pressure cells, seepage measuring weirs** and other monitoring;
- Access for **further grouting** during the dam's life;
- Routing of cables and services.

**Why the other options fail.** The spillway discharge (c) passes over or through dedicated spillway bays and their energy dissipaters; **penstocks** (d) are separate conduits, sometimes embedded in the dam but never in the drainage gallery.

**The stability requirements the gallery helps satisfy** (IS 6512):

> Resultant within the **middle third** → **no tension at the heel**
> Factor of safety against **overturning** ≥ 1.5
> **Shear friction factor** against sliding ≥ 4 to 5

All three are computed with uplift **included as a load**, which is why reducing it is worth the cost of the gallery. And note from Set 3 Q93 that **buckling is not** a mode of failure for such a massive section — the real modes are overturning, sliding, tension, crushing and **piping**.

examTip.trick: **Uplift** acts upward on the base and reduces the effective weight, cutting both the sliding and the overturning resistance. A drainage gallery with relief holes near the heel **intercepts the seepage and relieves the pressure**.
examTip.mnemonic: **A grout curtain plus a drainage gallery reduces the uplift at the drain line to about ONE THIRD of the reservoir head.** The **drainage is more reliable than the grouting** — which is why both are used and why the drains are inspected and re-drilled over the dam's life. Uplift is the force most often underestimated.

questions.stem: A gravel trap in the headworks of a run-of-river plant is provided immediately after the intake to:
options: Remove the coarse bed load before it enters the conveyance system
Remove dissolved minerals from the water
questions.solution:
**To remove the coarse bed load before it enters the conveyance system.**

A gravel trap is a short widened and deepened section immediately downstream of the intake. The abrupt reduction in velocity lets the **coarse fraction** — gravel, pebbles and coarse sand rolling along the river bed — drop out, from where it is flushed back to the river.

It is the **second** of a graded series of sediment defences, each sized for a different fraction:

| Device | Removes | Position |
|---|---|---|
| **Trash rack** | **Floating debris**, logs, branches, plastic | At the intake |
| **Gravel trap** | **Coarse bed load** — gravel, coarse sand | Immediately after the intake |
| **Settling basin** | **Finer suspended sediment**, down to 0.1–0.2 mm | Before the headrace |
| Forebay | Final settling; balancing storage | Before the penstock |

The sequence runs **coarse to fine**, and each stage exists so the next is not overwhelmed by material it was never designed to handle. Sending gravel into a settling basin would fill it within days.

**Why sediment control dominates Nepali headworks design.** Himalayan rivers carry very high loads of hard **quartz and feldspar** — minerals harder than the steel of a turbine runner. Passed through the machine at high velocity that sediment:

- **abrades** buckets, guide vanes and liners;
- destroys the profile the runner was designed to, so efficiency falls;
- requires the unit to be dismantled for repair, losing generation as well as money.

Abrasion damage rises **steeply with head**, which is why a high-head **Pelton** scheme must remove particles down to about **0.1 mm** while a low-head Francis can tolerate 0.2 mm.

**Why the other options fail.** Dissolved minerals (b) are not removed by any settling structure — only by chemical treatment, and they do no harm here. Discharge is measured by a **weir or flume** (c). Storage for peaking is the job of a **forebay or pondage** (d).

**Design essentials** for the trap itself: velocity reduced enough for the target grain size to settle, a **hopper-shaped floor** sloping to a flushing outlet, and a **flushing gate** discharging back to the river below the intake. Flushing must be possible **without shutting the plant down**, or the trap becomes a liability every time it fills.

examTip.trick: Sediment is removed in **stages by size**: a **gravel trap** at the intake takes out the coarse **bed load** (rolling stones), and a **settling basin** further along removes the finer **suspended** sand.
examTip.mnemonic: **Coarse first, fine second — a settling basin cannot handle boulders.** The reason both matter: **quartz sand ERODES turbine runners fast**, and a Pelton needle or Francis runner can lose its profile in a single Himalayan monsoon.

questions.stem: A side intake in a run-of-river scheme is generally preferred to a frontal intake on a Himalayan river because it:
options: Allows a larger discharge to be diverted
Draws water from the surface layer, which carries less sediment
questions.solution:
**Because it draws from the surface layer, which carries less sediment.**

Sediment concentration in a river is **greatest near the bed** and least at the surface, and coarse material travels along the bed as bed load. A **side intake**, set into the bank with its sill raised above the bed, therefore skims the **cleaner upper layer** while the sediment-laden bottom flow passes on downstream.

That is the same principle exploited by a **silt excluder** at an irrigation headworks, whose tunnels skim the dirty bottom layer away while clearer water passes over their roofs into the canal.

**Why it matters on a Himalayan river.** The sediment load is exceptionally high and exceptionally abrasive — hard quartz and feldspar, harder than runner steel. Every tonne kept out of the intake is a tonne that:

- does not have to be settled out downstream (smaller settling basin);
- does not abrade the turbine;
- does not have to be flushed, with the water and generation that flushing costs.

So excluding sediment **at source** is far cheaper than extracting it later. That is the general rule for the whole headworks: **prevention upstream, extraction only for what gets through.**

**Further advantages of a side intake:** it is **less exposed to floods and debris** than a structure in the main current, and it can be located on the **outer bank of a bend**, where the helicoidal flow sweeps bed load towards the *inner* bank and away from the intake — a useful piece of river behaviour to exploit deliberately.

**Why the other options fail.** A side intake is not inherently cheaper (a) — it needs bank works and careful alignment. It does not permit a larger diversion (b); if anything the approach conditions limit it. And a **trash rack is required regardless** (c) — floating debris must be excluded from any intake.

**The intake types**, for orientation:

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Side intake** | Set in the bank; **skims the surface layer**; the usual choice on sediment-laden rivers |
| **Frontal intake** | Faces the flow directly; simple, but takes bed load straight in |
| **Trench (bottom rack) intake** | A screened trench across the bed; suits steep, boulder-strewn mountain streams |
| Drop / Tyrolean intake | Similar; water falls through a bar rack into a trench |

The **trench or Tyrolean** intake is worth noting as the other common Nepali solution, used on very steep streams where a bank structure is impractical — it accepts bed load deliberately and flushes it, rather than trying to exclude it.

examTip.trick: Sediment concentration is **highest near the bed** and lowest at the surface. A side intake drawing from the **upper layer** therefore takes the cleanest water available.
examTip.mnemonic: **Draw from the surface, and place the intake on the OUTSIDE of a bend** — where the secondary (helical) current sweeps the bed load toward the inside, leaving cleaner water at the outer bank. That single siting decision removes more sediment than any downstream structure.

questions.stem: An anchor block on a penstock is provided to:
options: Support the weight of the penstock only
Resist the thrust developed at bends and changes of section
Allow free longitudinal movement of the pipe
Reduce the head loss at bends
questions.solution:
**To resist the thrust developed at bends and changes of section.**

Water flowing round a bend changes direction, so its **momentum changes** — and by the momentum equation that requires a force. The pipe must deliver it, and the anchor block delivers it to the ground:

> **F = ρQ(v₂ − v₁)** plus the pressure force **pA** on each face

At a high-head penstock both terms are large: internal pressure of several hundred metres of head acting on the pipe's cross-section produces an enormous unbalanced thrust at any bend. An anchor block is a **massive concrete mass**, keyed into rock where possible, that holds the pipe rigidly in position against it.

**Where anchor blocks are placed:** at every **horizontal or vertical bend**, at changes of **diameter**, and at intervals on long straight runs to break up the accumulated frictional and gravity thrust.

**The distinction from a support pier**, which option (a) describes:

| Element | Function | Movement allowed |
|---|---|---|
| **Anchor block** | **Resists thrust**; holds the pipe rigidly | **None** |
| **Support pier (saddle)** | Carries the **weight** of pipe and water | **Slides longitudinally** |
| **Expansion joint** | Absorbs **thermal movement** | Longitudinal, freely |

So weight is carried by the piers, thrust by the anchors, and thermal movement by the expansion joints — three jobs, three elements. Option (c) is exactly what an anchor block must **prevent**, and it is the expansion joint's role instead.

The standard arrangement is therefore: **anchor block – expansion joint – several sliding support piers – expansion joint – anchor block**, so each pipe length between anchors is free to expand against a joint without transmitting that movement into the anchor.

**Why option (d) is wrong.** The bend loss h_L = k V²/2g depends on the bend's **radius and geometry**, not on how it is supported. A long-radius bend has a much lower k than a sharp mitred one — but that is a hydraulic choice made independently of anchoring.

**The related penstock design items:**

| Item | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Wall thickness** | Hoop stress **t = pD/2σ**, with p including the **water-hammer** rise |
| **Economic diameter** | Capital cost of a larger pipe against the lifetime value of head lost to friction |
| Velocity | **5 – 8 m/s** in high-head schemes |
| **Surge protection** | Surge tank or pressure relief valve, limiting Δh |
| Corrosion protection | Lining, coating, cathodic protection |

examTip.trick: At every **bend and change of section** the penstock develops an unbalanced thrust that would push the pipe out of line and pull the joints apart. An anchor block ties it to the ground.
examTip.mnemonic: **Anchor blocks resist thrust and hold the pipe in position; SUPPORT PIERS between them carry only the weight and ALLOW AXIAL MOVEMENT.** Between anchors an **expansion joint** accommodates thermal movement — because a fully restrained pipe develops **σ = αΔT·E** regardless of its length.

questions.stem: A generator with 20 poles running at a frequency of 50 Hz must rotate at a synchronous speed of:
questions.solution:
**300 rpm.**

> **N = 120 f / P**

where f is the frequency in Hz and P the number of poles.

**Substituting:**
> N = 120 × 50 / 20 = **300 rpm** ✓

Common combinations at 50 Hz, worth recognising:

| Poles | Synchronous speed |
|---|---|
| 2 | 3000 rpm |
| 4 | **1500 rpm** |
| 10 | 600 rpm |
| **20** | **300 rpm** |
| 40 | 150 rpm |

So the distractors are simply the neighbouring pole numbers — 4, 10 and 40 — which is why the arithmetic must be done rather than guessed.

**Why this matters for turbine selection.** The generator's speed is **not free**: it is fixed by the grid frequency and the pole count, and only whole numbers of pole **pairs** are possible. So the turbine must be designed to run at one of a discrete set of speeds, and that constraint feeds back into the machine choice through **specific speed**:

> **N_s = N√P / H^{5/4}**

| N_s (kW units) | Turbine | Head |
|---|---|---|
| 10 – 35 | **Pelton**, single jet | > 250 m |
| 35 – 60 | Pelton, multi-jet | High |
| 60 – 300 | **Francis** | 25 – 250 m |
| 300 – 1000 | **Kaplan** | < 25 m |

The practical consequence: a **low-head** plant has a low H, so to reach a workable specific speed it needs a **high N** — few poles, fast machine. A **high-head** Pelton needs a low N_s, so it runs slowly and needs **many poles**, hence a physically large generator. Twenty poles at 300 rpm is characteristic of a medium- to high-head machine.

Where the required turbine speed and a sensible generator speed cannot be reconciled directly, a **speed increaser (gearbox)** is used — common on small and micro hydro plants, and avoided on large ones because of the losses and maintenance it adds.

**Holding that speed** is the **governor's** job: it senses the shaft speed and adjusts the **water flow** — wicket gates on a reaction turbine, the spear valve and deflector on a Pelton — so that N, and hence the frequency, stays constant as the electrical load varies. And the machine must survive **runaway speed** if the load is lost and the governor fails: roughly **1.8 × normal for a Pelton, 2.0–2.2 for a Francis, and 2.5–3.0 for a Kaplan**.

examTip.mnemonic: **N = 120f/P — more poles, slower speed.** That is why **low-speed turbines (Kaplan, low-head Francis) need generators with MANY poles** and are physically large, while a high-speed Pelton can drive a compact 4- or 6-pole machine. The turbine's speed and the generator's pole count are chosen together.

questions.stem: In the Nagpur road plan, the road network pattern adopted was the:
questions.solution:
**The star and grid pattern.**

The **Nagpur road plan (1943–61)**, the first systematic road development plan of the subcontinent, adopted a **star and grid** network and classified roads into five categories:

| Class | Character |
|---|---|
| **National Highway** | Main arterial routes across the country |
| **State Highway** | Within a state, connecting to national highways |
| **Major District Road** | Within a district |
| **Other District Road** | Lower-order district roads |
| **Village Road** | Village to the nearest road of higher class |

Its target was a road **density** of 16 km per 100 km², computed by the well-known Nagpur formula from the numbers of towns and villages to be served.

The successive plans, each with its own pattern:

| Plan | Period | Pattern | Density target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Nagpur** | 1943–61 | **Star and grid** | 16 km/100 km² |
| **Bombay** | 1961–81 | **Square grid** | 32 km/100 km² |
| **Lucknow** | 1981–2001 | — | 82 km/100 km² |

So the patterns progressed from star-and-grid to a denser square grid as the network matured — which is why option (b), radial and circular, is the distractor: that is an **urban** pattern for a city radiating from a centre, not a national plan.

**Nepal's own classification** is the one that matters more for this examination, and it is **functional** rather than geometric:

| Class | Designation | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **National Highway** | **H** | Main arterial routes (e.g. H01 Mahendra Highway) |
| **Feeder Road** | F | District headquarters and economic centres to the highways |
| **District Road** | D | Traffic within a district |
| **Urban Road** | U | Within municipal areas |

Nepal's roads are separately classified by **terrain**, which governs the geometric standards applied: **Plain** (up to 10% cross slope), **Rolling** (10–25%), **Mountainous** (25–60%) and **Steep** (over 60%). The same functional class carries very different design speeds in different terrain — a national highway is designed for 120 km/h in the plains but as little as 40 km/h in steep country.

And note that a road is also described by **surface type** — earthen, gravelled or blacktopped — which is a construction description, not a classification of function.

examTip.trick: The Nagpur plan (1943–61) laid out India's first systematic road development framework, adopting a **star-and-grid** network geometry and classifying roads as NH, SH, MDR, ODR and Village Roads.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nagpur → star and grid; Bombay (1961–81) → hexagonal (Lucknow) pattern.** The classification into a functional hierarchy is the enduring contribution — **National Highway, Feeder, District, Urban** in Nepal's own system serves the same purpose.

questions.stem: In a traffic origin–destination study, the most suitable method for a large urban area is the:
questions.solution:
**The home interview method.**

An origin–destination (O–D) study establishes **where trips begin and end**, which is the foundation of transport planning — it determines desire lines, and hence where new roads or improvements are actually needed.

For a **large urban area** the home interview method is the standard because it captures what the others cannot:

| Advantage | Reason |
|---|---|
| **All trips**, including those wholly inside the study area | Roadside methods catch only vehicles crossing a survey station |
| **Trip purpose** | Work, education, shopping, social — essential for modelling |
| **Socio-economic data** | Income, vehicle ownership, household size — the variables that *explain* trip generation |
| **All modes**, including walking and public transport | Roadside interviews sample vehicles, not people |

That third row is decisive for planning: only household data lets trip generation be **modelled and forecast**, rather than merely described as it is today.

Its cost is that it is **expensive and slow**, so it is conducted on a **sample** — typically 1 to 10% of households, higher in smaller towns.

**The alternatives and where each fits:**

| Method | How | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Home interview** | Household survey | **Large urban areas**; comprehensive planning |
| **Road-side interview** | Drivers questioned at a station | Through traffic; bypass studies |
| **Registration number** | Numbers recorded at entry and exit, then matched | **Cordon** studies; quick and cheap |
| **Tag on vehicle** | Card fixed at entry, collected at exit | Small areas, short duration |
| Return post card | Cards handed out, returned by post | Cheap, but **low response rate** |

The **registration number** method is the practical choice for a cordon survey — it needs no cooperation from drivers and causes no delay — but it yields only the origin and destination *zones*, with no purpose or household information.

**What the study produces:** an **O–D matrix** (trips from each zone to each other zone), **desire lines** drawn between zone centroids with width proportional to trip volume, and the inputs to the four-stage transport model — **trip generation, trip distribution, modal split and traffic assignment**.

The practical relevance in Nepal: Kathmandu Valley's congestion is a distribution problem as much as a capacity one, and a proper O–D study is what distinguishes a road that relieves demand from one that merely moves the queue.

examTip.trick: For a **large urban area** the trips are too numerous and varied to intercept at the roadside. The **home interview** samples households directly and captures **all** their trips, including those by every mode.
examTip.mnemonic: **Home interview for a large area (comprehensive but expensive); ROADSIDE INTERVIEW for a cordon or screen line; REGISTRATION NUMBER or TAG methods for a small area or a single facility.** The output is an **O–D matrix**, and it is the foundation of every transport model.

questions.stem: A summit (crest) vertical curve is designed principally on the basis of:
questions.solution:
**Stopping or overtaking sight distance.**

On a **summit** curve the road surface itself obstructs the view — a driver approaching the crest cannot see over it. The curve must therefore be long enough (flat enough) that the available sight distance meets the requirement: **SSD** as a minimum, and **OSD** where overtaking is to be permitted.

Comfort is **not** the governing criterion on a summit, because the centrifugal force there acts **upward**, *opposing* gravity — so it reduces the effective weight on the vehicle and is felt as relief rather than discomfort.

**The contrast with a valley (sag) curve** is the whole point of the question:

| | **Summit (crest)** | **Valley (sag)** |
|---|---|---|
| Centrifugal force | **Upward** — opposes gravity | **Downward** — adds to gravity |
| Governing criterion | **Sight distance (SSD / OSD)** | **Headlight sight distance at night**, and **passenger comfort** |
| Why | The road surface blocks the view | By day the view is unobstructed; at **night** the headlight beam shoots up off the curve |
| Comfort | Not critical | **Critical** — the added force is felt as a jolt |

So options (a) and (b) are the **valley** curve criteria, offered as distractors.

**The design relations for a summit curve**, with L the curve length and N the deviation angle:

> **If L > S:**  L = N S² / (2(√h₁ + √h₂)²)
> **If L < S:**  L = 2S − (2(√h₁ + √h₂)²)/N

with the standard eye height **h₁ = 1.2 m** and object height **h₂ = 0.15 m** for SSD (and 1.2 m for both when checking OSD, since the object is another vehicle).

Both cases must be tried, and the one satisfying its own condition adopted.

**Vertical curves are parabolic**, not circular, because a parabola gives a **constant rate of change of grade** — the smoothest transition and the simplest to set out by offsets from the tangent.

A practical note for hill roads: providing full **OSD** over every summit is often impossible in mountainous terrain, so overtaking is prohibited and only **SSD** is provided — which is why no-overtaking zones cluster at crests and on the approaches to blind bends.
