examTip.trick: On a **summit** curve the road surface itself blocks the sight line, so the curve length is set by **sight distance**. On a **valley (sag)** curve the limit is different — **headlight** reach at night and **passenger comfort**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Summit → SIGHT DISTANCE (the crest blocks the view). Valley → HEADLIGHT distance and COMFORT (the sight line is unobstructed by day).** Two curve types, two entirely different governing criteria — a standard examination discriminator.

questions.stem: Grade compensation on a horizontal curve is provided because:
options: The superelevation reduces the effective gradient
The curve resistance adds to the grade resistance
Drainage becomes difficult on a curve
Sight distance is reduced on a curve
questions.solution:
**Because the curve resistance adds to the grade resistance.**

A vehicle climbing a gradient already works against **grade resistance**. On a curve it must additionally overcome **curve resistance** — the loss caused by the tyres having to be dragged sideways as the vehicle is turned, and by the rear wheels tracking a tighter radius than the front. The two resistances **add**, so a gradient that a loaded truck can just manage on a straight becomes impassable on a sharp curve.

**Grade compensation** flattens the gradient through the curve to keep the total resistance within what the vehicle can deliver.

**The IRC rule:**

> **Grade compensation = 30/R + 75/R percent**, subject to a maximum of **75/R**

where R is the curve radius in metres. And an important limitation:

> **No compensation is applied where the gradient is flatter than 4%**

because at such grades the combined resistance is not critical, and flattening further would create drainage problems.

**A worked illustration.** For R = 50 m: 75/50 = 1.5%. So a ruling gradient of 6% would be eased to **4.5%** through the curve.

**Where this shows up most sharply** is the **hairpin bend** on a hill road. Nepal Road Standard 2070 limits the longitudinal gradient there to **4%** — *lower* than the ruling gradient of 5 to 7% used on the open hill road — precisely because the radius is as small as 15 m and the curve resistance is at its greatest. The other hairpin parameters follow the same logic: design speed 20 km/h, minimum radius 15 m, minimum transition 15 m, and maximum superelevation 10%.

**Why the other options fail.** Superelevation (a) counters **centrifugal force**; it does not change the longitudinal gradient. Drainage (c) is a reason **not** to over-flatten a grade, so it argues against compensation rather than for it. Reduced sight distance (d) is a real problem on curves, but it is addressed by **setback distance** and clearing the inside of the curve, not by altering the gradient.

The related gradient classification: **ruling** (the design value), **limiting** (steeper, where terrain demands), **exceptional** (short unavoidable stretches) and **minimum** (about 1 in 200 to 1 in 500, needed for drainage in a lined side drain).

examTip.trick: A vehicle on a curve already faces **curve resistance** from tyre scrub. Adding a steep gradient on top of it makes the total resistance excessive — so the **gradient is EASED** on the curve.
examTip.mnemonic: **Grade compensation = (30 + R)/R percent, subject to a maximum of 75/R** — and it is **not applied on grades flatter than 4%**, where the total resistance is not a problem. Failing to compensate is why trucks stall on tight hairpin bends.

questions.stem: The softening point of bitumen is determined by the:
questions.solution:
**The ring and ball test.**

A sample of bitumen is cast in a brass **ring** and a steel **ball** of 3.5 g placed on it. The assembly is heated in a water or glycerine bath at a controlled rate of **5°C per minute**, and the **softening point** is the temperature at which the bitumen softens enough for the ball to sink through and fall a distance of **25 mm**.

Typical values are **35 to 70°C** depending on grade.

**What it tells the engineer.** Bitumen has no sharp melting point — it softens gradually — so the softening point is a measure of its **susceptibility to temperature**, and specifically of the temperature at which it will begin to flow in service. A **higher** softening point means a **harder, less temperature-susceptible** binder.

That makes it the test for selecting a grade by climate:

| Climate | Requires |
|---|---|
| **Hot** | **High** softening point — resists **bleeding and rutting** |
| **Cold** | Lower softening point — stays flexible, resists **cracking** |

Nepal spans both extremes within one road network, which is why grade selection varies by region.

**The bitumen tests, each measuring a different property** — this is the set the options are drawn from:

| Test | Measures | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| **Penetration** | **Consistency / hardness** | Needle, **100 g, 5 s, 25°C**; result in 0.1 mm units |
| **Ductility** | **Ability to stretch without breaking** | Briquette pulled at 50 mm/min, **27°C**; minimum **50 cm** |
| **Softening point** | **Temperature susceptibility** | **Ring and ball**, 5°C/min rise |
| **Float** | Consistency of **hard** bitumen, too stiff for penetration | Float in a water bath |
| Viscosity | Flow resistance | At 60°C and 135°C |
| Flash and fire point | **Safety** in heating | Pensky-Martens; flash ≥ 175°C |
| Loss on heating | Volatiles present | — |
| Specific gravity | Quality control | ≈ 0.97–1.02 |

The **float test** (option c) is the near miss worth noting: it measures consistency too, but is used for **hard** bitumens on which the penetration test would register almost nothing.

**The trend in practice** is away from penetration grading towards **viscosity grading** (IS 73:2013, grades VG-10 to VG-40), because viscosity at 60°C — close to the maximum pavement temperature — correlates better with in-service performance than a needle test at 25°C.

examTip.trick: The **ring and ball** test heats a bitumen disc supported in a ring with a steel ball on it; the softening point is the temperature at which the bitumen sags enough for the ball to fall a set distance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bitumen has no sharp melting point — it softens gradually, which is why the test defines an arbitrary but reproducible reference.** The specification set: **penetration (hardness), softening point (temperature susceptibility), ductility (≥50 cm), flash point (safety), viscosity (mixing and laying temperatures).** No single test characterises it.

questions.stem: A flaky aggregate is one whose least dimension is less than:
questions.solution:
**Less than 0.6 times its mean dimension.**

> **Flakiness index** = the percentage by weight of particles whose **least** dimension is **less than 0.6** of their mean dimension
> **Elongation index** = the percentage whose **greatest** dimension exceeds **1.8** times their mean dimension

So option (b), 1.8, is the **elongation** criterion — the intended trap, since the two indices are always taught together.

Both are determined by passing the aggregate through special gauges: a **thickness gauge** with slotted openings for flakiness, and a **length gauge** for elongation.

**Permissible limits:**

| Index | Maximum |
|---|---|
| **Flakiness** | **25%** (15% for some surfacing works) |
| **Elongation** | **15%** |
| Combined | 40% |

**Why particle shape matters so much:**

| Problem with flaky or elongated particles | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Break easily** under compaction and traffic | The gradation changes after laying; fines are generated |
| **Poor interlock** | They lie flat and slide over one another instead of keying |
| **Higher voids** | More binder or cement needed for the same result |
| **Reduced workability** in concrete | Higher water demand, hence lower strength |
| Weak planes | Lower crushing and impact resistance |

The most serious is the first: an aggregate that satisfies every strength test in the laboratory can still fail in the road if it **fractures during rolling**, because the compacted layer then has a quite different gradation from the one designed.

**The preferred shape** is **cubical and angular** — angular for interlock, cubical so it does not break. **Rounded** river gravel gives good workability but poor interlock; **flaky and elongated** particles are undesirable in every application.

The shape descriptors: rounded, irregular, **angular**, flaky, elongated, and flaky-and-elongated.

**Where shape enters the specification.** Flakiness and elongation limits appear alongside the strength and durability tests, and the four should be seen as a set testing different things:

| Test | Property |
|---|---|
| **Flakiness / elongation index** | **Shape** |
| Impact value | Resistance to **sudden shock** |
| Crushing value | Resistance to **gradual load** |
| Los Angeles abrasion | Resistance to **wear** |
| Soundness | Resistance to **weathering** |
| Water absorption | Porosity |

examTip.trap: **Flakiness** and **elongation** are easily swapped: flakiness concerns the **LEAST** dimension (thickness), elongation the **GREATEST** (length).
examTip.trick: **Flaky: least dimension < 0.6 × mean. Elongated: greatest dimension > 1.8 × mean.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Flaky = thin (0.6); elongated = long (1.8).** Both are undesirable because they **break easily under the roller and compact into a layered structure with high voids.** Combined index limits are typically 30–40% for pavement work.

questions.stem: A traffic sign with a red border and a triangular shape is a:
questions.solution:
**A cautionary (warning) sign.**

Traffic signs are classified by **shape and colour**, so that the *type* of message is recognised before the symbol itself is read — which matters at speed and in poor visibility.

| Class | Shape | Colour | Message |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cautionary (warning)** | **Equilateral triangle**, apex up | **Red border**, white background, black symbol | **Warns of a hazard ahead** — bend, gradient, school, narrow bridge |
| **Mandatory / regulatory** | **Circular** | Red border, or blue for positive instructions | **Must be obeyed** — speed limit, no entry, one way |
| **Informatory** | **Rectangular** | Blue or green background | **Guides** — direction, distance, facilities |

Two signs break their own shape rule deliberately, because they are the most critical and must be unmistakable even if partly obscured or seen from behind:

| Sign | Shape |
|---|---|
| **STOP** | **Octagon** |
| **GIVE WAY** | **Inverted triangle** |

**The distinction that carries legal weight.** A **mandatory** sign is enforceable — disobeying it is an offence. A **cautionary** sign carries no penalty for proceeding; it warns, and the driver must then exercise judgement. That is why the two use different shapes rather than merely different symbols.

**Where signs sit among traffic control devices**, all governed by IRC 67:

| Device | Function |
|---|---|
| **Signs** | Convey regulation, warning or information |
| **Road markings** | Channelise and delineate — centre line, edge line, stop line, zebra crossing |
| **Traffic signals** | Assign right of way in **time** at an intersection |
| **Islands and channelisation** | Assign it in **space** |

The requirements a sign must meet to work at all: it must **command attention**, convey a **clear and simple meaning**, allow **adequate time to respond** (hence placement well in advance of the hazard), and **command respect** — which is why signs that are ignored, such as a speed limit set unrealistically low, actively undermine the whole system.

**Retro-reflective sheeting** is required for night visibility, since a sign that cannot be read after dark is worse than none — it gives the appearance of a signed road without the substance.

examTip.trick: Traffic signs are classified by **shape and colour**: **circular** signs are **mandatory/regulatory**, **triangular** signs are **cautionary/warning**, and **rectangular** signs are **informatory**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Triangle warns, circle commands, rectangle informs.** The red border marks the first two as compulsory to obey. That shape coding is deliberate — it lets a driver classify a sign before reading it, and it works even when the legend is obscured.

questions.stem: A collision diagram in accident studies is used to show:
options: The total number of accidents per year on a network
The type and manner of collisions at a particular location
questions.solution:
**The type and manner of collisions at a particular location.**

A **collision diagram** is a schematic plan of one intersection or road section on which every recorded accident is drawn with **arrows** showing the direction and movement of each vehicle involved, together with symbols for the type of collision, the severity, and often the date, time and weather.

It is not a statistical summary but a **diagnostic** tool: because the accidents are drawn in their actual positions and movements, a **pattern** becomes visible that a table of numbers conceals.

**What patterns reveal, and the remedy each suggests:**

| Pattern on the diagram | Likely cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Many **right-turn** collisions | Conflicting turning movements | **Channelisation**, a dedicated turning phase |
| Many **rear-end** collisions | Sudden stopping; inadequate sight distance | Improve **SSD**, advance warning, signal timing |
| Many **right-angle** collisions | Right of way not clear | **STOP/GIVE WAY**, or signals |
| Accidents concentrated **at night** | Poor visibility | **Lighting**, retro-reflective signs and markings |
| Accidents concentrated **in the wet** | Loss of friction | **Skid resistance**, drainage, camber |
| **Pedestrian** collisions | No safe crossing provision | Zebra crossing, refuge, footpath |

That is the value of the tool: it converts an accident record into a **specific engineering intervention** rather than a general call for care.

**The companion tool** is the **condition diagram** — a scaled plan of the same location showing the physical features: road width, surface, obstructions, sight lines, signs, markings, drainage and abutting development. The two are read together, the collision diagram showing *what happens* and the condition diagram *why it might*.

**Why the other options describe different things:** total accident numbers (a) come from **accident statistics** and are normalised as accident **rates** per 100 million vehicle-kilometres for comparison; costs (c) belong to the **economic** appraisal of a safety improvement; and speed distribution (d) comes from a **spot speed study**, whose percentiles give the speed limit (85th), the geometric design speed (98th) and the minimum limit (15th).

The systematic approach these feed is the identification of **black spots** — locations with an accident frequency or rate significantly above the network average — followed by diagnosis, treatment, and **before-and-after** evaluation to confirm the treatment worked.

examTip.trap: **Collision diagram** and **condition diagram** are different tools and are easily confused.
examTip.trick: A **COLLISION diagram** is a schematic showing each accident by **type and direction of movement** using standard arrows — it reveals the **pattern**. A **CONDITION diagram** is a scale plan showing the **physical features** — sight obstructions, surface, markings, drainage.
examTip.mnemonic: **Collision diagram shows WHAT is happening; condition diagram shows WHY it might be.** Used together they diagnose a blackspot — the pattern points to a cause, and the physical layout confirms it.

questions.stem: In Westergaard's analysis of rigid pavements, warping stresses arise because of:
options: The wheel load applied at the slab edge
Friction between the slab and the subgrade
Shrinkage of the concrete during curing
A temperature difference between the top and bottom of the slab
questions.solution:
**A temperature difference between the top and bottom of the slab.**

A concrete pavement slab is exposed on top and insulated below, so a **temperature gradient** develops through its depth:

| Time | Gradient | Slab tries to |
|---|---|---|
| **Day** | Top **hotter** | **Curl downward** at the edges (convex up) |
| **Night** | Top **cooler** | **Curl upward** at the edges (concave up) |

The slab's own **self-weight** and the restraint of adjacent slabs prevent that curling, and the resulting restraint stresses are the **warping (temperature) stresses**. They are largest where the gradient is steepest — around midday and just before dawn.

**The three stress systems in a rigid pavement**, which must be distinguished:

| Stress | Cause | Relieved by |
|---|---|---|
| **Load stress** | Wheel load — analysed at the **interior, edge and corner** | Slab thickness |
| **Warping stress** | **Temperature gradient** through the depth | **Warping joints**, along the centreline |
| **Frictional stress** | Uniform temperature change resisted by **subgrade friction** | **Expansion and contraction joints** |

So option (b) describes the **frictional** stress — caused by a *uniform* temperature change, not a gradient — and it is relieved by a quite different joint. That is the distinction the question is testing.

**Which combination governs the design:**

> **Critical combination = load stress + warping stress**

evaluated at the edge and corner, since those are the weakest positions. Westergaard gave the load stress equations for the three positions, and **Bradbury's coefficients** give the warping stress from the gradient, slab dimensions and the **radius of relative stiffness**

> l = [Eh³/(12k(1 − μ²))]^{1/4}

where k is the **modulus of subgrade reaction** — the parameter on which rigid pavement design rests, in contrast to the **CBR** used for flexible pavements.

**The joints that manage all this:**

| Joint | Relieves | Spacing |
|---|---|---|
| **Expansion** | Expansion in hot weather | 50 – 140 m |
| **Contraction** | Shrinkage and contraction | ≈ 4.5 m (plain) |
| **Warping** | Curling stresses | Along the longitudinal centreline |

with **dowel bars** transferring load across joints while permitting movement, and **tie bars** holding longitudinal joints together.

Note that **shrinkage** (option c) is real but is a construction-stage effect handled by contraction joints and curing, not what Westergaard's warping analysis addresses.

examTip.trick: Westergaard analysed three stress systems in a rigid pavement slab: **wheel load** stresses (interior, edge and corner), **WARPING (temperature)** stresses from a top-to-bottom temperature difference, and **friction** stresses from restrained expansion.
examTip.mnemonic: **Warping stresses come from the TEMPERATURE GRADIENT through the slab, not the average temperature.** By day the top is hotter and the slab tries to curl **downward** at the edges; by night the reverse. The restraint of its own weight then induces stresses **comparable in size to the wheel load stresses** — which is why they cannot be neglected.

questions.stem: A prime coat in bituminous road construction is applied:
options: On a granular base, to plug voids and provide a bond for the layer above
To fill cracks in an existing pavement
questions.solution:
**On a granular base, to plug the surface voids and provide a bond for the bituminous layer above.**

A prime coat is a **low-viscosity** bituminous material — a cutback or emulsion — sprayed on a porous, non-bituminous surface. It penetrates a few millimetres, seals the voids, binds the loose surface fines, and gives the overlying bituminous layer something to adhere to.

The three coats are constantly confused, and the distinction is simply **what lies below**:

| Coat | Applied on | Purpose | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prime coat** | **Granular (non-bituminous)** base | **Penetrate and seal**; provide bond | 7 – 10 kg/10 m² |
| **Tack coat** | **Existing bituminous** or primed surface | **Bond** two bituminous layers | 2 – 3 kg/10 m² |
| **Seal coat** | **The finished surface** | **Waterproof** and provide texture | Varies with type |

So the prime coat goes **onto granular material**, the tack coat **between bituminous layers**, and the seal coat **on top of everything**. Options (b) and (c) name the tack and seal coats respectively, and (d) describes **crack sealing** with plastic bitumen — a maintenance operation, not a construction coat.

**Why a prime coat is needed at all.** A granular base is porous and dusty. Without priming:

- the bituminous layer above **does not bond** and can slip or delaminate;
- **water** enters the base through the voids;
- **dust** on the surface prevents adhesion entirely.

**Why a tack coat cannot substitute for it.** A tack coat is more viscous and is designed to remain **on** the surface as a sticky film, not to penetrate. On a porous granular base it would sit on top of the dust and fail to seal the voids — so each coat is formulated for its own job.

**Where they sit in the pavement**, to fix the sequence:

> subgrade → sub-base → base course → **PRIME COAT** → binder course → **TACK COAT** → wearing course → **SEAL COAT**

**Practical requirements:** the surface must be **clean, dry and swept** before priming; the primed surface is left to **cure** until it is tacky but not runny before the next layer is laid; and traffic is kept off in the meantime. Applying a bituminous layer onto an uncured or dusty prime coat is a common cause of early **delamination**.

examTip.trick: A **prime coat** is a low-viscosity binder applied to an **absorbent granular base** — it penetrates, plugs the surface voids and provides a bond for the bituminous layer above.
examTip.mnemonic: **PRIME on a granular base (penetrates); TACK on an existing bituminous or concrete surface (bonds, does not penetrate); SEAL coat on top of the finished surface (waterproofs and provides skid resistance).** Three coats, three different jobs — and applying the wrong one gives a layer that delaminates.

questions.stem: A drawing prepared to a scale of 1 : 50 means that:
options: The drawing is 50 times larger than the object
1 mm on the drawing represents 50 cm on the object
1 unit on the drawing represents 50 of the same units on the object
The object is drawn at full size
questions.solution:
**One unit on the drawing represents 50 of the same units on the object.**

A scale is a **ratio of like quantities**, so it is dimensionless — 1 mm on paper represents 50 mm on the object, 1 cm represents 50 cm, and so on. That is why option (b) is wrong: it mixes mm with cm and so states a scale of 1:500.

The scale is expressed as the **representative fraction**:

> **RF = drawing size / actual size**

| RF | Scale type | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **RF < 1** | **Reducing** | **Maps, buildings, site plans** — the object is bigger than the paper |
| RF = 1 | **Full size** | Ordinary machine drawings |
| **RF > 1** | **Enlarging** | Small components — a watch part, a bolt thread |

So 1:50 is a **reducing** scale, and option (a) reverses it — that would be 50:1.

**The recommended scales** follow a decimal-and-halving progression, which keeps them convenient to read off and consistent between drawings:

> Reducing: **1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 1:200, 1:500, 1:1000**
> Enlarging: 2:1, 5:1, 10:1

**Typical civil engineering uses:**

| Drawing | Scale |
|---|---|
| Site / location plan | 1:500 – 1:1000 |
| **Building plans, sections, elevations** | **1:50 – 1:100** |
| Detail drawings (joints, reinforcement) | 1:5 – 1:20 |
| **Topographic map** | 1:25 000 – 1:250 000 |
| Cadastral plan | 1:500 – 1:5000 |

Note the terminology trap: a **large-scale** map has a **large RF** and covers a **small area in great detail** (1:500), while a **small-scale** map covers a **large area with little detail** (1:1 000 000). The words describe the fraction, not the area.

**Why a graphical scale is drawn on the sheet.** Paper shrinks and drawings are photocopied and reduced, so the stated ratio may no longer hold. A **scale bar** drawn on the sheet scales with the reproduction and remains correct — which is why every map and site plan carries one.

And note the √2 logic running through the drawing standards as one system: **sheet sizes** (A0 to A4, each halved), **lettering heights** (2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm) and line thicknesses all step in the same ratio, so a drawing reduced from A1 to A2 keeps its proportions and remains legible.

examTip.trick: A scale of **1:50** is a **reducing** scale: **one unit on the drawing represents 50 of the same units on the object**.
examTip.mnemonic: **LARGE scale = a SMALL area shown in great detail (1:10, 1:50); SMALL scale = a LARGE area in little detail (1:1000).** The naming feels backwards until you remember it refers to the size of the **fraction**, not the area covered. And **always draw a graphical scale bar** — it survives photocopying and reduction, where a written ratio does not.

questions.stem: In a sectional view of an engineering drawing, the cut surface is indicated by:
options: Hatching with thin lines, usually at 45°
questions.solution:
**Hatching with thin continuous lines, usually at 45°.**

A **sectional view** shows the object as if cut through, so that internal features appear as **visible outlines** rather than hidden dashed lines. The surface actually cut by the plane is identified by **hatching** (section lining).

The conventions (IS 10714 and IS 11669):

| Convention | Rule |
|---|---|
| Hatching lines | **Thin continuous**, at **45°** to the principal outline |
| Adjacent parts | Hatched at **different angles or spacings**, so the parts are distinguishable |
| The same part in different views | Hatched **identically** throughout |
| Large areas | Hatching may be limited to a **band along the outline** |
| **Thin sections** (gaskets, sheet) | May be shown **solid black** |
| **Hidden lines** | **Omitted** in the sectioned portion — they are now visible |

Option (c) is therefore correct only for the special case of a very thin section, and option (d) is precisely what sectioning **removes**.

**The parts that are conventionally NOT sectioned**, even when the cutting plane passes through them — a point frequently examined:

> **Shafts, bolts, nuts, screws, rivets, keys, pins, ribs, webs, gear teeth and rolling elements**

Ribs and webs are excluded because hatching them would give a misleading impression of solidity where the part is in fact a thin plate.

**Where the cutting plane is shown.** On the adjacent view, by a **thin chain line thickened at its ends and at every change of direction**, with arrows giving the direction of viewing and capital letters identifying the section (A–A, B–B).

**The types of section:**

| Type | Cut |
|---|---|
| **Full section** | Right through the object |
| **Half section** | Half sectioned, half external — shows both at once |
| **Offset section** | Cutting plane stepped, to pass through several features |
| **Revolved / removed** | A local section rotated into place, or placed elsewhere |
| **Broken-out (partial)** | A small area only, bounded by a **break line** |

**Why sections matter in civil engineering** rather than only in machine drawing: a building or a structure is understood chiefly through its **sections** — a wall section showing the DPC, plinth and foundation, a beam section showing the reinforcement layout, a road cross-section showing camber, shoulders and drains. In each case the section is where the information a contractor actually needs is conveyed.

examTip.trick: **Hatching (section lining)** with thin continuous lines at **45°** marks the material actually **cut** by the section plane — not everything visible beyond it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hatch only what the knife touches.** Adjacent parts are hatched in **opposite directions or at different spacings** so they can be told apart. And by convention, **ribs, webs, shafts, bolts and fasteners are NOT hatched** even when the plane passes through them — hatching them would misrepresent the shape.

questions.stem: The sinking fund method of depreciation provides for replacement by:
options: Setting aside a uniform annual amount that accumulates with interest to the replacement cost
Writing off a fixed percentage of the reducing book value each year
Charging a constant amount each year with no interest
Charging depreciation in proportion to output
questions.solution:
**By setting aside a uniform annual amount which accumulates with interest to the required sum.**

The sinking fund method recognises that money set aside **earns interest**, so the annual deposit needed is less than a simple division of the amount to be recovered:

> **A = (C − S) × (A/F, i, n) = (C − S) × i / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]**

where C is the initial cost, S the salvage value, i the interest rate and n the useful life. The factor **i/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** is the **sinking fund factor**.

That interest term is what distinguishes it from **straight line** depreciation, which charges a constant (C − S)/n with no interest credit at all — option (c).

The methods compared:

| Method | Annual charge | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Straight line** | **(C − S)/n**, constant | Simplest; no interest |
| **Sinking fund** | **(C − S) × sinking fund factor**, constant | **Includes interest**; provides the replacement fund |
| **Declining balance** | Fixed **% of the reducing book value** | **Accelerated** — heavy early charge |
| Sum-of-years-digits | Decreasing | Accelerated |
| **Production units** | Per **unit of output** | Suits plant with variable use |

So option (b) is the **declining balance** method and (d) the **production units** method — both real, both different.

**A worked feel for the difference.** For C − S = Rs 100,000 over 10 years at 8%: straight line sets aside Rs 10,000 a year, while the sinking fund needs only

> 100,000 × 0.08/[(1.08)¹⁰ − 1] = 100,000 × 0.069 = **Rs 6,900**

The accumulated interest supplies the difference — which is precisely the point of the method.

**Why the choice matters beyond bookkeeping.** Depreciation feeds directly into **replacement analysis**: the decision whether to keep or replace a machine compares the **equivalent uniform annual cost** of retaining it — which *rises* as maintenance grows and remaining value falls — against the EUAC of a new one. The economic life is the year in which the two cross.

And note the valuation terms that accompany it, routinely confused: **book value** (cost less accumulated depreciation), **salvage value** (worth at end of life, sold **intact**), **scrap value** (worth of the **dismantled materials**) and **replacement value** (cost of an equivalent new asset at current rates). Salvage value can even be **negative** where disposal, demolition or site restoration costs money.

examTip.trick: The **sinking fund** method sets aside a **uniform annual amount** which, **accumulating at interest**, exactly equals the replacement cost at the end of the asset's life.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sinking fund: A = (F × i)/((1+i)ⁿ − 1).** Compare the others: **straight line** writes off an equal amount each year (simplest); **declining balance** writes off a fixed percentage, so it depreciates faster early on — which is closest to how plant actually loses value.

questions.stem: The minimum attractive rate of return (MARR) used in project appraisal represents:
options: The rate at which the NPV becomes zero
The average return earned on all past projects
The rate of inflation expected over the project life
The lowest rate of return the organisation is willing to accept on an investment
questions.solution:
**The lowest rate of return the organisation is willing to accept on an investment.**

The MARR is a **hurdle rate** set by the organisation, not computed from a project. It reflects:

| Component | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **Cost of capital** | What the organisation pays for funds — interest, or the weighted average cost of debt and equity |
| **Risk premium** | Higher for uncertain projects |
| **Opportunity cost** | The return available on the next-best alternative |
| Capital rationing | Raised when funds are scarce relative to opportunities |

**Its role is as the standard of comparison**, and it appears as the benchmark in every criterion:

> **IRR ≥ MARR** → accept
> **NPV computed at the MARR ≥ 0** → accept
> **Δ IRR ≥ MARR** for each increment in an incremental analysis → accept the larger alternative

Option (a) is the definition of the **IRR** — the rate at which NPV vanishes. The distinction is essential: the **IRR is an output** of the project's cash flow, while the **MARR is an input** set by the organisation. Confusing them is the commonest error in this topic.

| | **IRR** | **MARR** |
|---|---|---|
| Source | **Computed** from the project's cash flow | **Chosen** by the organisation |
| Varies with | The project | The organisation, and the risk class |
| Role | The result to be judged | The **standard** to judge it against |

**Why the MARR must exceed the cost of capital.** Investing at exactly the cost of capital creates no value and leaves no margin for the risk that the forecast is wrong. Typical practice sets the MARR several points above the borrowing rate.

**Two cautions on using it:**

1. Comparing **individual** IRRs against the MARR does **not** correctly rank mutually exclusive alternatives — a small project with a spectacular rate can leave most of the capital idle. The remedy is **incremental analysis**, testing each additional increment of investment against the MARR.
2. The MARR must be consistent with how the cash flows are expressed. A **nominal** (money) MARR goes with cash flows in current prices; a **real** MARR with constant-price flows, related by (1 + i_nominal) = (1 + i_real)(1 + f). Mixing the two — option (c)'s confusion — systematically distorts the appraisal.

For **public** projects the equivalent hurdle is the **social discount rate**, and the criterion is usually the **B/C ratio ≥ 1** or the **EIRR** against that rate, computed on shadow prices and including externalities.

examTip.trick: The **MARR** is the organisation's threshold — the return below which it would rather do something else with the money. It is set from the **cost of capital plus a risk premium**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Accept if IRR > MARR, or equivalently if NPV computed AT the MARR is positive.** The two criteria agree for a simple project. For **mutually exclusive** alternatives, however, **NPV is the safer criterion** — IRR can rank them wrongly, and incremental analysis is then needed.

questions.stem: Crashing a project schedule means:
options: Extending the project duration to reduce resource peaks
Deliberately shortening activity durations by adding resources, at extra cost
Recomputing the network after a delay
questions.solution:
**Deliberately shortening activity durations by adding resources, at extra cost.**

Crashing compresses the project by spending money — overtime, extra crews, additional plant, or a faster construction method. It is the practical expression of the **time–cost trade-off**.

**The two cost streams pull in opposite directions:**

| Cost | Behaviour as duration shortens |
|---|---|
| **Direct cost** (labour, plant, material) | **Rises** — crashing is inefficient |
| **Indirect cost** (overheads, supervision, site establishment, financing) | **Falls** — fewer days to pay for |
| **Total cost** | Falls, then rises — a **minimum** exists |

That minimum is the **optimum duration**, and finding it is the object of the exercise. Shortening beyond it costs more than it saves.

**The cost slope** is the key quantity:

> **Cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost) / (normal duration − crash duration)**

that is, the **extra cost per day saved**.

**The procedure:**

1. Identify the **critical path** — only critical activities can shorten the project.
2. Among them, crash the activity with the **lowest cost slope** first.
3. Recompute the network: **the critical path may change**, and a previously non-critical path may become critical.
4. Repeat until the target duration is reached, or until further crashing raises the total cost.

Step 3 is where the method is most often applied wrongly. Once a parallel path becomes critical too, **both** must be crashed simultaneously to gain another day — so the cost per day rises in steps.

**Why crashing a non-critical activity is wasted money.** It has float, so shortening it changes nothing about the project duration. That is why option (c) is wrong, and why the critical path must be identified before any money is committed.

**Distinguish crashing from the resource techniques**, which option (a) names:

| Technique | Constraint | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| **Crashing** | **Time** — shorten it | **Reduced**, at extra cost |
| **Resource levelling** | **Resources** fixed | May **extend** |
| **Resource smoothing** | **Duration** fixed | Unchanged; activities shifted within float |
| Fast tracking | — | Reduced by running activities **in parallel**, at extra **risk** rather than extra cost |

**Fast tracking** is the alternative worth knowing alongside it: overlapping activities that would normally be sequential buys time without direct extra cost, but increases the risk of rework if the earlier activity changes.

Crashing is also the standard response when a project has fallen behind and the **completion date is contractual** — weighed against the **liquidated damages** that lateness would incur.

examTip.trick: Crashing shortens the **critical path** by adding resources — overtime, extra crews, more plant — at extra cost. It is only worth doing on **critical** activities, since shortening a non-critical one changes nothing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Crash the CRITICAL path, cheapest activity first — and re-identify the critical path after every step, because it can SHIFT.** The optimum is where the rising direct cost meets the falling indirect cost. Compare **FAST-TRACKING**, which overlaps activities instead of resourcing them harder — no extra cost, but added risk of rework.

questions.stem: In PERT, the standard deviation of an activity duration is taken as:
questions.solution:
**σ = (t_p − t_o)/6.**

PERT models each activity duration as a **beta distribution** from three estimates, and assumes the range from optimistic to pessimistic spans approximately **six standard deviations**:

> **σ = (t_p − t_o)/6**,  and **variance σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²**

alongside the expected duration

> **t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6**

Note what σ depends on: **only the two extremes**. The most likely value t_m affects the expected time but **not** the standard deviation — which is why option (d) is wrong. And option (b) **adds** rather than subtracts, so it could not be a measure of spread at all.

**How the variance is used**, which is the whole reason PERT exists:

1. Compute t_e for every activity and find the **critical path** in the usual way.
2. Sum the **variances of the activities on that path** — variances add, standard deviations do not:

> **σ_project = √(Σσ²)**

3. Because the sum of many independent distributions tends to normal, the probability of finishing by any target date T follows from the standard normal deviate:

> **Z = (T − T_e)/σ_project**

That probability statement is what PERT delivers and CPM cannot. A manager can say *"we have an 85% chance of finishing by June"* rather than quoting a single bare date — which is a far more honest representation of a novel project.

**The comparison:**

| | **CPM** | **PERT** |
|---|---|---|
| Durations | **Deterministic**, one estimate | **Probabilistic**, three estimates |
| Orientation | **Activity**-oriented | **Event**-oriented |
| Suits | **Repetitive** work — construction | **Novel** work — research, development |
| Cost | Handles the **time–cost trade-off** (crashing) | Time only, in its original form |

**A known limitation worth stating.** PERT sums the variances of the **critical path only**. A **near-critical** path with high variance can easily overtake it, so the computed probability of on-time completion is **optimistic** — sometimes substantially. Monte Carlo simulation addresses this by sampling all paths, and is what modern software does.

In practice the two methods have largely merged: planning software computes network logic with deterministic durations, displays it as a bar chart, and offers probabilistic simulation as an option.

examTip.trick: PERT assumes a **beta distribution** whose range is spanned by the optimistic and pessimistic estimates, giving **σ = (t_p − t_o)/6** — because a normal distribution's range is about six standard deviations.
examTip.mnemonic: **Expected time (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6; standard deviation (t_p − t_o)/6; VARIANCE the square of that.** Project variance is the **sum of the variances of the CRITICAL activities only** — and the probability of meeting a target date follows from **Z = (T_target − T_expected)/σ_project**.

questions.stem: In an item-rate (unit-price) contract, the contractor is paid on the basis of:
options: A single lump sum for the whole work
Actual cost plus an agreed percentage
A percentage above or below the estimated cost
Quantities actually executed, measured at the tendered rates
questions.solution:
**Quantities actually executed, measured at the tendered rates.**

In an item-rate contract the employer supplies a **bill of quantities** with estimated quantities for each item, and the contractor quotes a **rate** against each. Payment is then the sum of (actual measured quantity × tendered rate), so the final value varies with the work actually done.

This is the **commonest form for civil engineering works**, because quantities in construction can rarely be fixed exactly in advance — excavation depths, foundation levels and ground conditions all vary from the drawings.

**The contract types compared:**

| Type | Payment basis | Risk of quantity variation | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Item rate (unit price)** | **Measured quantity × tendered rate** | **Employer** | **Most civil works**; quantities uncertain |
| **Lump sum** | One fixed price for the defined work | **Contractor** | Well-defined work, complete drawings |
| **Cost plus percentage** | Actual cost + agreed % | **Employer** entirely | Emergency work; scope unknown |
| Cost plus fixed fee | Actual cost + fixed fee | Employer, but fee capped | Better incentive than % |
| **Percentage rate** | A % above or below the employer's estimate | Employer | Where the estimate is reliable |
| Labour rate | Labour only; employer supplies material | Employer | Departmental work |

So option (a) is **lump sum**, (b) **cost plus percentage**, and (c) **percentage rate** — all genuine forms, which is what makes the question worth asking.

**Note the perverse incentive in cost-plus-percentage:** the contractor's fee **rises with the cost**, so there is no incentive to economise. It is used only where the scope genuinely cannot be defined — emergency or repair work — and a **fixed fee** version is preferred wherever possible.

**Why measurement conventions matter so much in an item-rate contract.** Since payment follows measurement, the rules must be unambiguous — which is the whole purpose of **IS 1200**: brickwork in m³ with no deduction for openings up to 0.1 m², plaster in m² with the limit at 0.5 m², steel by weight with laps included, excavation on authorised dimensions. Disputes on site far more often concern **how something was measured** than the rate applied to it.

**The related instruments** under Nepal's Public Procurement Act 2063: **bid security** (2–3%, guarantees the bid), **performance security** (5–10%, guarantees performance), **retention money** (withheld against defects), **mobilisation advance** (against a bank guarantee), and **variation orders** valued at the contract rates wherever the work is of the same character.

examTip.trick: In an **item-rate (unit-price)** contract the bidder quotes a **rate per unit** for each item, and payment is for the **quantities actually executed**, measured on site.
examTip.mnemonic: **Item rate: quantities vary, rates are fixed — suits work whose extent is uncertain (earthwork, foundations), and the EMPLOYER carries the quantity risk. LUMP SUM: one price for the whole, suits fully designed work, and the CONTRACTOR carries the risk.** Who carries which risk is the real distinction between contract types.

questions.stem: Liquidated damages in a construction contract are:
options: A pre-agreed sum deducted for each day or week of delay in completion
The contractor's claim for additional payment
A bonus paid for early completion
The retention money released at the end of the defect liability period
questions.solution:
**A pre-agreed sum deducted for each day or week of delay in completion.**

Liquidated damages (LD) are fixed **in the contract itself**, before any delay occurs, as a stated amount per unit of time — commonly a small percentage of the contract price per week, subject to an overall ceiling of about **10%**.

**Why they are pre-agreed rather than proved.** Establishing the employer's actual loss from a late completion would be difficult and contentious — lost revenue, extended supervision, consequential effects on other contracts. Fixing the figure in advance:

| Advantage | For whom |
|---|---|
| No need to **prove** actual loss | Employer |
| **Certainty** of the maximum exposure | Contractor |
| Avoids litigation over quantum | Both |

**The legal requirement that governs them.** LD must be a **genuine pre-estimate of the likely loss**, not a punishment. A sum set extravagantly above any conceivable loss is a **penalty**, and a penalty is generally unenforceable — the distinction between liquidated damages and a penalty is the central legal point of the topic.

**The contractor's defence: extension of time.** LD can only be levied for delay that is the **contractor's responsibility**. Where the delay is caused by the employer or by a neutral event, the contractor is entitled to an **extension of time (EOT)**, and LD cannot run for that period. The usual grounds:

| Ground for EOT | Example |
|---|---|
| **Employer's delay** | Late possession of site, late drawings or decisions |
| **Variations** | Additional work instructed |
| **Force majeure** | Earthquake, flood, strike, epidemic |
| Exceptionally adverse weather | Beyond what was foreseeable |
| Suspension ordered by the employer | — |

So a **variation order** matters twice over: it changes the price *and* may protect the contractor from LD by justifying an EOT. That is why variations must be issued **in writing and before the work is done**.

**Why the other options are different instruments:**

| Instrument | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Liquidated damages** | **Deduction for delay** |
| **Claim** | The contractor's **application** for extra time or money |
| **Bonus / incentive** | Payment for **early** completion — the mirror of LD, occasionally used |
| **Retention money** | Withheld from each bill against **defects**, released after the defect liability period |

Under Nepal's **Public Procurement Act 2063** and the PPMO documents, the LD rate and its ceiling are stated in the contract, and continued delay beyond the ceiling becomes a ground for **termination** rather than further deduction.

examTip.trick: Liquidated damages are a **pre-agreed** sum, fixed at the time of contract as a **genuine estimate of the employer's loss** from delay — not a penalty, and not proved after the event.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pre-agreed and compensatory, not punitive — a sum that is a PENALTY rather than a genuine estimate is unenforceable.** Typically 0.05–0.1% of the contract value per day, capped at about 10%. The contractor's defence is an **extension of time** for delays that were the employer's responsibility or beyond both parties' control.

questions.stem: An engineer asked to certify work that they know does not comply with the specification should:
options: Certify it, since the client has accepted the work
Certify it but record a private note of the discrepancy
Refuse to certify, report the non-compliance and require it to be remedied
Certify it if the non-compliance does not affect appearance
questions.solution:
**Refuse to certify, report the non-compliance, and require it to be remedied.**

Certification is a **professional representation** that the work conforms to the specification. Certifying work known to be non-compliant is a **false statement** — and one on which the employer, future owners and the public will rely.

The governing principle is the first canon of every engineering code of ethics:

> **Hold the safety, health and welfare of the public paramount.**

The engineer's duties to the client and to the employer are real, but they are **subordinate** to that. Where they conflict, the public interest prevails.

**Why the softer options fail:**

| Option | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Certify because the client accepted it (a) | The client **cannot waive** a standard that protects third parties and future occupants |
| Certify with a private note (b) | The certificate is what others rely on; a private record protects the engineer's conscience, not the public. It is arguably worse — it proves the engineer knew |
| Certify if appearance is unaffected (d) | Compliance is about **performance and safety**, not appearance. Cover, compaction and reinforcement are all invisible once complete |

That last point is worth dwelling on: the defects that matter most in construction — **inadequate cover, poor compaction, missing stirrups, wrong bar placement** — are precisely the ones that become invisible. Certification exists because they cannot be inspected later.

**The proper course of action:**

1. **Record** the non-compliance factually, with measurements and photographs.
2. **Notify** the contractor and the employer **in writing**.
3. **Withhold** the certificate and the associated payment for that work.
4. Require **rectification**, or a formally justified and documented **engineering assessment** if the departure can be accepted on technical grounds.
5. If overruled, **escalate** — and if the matter concerns safety, report it to the authority concerned.

Step 4 admits an important nuance: not every departure requires demolition. A non-compliance may be acceptable if a **competent engineering assessment** shows the work still meets its performance requirements — but that assessment must be explicit, documented and signed, not an informal accommodation.

**The consequences in Nepal.** The **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055** makes professional misconduct a disciplinary matter, and the Council may **suspend or cancel registration** — removing the right to practise. False certification also carries liability in contract and in tort, and criminal liability where a failure causes injury.

This is the same principle that governs a **conflict of interest**: the test is whether the decision would survive disclosure. If certifying would embarrass you were the facts later known, it must not be certified.

examTip.trick: The engineer's certificate is a professional statement that the work complies. Certifying non-compliant work is a **false statement**, whatever the commercial pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Refuse, report, require remedy — all three, in writing.** This follows directly from the first principle of every engineering code: **the safety, health and welfare of the PUBLIC is paramount**, ranking above duty to client or employer. An engineer who certifies under pressure has surrendered the thing that makes the certificate worth anything.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Nepal Engineering Council?
options: Registering engineers and maintaining the register
Fixing the fees and salaries payable to engineers in private practice
Recognising engineering qualifications and accrediting programmes
Taking disciplinary action for professional misconduct
questions.solution:
**Fixing the fees and salaries payable to engineers** is not a function of the Council.

The Council is a **regulator of competence and conduct**, not a wage-fixing body. Remuneration is a matter for the market, for employment contracts, and — for public works — for the government's own rate schedules. A professional **association** may publish recommended fee scales, but the Council does not set them.

**What the Council does do**, under the **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055 (1998)**:

| Function | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Registration** | Maintains the register; issues certificates in categories **A (General), B (Professional), C (Foreign)** |
| **Examination** | Conducts the **registration (license) examination** — the one this syllabus serves |
| **Recognition of qualifications** | Recognises degrees and **accredits** engineering programmes |
| **Regulation of conduct** | Enforces the code of ethics; investigates misconduct and may **suspend or cancel registration** |
| Scope of practice | Determines what work each category may undertake |

So options (a), (c) and (d) are all core statutory functions.

**The distinction that underlies the whole topic** — Council versus Association:

| | **Nepal Engineering Council (NEC)** | **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)** |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | **Statutory regulator**, created by the Act | **Voluntary** membership body |
| Joining | **Registration is mandatory** to practise | By choice |
| Powers | **Licensing**; examination; **suspend or cancel** registration | Advocacy, networking, professional development |
| Interest served | **The public** | **Its members** |

That last row is the essential point: a regulator exists to protect the **public**, an association to advance its **members' interests**. Fee-fixing belongs to the second kind of body, not the first — which is exactly why it is the odd one out here.

The two are nonetheless linked: the **NEA President and five NEA-elected engineers** sit on the Council, alongside seven government nominees, two Council nominees, a Campus Chief, a representative of the Institute of Engineering, and the **Registrar as Member-Secretary**.

**The practical consequence to carry.** Registration is a **legal prerequisite to practising engineering in Nepal** — for Nepali and foreign nationals alike. Signing, designing or certifying engineering work without it is an offence, not merely an irregularity. And the price of that licensed status is accountability: the same Council that grants the right to practise can remove it.

examTip.trap: Read the question — it asks which is **NOT** a function of the Council.
examTip.trick: A regulator's functions are **registration, setting standards of education and practice, maintaining a register, and disciplinary action**. Setting **fees and salaries** is a commercial matter for the market or a professional association, not a statutory regulator.
examTip.mnemonic: **The Council REGULATES; the Association REPRESENTS.** Registration with the NEC is a **legal requirement to practise**; membership of the Nepal Engineers' Association is voluntary. Keeping those two roles apart answers most institutional questions on the paper.
